title: dramatic monologue|the ocean during a storm
text:
The Ocean's Lament

I was the cradle, the glass-green calm,
the whisper lulling the shore to sleep.
You walked my edges with open palms
and never asked what the deep dark keeps.

Now hear me roar what I held in stone—
the weight of a thousand sunken ships,
the sailors' bones I have made my own,
the prayers still frozen on drowned men's lips.

You built your towns on my patient back
and dared to name me "gentle" and "kind."
I am the hunger, the endless black,
the oldest rage that your kind will find.

The wind is my herald, the lightning's mine,
the thunder answers my beckoning cry.
I take the harbor, I take the shrine,
I drag the boats down and watch them die.

Do not mistake me for what I show
when the sun is high and the gulls are loud.
I am the terror beneath the glow,
the flood that swallows the tall and proud.

Kneel on your cliffs and watch me climb—
I am the storm, and I am the sea.
I have been waiting since the birth of time
to show you how small your kingdoms be.

title: poem in tercets|a factory town after the plant closed
text:
The last shift’s overtime is a fossil
in the payroll ledger. Rain varnishes
the dead smokestack’s brick throat.

At the Kwik Mart, a clerk rotates
the hot dog rollers. Their small, even heat
is the only industry left on this block.

The chain-link by the old lot has grown
a beard of milkweed. A shopping cart
sleeps on its side like a downed satellite.

Someone has stenciled a door
on the cinderblock wall of the plant.
It is always closed. It is always being painted.

The river, that slow brown conveyor,
carries the town’s reflection past the town.
It does not clock in. It does not clock out.

In the bar, the jukebox is a reliquary
of sad guitars. A man feeds it quarters
like he’s paying a toll to somewhere else.

The whistle is a ghost that only dogs
and the very old can hear. It sounds
like a fork lifted from a plate, and set down.

title: sequence of haiku|autumn leaves in a cemetery
text:
Autumn Leaves in a Cemetery

Red maple drifts down—
a name half-hidden in moss
under the cold stone

Wind through iron gates
lifts a scarf of fallen leaves
over sleeping rows

One oak leaf settles
on a grave without flowers—
brief, quiet tribute

Bare branches above
count the stones the leaves have touched
then let go again

title: Petrarchan sonnet|the sound of a train at night
text:
The radiator ticks. I can’t sleep. Again
I’m at the window, third floor, no screen, just glass
still smudged from where my palm pressed, weeks ago. The grass
isn’t mine—it’s the lot’s. Then the far-off grain
of a horn, two notes, flat, like a man in pain
who’s stopped trying. My father sold insurance. Pass.
Don’t think about it. The tracks run behind the VFW, brass
shells in a bucket by the door, a flag in rain.
The diesel comes through the cut like a cough
that won’t clear. My coffee’s cold. The cat
won’t look at me. I count the cars—twelve, a flat
car, twelve—and the window hums, and the sound comes off
the overpass and thins to a wire, a wire, a wire,
and the house settles its weight, and nothing’s on fire.

title: ballad in quatrains|a jazz club in the rain
text:
The neon bleeds across the wet black street,
A saxophone begins its slow complaint;
The rain keeps time with every aching beat,
And paints the windows with a weeping saint.

The bassman’s fingers walk the wooden floor,
A cigarette burns low between his lips;
The drummer dreams of someone at the door,
While thunder rolls like drums in fingertips.

Blue smoke has settled on the empty chairs,
The piano player’s hands are lost in keys;
A woman laughs, then folds into her prayers,
And all the world dissolves by slow degrees.

The rain will wash the morning clean again,
The neon will forget what it has seen;
But something in the music will remain—
A blue and burning room, a rain-washed scene.

title: spoken-word poem|a garden after the gardener has died
text:
I. What the Shears Remember

The shears still hang on the hook by the door,
jaws half-open like they're waiting for one more
conversation with the hedge.
Nobody told the roses.
Nobody told the roses, so they keep
climbing the trellis like a question
no one's left to answer,
throwing blooms at the sky
like they're flagging down a ride
back to last spring.

The mint has gone feral.
It's taking the path apart, stone by stone,
the way grief takes a schedule apart,
hour by hour, until the whole day
is just one long weed
you can't bring yourself to pull.

II. The Watering Can

The watering can sits tipped on its side,
dry as a sermon nobody stayed to hear.
The soil has learned to drink from the sky now —
learned the way children learn
to tie their shoes without you watching,
clumsy and certain at once.

The tomatoes are volunteering.
Nobody planted them there.
They rise through the cracked bed
like they heard the old man's voice
in the dirt and decided
to answer it in fruit.

And the gate — the gate still swings
the way he oiled it to,
soft complaint, soft return,
as if it hasn't heard the news.

III. What Grows Anyway

Here is the thing about a garden:
it doesn't know it's an elegy.
It only knows the light,
the long green argument with gravity,
the stubborn yes of seed to soil.

So the beans keep threading upward,
so the bees keep their appointments,
so the blackberries take the fence
like a slow applause
that won't stop,
that won't stop,
that won't —

The gloves are still in the shed.
The gloves are still in the shed,
curled like two hands
that finished their work
and forgot to let go.

And the garden,
the garden keeps growing
like it's trying to finish
what he started,
one green sentence at a time,
out loud,
to no one,
to everyone,
to the sun.

title: poem in tercets|moving out of a childhood home
text:
The tapedeck in the closet, its ribbon
unspooled like a field of black wheat.
We leave the door ajar for the dust.

The height chart on the doorframe
is a fossil of a smaller animal.
My palm fits the highest mark now.

In the kitchen, the linoleum
peels back from the corner,
a gray tongue tasting the subfloor.

The light switch in the hall
has a groove worn by thumbs.
We are all just passing through this plaster.

A wasp, dormant in the window frame,
wakes to the sound of boxes.
Outside, the moving truck idles, a blue lung.

title: free verse poem|a forest fire seen from far away
text:
Smoke on the Horizon

From the ridge road we stop the car
and watch the mountain burn.
A column of smoke stands over the pines
like a gray tree growing in reverse,
its roots unraveling into the sky.

The fire is small from here—
a flicker, a stubborn ember
someone forgot to put out.
We could cover it with a thumb.
We could turn away and it would still be there,
eating the hillside one green room at a time.

All afternoon the wind carries the smell of it,
faint as a memory of someone else's house.
Birds cross the valley in silence,
their small bodies pointed
toward wherever safety is.

By evening the smoke has leaned
into a long stain on the sunset,
and we drive home under a sky
the color of a wound
that doesn't hurt yet.

title: Shakespearean sonnet|commuting on a crowded subway
text:
The doors gasp shut. A man in surgical scrubs
is pressed against me, breathing through his mask.
My phone says 8:47. The lights all throb
a fluorescent headache. Someone's podcast blares
a chef describing butter. I don't ask
to move; my elbow's wedged in someone's bag,
a woman's braid is in my face, I drag
my coat sleeve free and grip the silver bar
that's slick with everyone. At Lorimer
the platform smells like rain and bleach, and half
the car gets off, then on again, a draft
of cold air hits my neck. I think of her—
the text I didn't answer, still unread,
the eggs I left out, hardening in the pan.

title: spoken-word poem|migrating geese over a frozen lake
text:
The lake is a closed eye.
A white scar of ice
stitched shut by the wind.

Then—the sound.
Not a song. A creaking,
a hundred hinges of hollow bone,
a torn silk rip across the sky’s gray throat.

They come.
A wavering line, a black stitch
pulled through the pale flesh of morning.
Each wingbeat a slow, deliberate pulse
against the cold that wants to keep them.

I stand at the shore,
a small heat in a vast indifference.
My breath is a ghost that leaves me
and does not look back.

Above the frozen eye,
they circle once. Twice.
A question asked in a language
of hunger and memory.
Is this the place? No.
This is only the map’s cold center.
The place is further. Always further.

They do not land.
They do not rest.
They are a promise the world makes to itself
and keeps moving to keep.

One call—sharp, thin,
a needle of sound
that threads the silence
and pulls it tight.

Then they are gone.
A fading script,
a last black letter
erased by the snow’s slow breath.

The lake stays.
A closed eye.
A white scar.
And in my chest,
the wingbeat remains—
a stubborn, migrating thing
that knows the way
but cannot say it.

title: spoken-word poem|commuting on a crowded subway
text:
I. Platform 6:42 AM

The yellow line sighs and the doors slide open
like a mouth that's been holding its breath all night.
We pour in, a liquid congregation,
shoulder to shoulder, elbow to rib,
strangers becoming a single organism
that breathes in unison when the car lurches.
Someone's coffee is a small religion,
someone's headphones leak a tinny chorus,
and I am pressed against a coat that smells like rain
and a man who's memorized the ceiling tiles
the way monks memorize a prayer.
We are not going anywhere.
We are being carried.

II. The Squeeze

This is the arithmetic of rush hour:
one more body always fits,
one more inch always exists
between the briefcase and the backpack,
between the mother and the man
who gives up his seat without a word,
a small kingdom surrendered.
The train rocks and we rock with it,
a field of wheat in a wind tunnel,
and for a moment I forget which arm is mine,
which hand grips the pole,
which breath is yours and which is the city's.
The announcement crackles, garbled, holy,
promising the next stop like a psalm.

III. Doors Open

Then the light—fluorescent, unremarkable, perfect—
and the organism exhales.
We spill out like coins from a pocket,
scattered, singular again,
each of us suddenly alone with our own heartbeat.
The platform swallows us and gives us back our names.
Somewhere behind me the doors close
on a car already filling with new strangers,
already becoming something else,
already forgetting
that for eleven stops
we were one body,
one pulse,
one long held breath
waiting to be let go.

title: blank verse meditation|a lost glove on a fence post
text:
The Lost Glove

A single glove upon a fence post rests,
its fingers open to the gray March air.
The wool is dark, the color of wet bark,
and stiffened now by frost that will not leave.
It waits as though a hand might still return,
as though the arm that wore it were not gone
down some long road the winter has erased.

I think of how it warmed a stranger's blood
against a morning colder than this one,
and how the small heat faded from its weave
until it held the weather like a cup.
The fence runs on beneath a heavier sky,
and I walk past, and leave it to the wind,
which worries at the thumb but cannot take
the shape of what it was, nor let it go.

title: ode|the first heartbreak
text:
Ode to the First Heartbreak

O first heartbreak, stern teacher of the young,
who came unasked when all the world was song,
and taught the tongue that only joy had spoken
the slower cadence of a chord once broken.

You were not loud. You were a quiet weather,
a gray that gathered in the smallest tether—
a text unread, a hallway turned away,
a name that lost its music in a day.

I thought the world had ended at your door,
that all the April I had known before
was spent, and I a beggar in the snow
of my own room, with nowhere else to go.

But you, harsh sculptor, chiseled at the stone
of what I was, and left me not alone—
you left me truer, tenderer, and wise
to hear the ache beneath another's eyes.

You broke the glass that held my single sky
and made me see how many heavens lie
in other hands, in other hearts' refrain—
and taught me how to hold, and lose, and love again.

So praise to you, first sorrow, sharp and kind,
who opened doors I could not see, though blind—
who made of me a vessel that could hold
both love and loss, and still not turn to cold.

title: poem in tercets|hope after a long illness
text:
The prednisone moon has finally waned.
Last night I slept six hours without the cough,
and dreamed of nothing—just a field, unplowed.

My wife has stopped
reading my face like a weather map.
She hums again. Off-key. The good way.

There's a robin who's been building something reckless
in the gutter of the garage—
twigs and a receipt, some kind of plastic string.

I watched him for an hour.
The string kept slipping. He kept picking it back up.
I don't know what I think about that.

The pills go in the cabinet now, not on the counter.
A small demotion. The pharmacist
says I look different, and I say it's the haircut.

At night the house settles with its old complaints,
and I let it. I let the radiator knock.
I let the screen door not quite latch.

title: pantoum|an abandoned railway station
text:
The signal's dark. The rails have gone to rust.
A schedule flutters, papery and tanned.
The platform edges gather dust on dust.
A name half-inked dissolves beneath the hand.

A schedule flutters, papery and tanned
where pigeons stitch their shadows into wire.
A name half-inked dissolves beneath the hand.
The benches hold the shape of no desire.

Where pigeons stitch their shadows into wire,
the clock has stopped its mineral display.
The benches hold the shape of no desire.
The turnstile lets the ivy have its way.

The clock has stopped its mineral display.
A suitcase sleeps unclaimed beneath the stair.
The turnstile lets the ivy have its way.
The wind reads notices to empty air.

A suitcase sleeps unclaimed beneath the stair.
The platform edges gather dust on dust.
The wind reads notices to empty air.
The signal's dark. The rails have gone to rust.

title: short lyric poem|an abandoned railway station
text:
I. Rusted Rails

The rails go nowhere, silver-brown,
threading the meadow's overgrown gown.
A semaphore, rust-locked, points to sky,
watching the empty clouds drift by.

II. The Waiting Room

The bench still holds a ghost of weight,
the timetable's last, forgotten date.
Through broken glass the ivy climbs,
keeping its own, more patient, times.

III. Departure

No whistle splits the quiet air,
no lantern swings, no one to care.
Only the wind, through grasses deep,
sings the trains to their endless sleep.

title: Shakespearean sonnet|teenage summer jobs
text:
The Summer Wage

When school is done and summer days are long,
The youth go forth to seek a humble wage,
To learn the world where labour makes its song
And write their names upon an early page.
The fry-cook stands amid the greasy heat,
The lifeguard watches o'er the chlorined pool,
The stockboy stacks the shelves with weary feet,
The camp counselor plays the cheerful fool.
Yet in these hours of toil a truth is found—
That money earned is sweeter than the rest,
That honest work doth make the spirit sound,
And put new sinew in a youthful breast.
   So let the summer pass in earnest trade,
   For thus are future men and women made.

title: free verse poem|a father teaching his daughter to drive
text:
The light is the color of a nickle
left in a parking lot all summer.
She adjusts the mirror, a small ceremony
of angles. The car is a borrowed Honda,
its dashboard a constellation of lint and warnings.

I tell her to feather the brake, a word
that hangs between us like a moth.
She does, and the car creeps forward
as if testing the thickness of the earth.
The cul-de-sac’s asphalt is a river
of dried tar, a black, slow-moving thing.

Her hands are at ten and two, but her knuckles
are white as the keys on a new piano.
I see her mother in the set of her jaw,
a stubbornness that has nothing to do with me.
We practice the three-point turn. The steering wheel
is a cold, hard coin she turns over and over
in her palms, looking for the side with the face.

The radio is off. The only music is the turn signal,
a steady, ticking insect. She checks her blind spot
like a swimmer taking a last breath before going under.
I want to tell her about the deer that will leap
from a ditch of Queen Anne’s lace, the patch of ice
that will make the world a spinning plate.
Instead, I say, *Good,* and the word feels
like a stone I’ve dropped down a well,
waiting for the sound of it hitting bottom.

title: Petrarchan sonnet|the ocean during a storm
text:
The radar’s green sweep found the anvil’s bruise
before the first gust hit the harbor wall.
We double-lashed the dory, let the squall
complain through stays. My father’s rubber shoes
still by the door, the coffee going cold—
I watched the swells build past the breakwater’s reach,
each crest a fist of white that seemed to teach
the pilings something older than the cold.
By three the windows shook. The barometer
fell past the mark he’d penciled years ago.
I thought of diesel, bilge, the radio
half-drowned in static, and the way the shore
just disappears—no lesson, nothing more
than water climbing where the stairs should go.

title: villanelle|moving out of a childhood home
text:
The keys lie cold within my palm.  
The rooms repeat their hollow sound.  
I carry out the final calm.  

The kitchen window keeps its charm—  
a square of light where dust motes drowned.  
The keys lie cold within my palm.  

The hallway holds a faded psalm  
of footsteps washed in evening brown.  
I carry out the final calm.  

The garden leans, a tired arm  
against the fence we never found.  
The keys lie cold within my palm.  

The attic breathes its cedar balm;  
the boxes breathe without a sound.  
I carry out the final calm.  

The door forgets its old alarm.  
The street is strange. The moon is round.  
The keys lie cold within my palm.  
I carry out the final calm.

title: ode|a wedding seen from the kitchen staff's view
text:
I. The Morning Prep

Before the guests arrive in silk and lace,
we chop and stir in this familiar place.
The stockpot simmers, sending up its steam,
while wedding bells are still a distant dream.
We polish glasses, line them in a row,
and watch the morning's pale and tentative glow.
The caterer is calling out the plan—
a choreography of pot and pan.

II. The Toast

The clinking starts; we hear it through the door,
a tide of laughter rising from the floor.
The best man's voice, the father's shaky pride,
the happy tears the bride cannot quite hide.
We pause, a colander of beans in hand,
and listen to a world we understand—
then back to work, the sauces needing whisking,
our own small toast unspoken, but unmissing.

III. The Last Plate

The chairs scrape back, the music starts to swell,
and out beyond us, stories start to tell.
We scrape the plates and stack them in the rack,
the cake's last crumbs, the lipstick on a glass.
The dishwasher begins its steady hum;
we wipe the counters, tired but overcome.
The kitchen light is harsh, the night is late—
we fed their joy, and cleared the final plate.

title: blank verse meditation|the ocean during a storm
text:
The Gale at Sea

The wind begins as whisper on the swell,
A rumor running gray across the deep.
The water, blind and breathing, heaves and climbs,
And what was glass becomes a broken field.

The clouds descend like judgment on the sea,
Unrolling shadow over miles of foam.
The lightning threads its white and crooked seam,
And thunder walks the caverns of the dark.

The waves rise up like walls without a door,
Then fall and drag the world down into troughs
Where sunlight never found a resting place.
The ocean has no memory of calm.

It shakes the poles of heaven with its voice,
It grinds the ancient stone to salt and sand,
And in the hollow spaces of the roar
The small heart learns the measure of its fear.

Yet in the violence there is a song,
A terrible and old and patient hymn,
As though the deep remembers what it was
Before the shores were drawn, before the light.

And when the storm has emptied out its lungs,
And spent its fury on the patient tide,
The sea will breathe again, and smooth its face,
And hold the wreckage gently as a grave.

title: sequence of haiku|the stars seen from a desert
text:
Cold sand keeps no score.
A satellite crosses out
a name I made up.

Coyote yelps — one
star goes wobbly in its glass.
The rest hold their breath.

Gas station sign dead.
Above it, the Dipper pours
nothing into nothing.

My breath fogs the lens.
A billion years of light waits
for me to wipe it.

Two stars, close enough
to seem one — like my parents
arguing softly.

The Milky Way: spilled
salt on a diner counter
nobody wipes up.

A meteor. Then
the silence after, thicker
than the desert is.

Dawn coming. The stars
don't fade — they're just outshouted
by a gas pump's glow.

title: pantoum|grief after a dog dies
text:
The Empty Leash

The leash still hangs beside the door,
its leather stiff, unused, and worn.
I listen for your claws on the floor,
and count the hours since you were gone.

Its leather stiff, unused, and worn,
the collar keeps a ghost of fur.
I count the hours since you were gone;
the silence holds no wag, no stir.

The collar keeps a ghost of fur—
a warmth my hands still half-believe.
The silence holds no wag, no stir;
the rooms forget how to receive.

A warmth my hands still half-believe,
the bowl still full beside the stair.
The rooms forget how to receive
the weight of you no longer there.

The bowl still full beside the stair,
I listen for your claws on the floor.
The weight of you no longer there—
the leash still hangs beside the door.

title: dramatic monologue|the stars seen from a desert
text:
The Stars, Seen from a Desert

Tonight the desert is a bowl of ink
held up to nothing, and the nothing spills.
I lie on my back in the cooling sand
and let the sky do what it will.

At first there is no sky. There is a hush
so wide it has a texture, like a cloth
drawn over the last blue. Then the first—
one star, so faint I think it is my pulse
arriving at the surface of my eye.

Then another. And the dark begins
to leak. Not light—the opposite of light,
a perforation, pinpricks in the black
that let the older darkness through. I see
the way a woman sees a thread of silver
in a coal seam, and pulls, and finds the seam
is everything, the mountain was a lie,
the world is made of thread.

I do not move.
I am afraid that if I shift my weight
the sky will slide off sideways like a plate
and shatter on the dunes. So I lie still
and let the numbers come: a thousand, then
ten thousand, then a number with no name,
a swarm, a blizzard, a white fever breaking
across the dark. The Milky Way unstitches
its long scar. I feel it on my face
like breath. Like someone leaning over me
who has been leaning here since I was born
and will lean here when I am sand myself.

This is the thing they never tell you: stars
are not above us. They are what we fell from,
and looking up is looking back, and back
is very far, and far is where the light
was young and did not know it would arrive
at such a late hour, at a woman
lying in a desert, crying, not from grief—

from the sheer arithmetic of it,
the way the sky keeps counting, counting, counting
and never once arrives at me, and yet
arrives. The sand is warm. The stars are cold.
I raise one hand and blot out Betelgeuse.
I am that large. I am that small. The dark
goes on being dark, and I go on
being the only thing out here that knows
it is alone, and calls that knowledge praise.

title: dramatic monologue|a father teaching his daughter to drive
text:
I. The Handbrake

This parking lot is Sunday-empty, good.
Now—mirrors first. No, not like that. You want
the horizon split across the glass, the road
behind you small enough to hold. Don't grip
the wheel like it owes you money. Loosen. There.
The car will tell you things if you let it.
Feel that? That shiver's just the engine
breathing. Now the clutch—easy, easy—find
the point where it starts to lean against you
like a dog that wants to run. That's the spot.
Hold it there. My hand's not on the brake.
My hand is nowhere. This is all your foot now,
and your foot is smarter than you think.

II. The Roundabout

Left lane, signal, and for God's sake *look*—
the mirror, then the blind spot, then the world.
You can't just take the gap because you want it;
you take it when it's given. See that truck?
He's got the right of way and he knows it, so
you wait. Waiting's half of driving. There—
now go, and don't apologize with the gas.
Commit. The roundabout rewards the sure
and punishes the hesitant. Second exit.
Signal. Signal. You signaled *after* turning—
the signal is a promise, not a eulogy.
I'm not gripping the door handle. I'm just
resting my hand here. That's a different thing.

III. The Hill

Stop. Right here, where the road tips up and all
you see is sky and hood. This is the hard part.
The fear's not wrong—the hill is real—but fear
is not instruction. Here's what you do:
clutch in, first gear, a little gas, and find
that leaning-place again, the one you know.
Now the brake comes off like you're setting down
a sleeping thing. Don't roll back. Don't roll back.
*There.* You feel how the car just—holds? That's you.
That's not the car. The car is only metal.
Now go, and when we crest this hill, don't stop
looking where you're going. I'll be here.
I've been here the whole time. I'm not letting go—
I'm just not holding on. There's a difference.
Now drive.

title: Petrarchan sonnet|a beekeeper in winter
text:
The Keeper's Frost

The hives stand silent in the frozen air,
like little monasteries deep in prayer;
the keeper walks among them, slow and grey,
and brushes frost from off the roof away.
He listens for the hum that is not there,
and thinks of summer, thick with golden care,
when all his drowsy kingdoms swam in day
and every field was his to sweep and weigh.

Now in the dark the clustered thousands keep
a slow and shivering warmth, a wing-bound fire,
and dream of clover under drifted sleep.
He leaves them honey, trusts the frugal choir,
and trudging home through snowdrifts, ankle-deep,
he keeps their small, fierce ember from the pyre.

title: spoken-word poem|an abandoned railway station
text:
The ticket booth's glass is a cataract.
Someone scratched a whole cosmology
into the paint with a key: *JESUS
WAS A LIAR,* and beneath it, smaller,
*so was I.* The bench has grown a spine
of splinters. I sit anyway.

The schedule's a fossil.
The 4:15 to Anywhere
is now a dialect of rust.
I think the tracks are a sentence
the ground forgot how to finish.

Here is the thing about silence:
it isn't empty. It's a room
where the furniture's been pushed
to the walls. A wasp works
the hollow of a light fixture,
building a paper city for no one.

A timetable's ghost is a hymn
in a language of leaving.
The turnstile's a broken metronome.
The semaphore's arm, stuck at *go,*
points at a horizon that's just
a rumor of hills.

I put my ear to the rail.
Not a rumble. Not a ghost train.
Just the cold iron thinking
its long, slow thought
about the weight it used to bear,
and the weeds coming up
through the ties like a slow,
green applause for the end of the show.

title: short lyric poem|a small-town Friday football game
text:
Friday Night Lights

The bleachers hum with hometown pride,
the field aglow beneath the night.
The whistle blows—the crowd alive,
as helmets catch the fading light.

A quarterback with muddy hands,
a cheer that rises with the moon.
The whole town leans against the stands,
and Friday sings its only tune.

title: blank verse meditation|grief after a dog dies
text:
The leash still hangs on the hook by the door—
blue nylon, chewed near the clasp.
I keep meaning to move it.
Some mornings I reach for it before I'm awake.

You were not a good dog, exactly.
You stole bread off the counter, you barked
at the mailman for eleven years straight,
you shed a second dog's worth of hair
into every corner of this house.

But you knew the sound of my car
three blocks away. You knew
when I was sad before I did,
and you'd press your heavy head
into my lap like a verdict.

The vet's office sent a card. I read it
standing in the kitchen, then put it
in the drawer with the takeout menus.
The last thing you ate was a hamburger.
You threw it up on the way home.
I laughed, then. That's the part
I can't explain to anyone—
how the worst night ends up
being the one you'd keep.

The house is very quiet now.
I've started talking to the radiator.
It ticks. I take that as an answer.

title: ballad in quatrains|a mother's hands
text:
I. Young Hands

Her hands were quick with ribbon, thread, and dough,
They braided hair and mended torn-up knees;
They knew each corner of the house, although
They never rested long in any ease.

II. Working Hands

Her hands grew cracked with dishes, soap, and cold,
They held the weight of groceries and years;
They rocked a fevered child and kept their hold
On courage through the night of borrowed fears.

III. Resting Hands

Her hands lie folded now, their labor done,
Soft as the sheets, and pale as winter light;
They gave their strength like coins to everyone—
And still they hold the dark and hold it tight.

title: blank verse meditation|a garden after the gardener has died
text:
The Gardener's Leave

The shears hang quiet on their iron hook,
And rust begins its slow, forgiving work
Upon the blade. The beds go unconfused
By any hand; the rose has spilled its red
Across the path and no one prunes it back.
The weeds ascend in green and ignorant rows,
Usurping ground they never would have dared
While he was here to pull them into light.

He knew the language of the soil—how
To read the thirst in drooping leaves, to hear
The aphid's faint and ruinous whisper. Now
The sprinkler ticks its dry, abandoned round,
And water pools in places he would chide.
The trellis lets the vine go where it will,
And nothing ties the wandering stem to form.

Yet in the compost heap the work goes on
Unsupervised—the peel and stem and leaf
Surrendering their shapes to something dark
And warm and patient. Underneath the moss
The seeds he never planted wait their turn,
And in the quiet rows the earth still turns
Its slow, unbothered alchemy of green.

The gate swings open to no one. The light
Falls equally on order and on ruin,
And both are beautiful, and both are his,
Though he has gone to ground himself, and grows
In some less tended garden, softly, on.

title: spoken-word poem|learning a second language as an adult
text:
The first word is a stone in my mouth.
I hold it there, a smooth, gray river rock
that tastes of nothing but its own weight.
*Buenos días*, I say to the cat,
who blinks and walks away, unimpressed
by my new currency.

The tongue is a muscle that forgets.
It wants the old roads, the familiar ruts
of *Wednesday* and *through*.
It trips on the rolled *r*, a pebble
sending it sprawling. It balks at the subjunctive,
that trapdoor in a sentence, that maybe-maybe-not
that opens under your feet.

I am a detective in a city of whispers.
I follow the breadcrumb trail of a preposition.
I learn that a table is feminine, but a problem is masculine,
and I think, *of course it is*.
I collect words like keys I find on the sidewalk,
none of them fit my own front door,
but I keep them anyway, a jangling pocketful
of maybe.

My mouth is a construction site.
New sounds are scaffolding, awkward and loud.
I am building a small, strange house
next to the one I've always lived in.
Some nights I stand on the porch of this new place
and listen to the rain on a different roof.
I don't know if it's home yet.
But I have learned the word for *window*,
and I know how to point at the moon.

title: ballad in quatrains|the first heartbreak
text:
The First Heartbreak

I met her by the willow tree,
When April skies were gray;
She promised she would wait for me
Until the close of day.

I carved our names upon the bark
With young and careless hand;
We walked together in the dark
Across the moonlit land.

She left a ribbon in my care,
A token soft and blue;
I wore it though the winds were bare,
And swore her heart was true.

But seasons turn and rivers run,
And promises grow cold;
I found her walking with someone
Beneath the autumn gold.

I passed her on the village street
And could not meet her eye;
My heart had learned its first defeat
And never told her why.

The willow by the water stands,
Its branches bowed and low;
I hold no ribbon in my hands,
But still the cold winds blow.

title: blank verse meditation|a jazz club in the rain
text:
The rain came down on Hector Street tonight
and the awning leaked above the door of Rudy's,
that same brown stain spreading like a bad decision.
Inside, the room was half a room.
Two couples at the bar, a man asleep
or doing a good job of it in the corner booth.
Elaine was working the coat check, which means
she wasn't working, just smoking by the radiator
and telling me her daughter moved to Tampa.
The trio started late. The bass player's hands
were cold, he said, and you could hear it,
that first chorus limping like a car with a bad valve.
Then the piano found the room and the room
found the piano, and the rain kept time
on the window in a way that wasn't time at all.
I thought about my father, who hated jazz,
who said it sounded like men arguing
in a language no one taught them.
He wasn't wrong. The tenor player stood up
and closed his eyes and went somewhere
I couldn't follow, and didn't want to.
Elaine brought me a beer I didn't order.
The bass player's hands were warm by then.
Outside, the streetlights did that thing they do
in rain, smearing themselves across the asphalt
like they've given up on being lights.
Nobody clapped when the song ended.
The piano player said, We'll take a break,
and nobody moved, and the rain went on
doing whatever it is rain does
when no one's listening.

title: sequence of haiku|a wedding seen from the kitchen staff's view
text:
The caterer's hands
fold napkins into white swans—
love stays in the oven.

Steam from the dish pit
rises past the swinging doors:
first dance, secondhand.

We plate the last course
as the bouquet leaves the room—
butter lamps still warm.

title: blank verse meditation|a library on a Sunday afternoon
text:
Sunday Hours

The reading room is hushed, but not with sleep.
The tall windows admit a slanted light
that falls across the long and empty tables,
and dust motes drift within it, slow as thought.
The shelves stand mute in their appointed rows,
and all the spines, worn smooth by other hands,
wait patient as a field beneath the snow.
No voice is here but what the pages keep—
the distant, turning whisper of a leaf,
the creak of a chair, the settling of a book.
Outside, the world goes by in Sunday clothes,
but here the hours are measured out in lines,
and time, grown gentle, folds its hands and stays.

title: poem in tercets|watching a parent grow old
text:
The trick is the shoes. He sits to tie them now,
a hush of breath before the daily knot,
the bunny ears a little out of practice.

*

He's taken up the weather like a trade.
At six he reads the barometric pressure
aloud, to no one, from the kitchen phone.

*

The mail arrives; he sorts it into piles
he will not touch again—the seed catalogs,
the bank, a letter from a friend two years dead.

*

I watched him eat a peach above the sink,
the juice conducting down his wrist like wire,
and for a moment he was thirty, summer,

*

then the tremor took the fruit back to his mouth
in sections, small and careful as a heist.
The stone he set aside. He set it down.

title: Petrarchan sonnet|insomnia and the refrigerator hum
text:
Nocturne with Appliance

The clock dissects the dark in even beats;
my mind, a tenant pacing rented floors,
rehearses conversations, closing doors
on arguments no daylight yet completes.
Beneath it all, the refrigerator greets
the silence with a hum that never bores—
a level psalm of compressors and chores,
the only prayer this hollow hour repeats.

O tireless servant, keep your steady tone,
a metronome for thought's unquiet tread;
you sing of milk and leftovers alone,
of ordinary mornings, warmth, and bread.
While sleep withholds the mercy of the stone,
your small machine orates me back to bed.

title: dramatic monologue|the sound of a train at night
text:
The 2:47 to nowhere, they call it,
but I know it's the 2:47 to Poughkeepsie
because my father took it every Sunday night
back to a job he hated in a town he hated
and I'd lie awake, six years old,
listening for that sound like a held breath let go.

It starts in the bones first—
that low hum you feel in your molars
before your ears even catch up.
Then the horn. Not a whistle, whatever they tell you.
A horn. Two notes, always two,
the second one a step lower like a question
losing its nerve halfway through asking.

The house would shake. Just slightly.
The water glass on my nightstand
would ring its little glassy ring
and I'd press my palm flat against the wall
to feel the whole world moving
without me, away from me,
carrying my father's gray coat
and his lunch pail and his tired hands
somewhere I couldn't follow.

There was a crossing down on Mill Street.
The horn would hit twice there,
then twice again a mile up at the depot,
and in between, this sound—
not silence exactly, but the rails cooling,
ticking like a clock that had given up on time.

I live in the city now.
The trains here are electric, they whine,
they don't have that diesel ache,
that smell of burnt matches and old rain.
But sometimes, late, when the windows are open
and the el train drags itself home,
I hear it. That second note.
That step down.

And I'm six again.
And the glass is ringing.
And my father is going
wherever it is
they go.

title: ode|the night shift at a diner
text:
The Night Shift at a Diner

The neon sign, a fractured, buzzin' hymn,
Bleeds pink and green across the asphalt dim,
And paints a halo on the coffee cup
A tired trucker, waking, holds it up.
The clock above the grill, a captive moon,
Has swept the floor and swept it clean too soon.
Its hands, like tired arms, have dragged the night
From black to blue, from blindness into sight.

The short-order cook, a ghost in grease and flour,
Works in the slow, deliberate, and late-hour
Cathedral of the spatula and flame.
He knows each customer has not a name,
But just a need: a plate of eggs and toast,
A refuge from the things they fear the most.
The hiss of bacon is a whispered prayer,
A small communion offered on the air.

A woman in a booth, her coat still on,
Sits with the ghost of someone who is gone.
She stirs her coffee, watches the slow swirl
Of cream become a galaxy, a world
Where she can briefly live before the sun
Burns off the fog and says the night is done.
Her spoon against the ceramic makes a sound
Like a small, steady heartbeat, safe and bound.

The waitress, wreathed in steam and second-hand,
Has learned to read the language of the hand
That holds a fork, the story in a sigh,
The way a stranger's shoulders start to cry
Without a sound. She wipes the counter clean,
A priestess of the vinyl and caffeine,
And slides a menu, plastic, worn, and vast,
A map of comfort for a night to last.

This is the kingdom of the fluorescent hum,
Where all the lost and lonely finally come
To sit beneath the flickering, holy light
And wait for morning's slow and welcome bite.
A place of grace in porcelain and chrome,
A temporary, greasy, sacred home,
Where every cup is filled, and every soul
Is, for a moment, made a little whole.

title: ghazal|coffee at dawn before anyone wakes
text:
I. First Light

The house is still; I spoon the dark before the dawn.
A quiet ritual, a spark before the dawn.

The kettle’s sigh is the only sound that stirs,
a promise murmured in the dark before the dawn.

Steam rises like a ghost of sleep, a wraith,
and curls against the window’s arc before the dawn.

I hold the warm ceramic in my hands and watch
the slow retreat of every mark before the dawn.

II. The Only Prayer

This bitter heat is the only prayer I know.
A grounding rite, a tether here, the only prayer I know.

The world’s demands are waiting just beyond the door,
a weight I am not ready to bear, the only prayer I know.

For now, the scent of roasted earth is sanctuary,
a shield against the coming care, the only prayer I know.

Each sip’s a small, deliberate act of staying put,
a whispered “yes” hung in the air, the only prayer I know.

III. The House Wakes

The floorboards creak, a sign the quiet’s almost done.
My solitude is a fading line, the quiet’s almost done.

A muffled cough, the distant sound of running water,
the day begins its slow design; the quiet’s almost done.

I drain the final, cooling sweetness from the cup,
a fleeting, personal divine, the quiet’s almost done.

The first “good morning” will dissolve this private world,
and leave the empty mug behind; the quiet’s almost done.

title: Shakespearean sonnet|a nurse finishing a twelve-hour shift
text:
The med-dispensing cart’s a squeaking ghost
I park beside the wall. My sneakers hiss
on tile. The breakroom microwave’s the most
loyal thing I know—its turntable spins
my cold coffee in circles. Someone’s purse
spills tampons, gum. I count the ceiling’s dots
like sheep. My scrubs wear someone else’s curse:
a stain shaped like a state I can’t place. Lots
of beeping dies behind me. In the glass
my face is photocopied, gray and thin.
I peel my badge off—lanyard like a lash—
and let the parking lot’s fluorescent grin
escort me out. The sun’s a rumor. Birds
are starting up like bad alarms. I’m words.

title: spoken-word poem|first snow in a hospital parking lot
text:
First Snow in a Hospital Parking Lot

The first flake doesn't announce itself.
It just arrives, like bad news,
like a diagnosis slipped under a door,
and then another, and another,
until the whole gray world is being rewritten
in a language no one has to translate.

I'm standing by the west entrance
where the ambulances idle,
where the smokers in gowns and wheelchairs
hold their IV poles like staffs
and tilt their faces up
to something softer than fluorescent light.

The parking lot is filling in—
the yellow lines, the handicap spaces,
the oil stains shaped like old regrets—
all of it going white,
all of it forgiven,
at least until the plows come.

Somewhere above us a window glows.
Someone is being told to wait.
Someone is being told to breathe.
Someone is holding a hand
that has grown very light in theirs.

And the snow keeps falling,
indifferent and generous,
catching in the bare trees
like a held breath,
like the pause before a doctor speaks,
like the moment after,
when you step outside
and the cold air tastes
of something clean.

I watch a nurse cross the lot
in sneakers, no coat,
phone pressed to her ear,
laughing at something
that has nothing to do with any of this.
She leaves a trail of dark footprints
that the snow is already closing,
already closing,
already closing.

This is how the world goes on.
Not with a bang.
With a flake.
With a flake.
With a flake.

title: pantoum|the stars seen from a desert
text:
The stars tonight are cheaper than I remember—
my brother’s old guitar still in the truck,
a cold that gets inside the coffee cup.
We drove four hours for a sky like this.

My brother’s old guitar still in the truck,
the dog asleep across the cooler lid.
We drove four hours for a sky like this.
He says the Milky Way looks like a spill.

The dog asleep across the cooler lid,
I count the Pleiades and lose my place.
He says the Milky Way looks like a spill
and tips his hat back, squinting at the haze.

I count the Pleiades and lose my place—
somewhere a semi downshifts on the grade.
He tips his hat back, squinting at the haze.
The fire’s down to coals we didn’t tend.

Somewhere a semi downshifts on the grade.
I find Orion’s belt, then lose it too.
The fire’s down to coals we didn’t tend.
He’s telling me about a girl in Tucson.

I find Orion’s belt, then lose it too.
The cold that gets inside the coffee cup—
he’s telling me about a girl in Tucson.
The stars tonight are cheaper than I remember.

title: spoken-word poem|hope after a long illness
text:
The X-Ray Is a Photograph of Snow

After the long winter of your body,
the technician’s voice is a thaw.
You lie inside the white tube’s hum,
a seed under the heavy, frozen ground.

They are looking for the storm’s signature,
the grey fist of it clenched in your lung,
the small, hard hailstone of it
tapping its code against a rib.

For months, the cough was a tenant
who paid no rent, who rearranged the furniture
of your sleep. The fever was a lamp
left on in an empty room.

But today, the radiologist studies the film
and says the word *clear* like a key
turning in a lock. Like the first bird
testing the silence after a blizzard.

You walk out into the parking lot.
The sun is a plain, uncomplicated coin.
The air is a clean sheet. You breathe it in.
You breathe it in. You breathe it in.

title: ode|teenage summer jobs
text:
I. First Light at the Diner

Before the sun has warmed the lot,
I tie the apron, learn the knot,
and stack the chairs from off the floor
while coffee brews behind the door.
The grill's first hiss, the plates' low clink,
the clock that never moves, I think—
I pour for men who tip in change
and call me "hon," and find it strange
how morning smells of toast and sweat,
how much of summer I forget
is measured out in refills, kind,
with all the windows left behind.

II. The Pool on Break

At noon I trade the tray for sun,
for chlorine air and everyone
who shouts my name from off the board
like I'm some hero they've adored.
I lifeguard mornings, scoop the leaves,
then count the hours the water weaves—
a dollar saved, a dollar spent,
a whistle blown, a compliment
from no one that I'll keep too long.
The radio plays the same sad song.
I'm tan and tired, broke and free,
and seventeen feels like the sea.

III. Last Shift, August

The register counts down the days;
the neon hums its tired praise.
I fold the apron, kill the light,
and step into the softer night
where August leans against the car
and tells me I have come this far—
a summer's worth of small mistakes,
of tips and towels, give and takes.
The pool is drained, the diner dims,
the radio forgives my hymns.
I drive home slow, the windows down,
one pocket light, one pocket town.

title: Petrarchan sonnet|time and memory
text:
The Fading Archive

Time is a thief who works with patient hands,
unthreading what the memory has spun;
he loosens every knot beneath the sun
and scatters grain across the shifting sands.
Yet memory, defiant, understands
the art of holding fast when day is done—
she keeps a lamp where fading echoes run
and writes her name where nothing else stands.

But time, relentless, turns the final page,
and memory, though fierce, must yield her claim;
the brightest moments dim with passing age,
and even love forgets to speak its name.
So let us hold each other while we may—
before the thief has stolen all away.

title: prose poem|a soldier writing home
text:
A Soldier Writing Home

The paper is a pale field under the lamp, and my pen moves across it like a patrol at dusk—slow, careful, measuring each line for what it can bear. Outside, the guns have gone quiet the way a heartbeat goes quiet, and I do not trust the silence. I write *I am well* and the words sit on the page like stones I have carried all day. I tell you the bread is good. I tell you the boots fit. I fold the truth into smaller and smaller squares until it fits inside an envelope, and the lies are not lies but a kind of armor I wear so you will not have to. Somewhere a man is laughing, and somewhere a man is not, and I am here in the between, writing your name at the top of the page like a prayer I am afraid to finish. The candle shortens. The night deepens. I sign it *with love*, and the word feels heavier than my rifle, lighter than my fear, and I send it out into the dark the way a soldier sends everything—hoping it arrives, hoping it is enough, hoping the morning comes gentle to the both of us.

title: Shakespearean sonnet|the ocean during a storm
text:
The wind off Hatteras has torn the sky
to rags. I stand where my grandfather stood,
his name half-eaten from the jetty wood,
and watch the gray come down. The gulls won't fly.
They huddle under the pavilion, eye
the churning green. Last night I understood
how little holds—a piling in the flood,
a rope, a voice. The waves stack up and die
against the rocks and stack again. My coat
is soaked through at the shoulders. Someone's chair
tumbles past the breakers, leg over leg.
I think of how he drowned out past the throat
of Ocracoke, and how the water there
gave nothing back—not even, then, the egg
of his lunch pail, they said. The rain comes slant.
I should go in. I don't. I never can.

title: blank verse meditation|insomnia and the refrigerator hum
text:
The hour when nothing answers but the hum
of the refrigerator, keeping its cold
covenant with the dark. I lie and count
the small contractions of the house—the tick
of settling wood, the pipes' faint asthmatic
sigh—and listen to that motor's steady
monologue, the only voice still speaking
in a tongue I almost understand.

Last night I stood barefoot on the kitchen tile
and opened it: the brief and blinding church
of light, the shelves arranged like offerings—
the milk, the wilting parsley, the half-lemon
wrapped in its shroud of plastic. I closed the door
and let the darkness heal again, and felt
the compressor shudder into being, patient
as a heart that will not stop.

Somewhere a dog barks twice and thinks better of it.
The ceiling holds its pale, indifferent face
above me. I have memorized the grain
of it, the hairline crack that runs from corner
to corner like a river on a map
of someplace I have never been. The hum
goes on. It is the sound of something keeping,
which is the closest thing to being kept.

I think of all the sleepless in their rooms—
the woman in the next apartment turning
her pillow like a phrase she cannot parse,
the man upstairs who paces, paces—each
of us awake inside a small machine
that labors through the night to keep us cold,
to keep us whole, to keep the milk from souring
before the morning comes. The hum, the hum.

And then the window grays. The refrigerator
clears its throat and rests. A bird begins
its first uncertain sentence, and I close
my eyes at last, and let the quiet take me
like a hand that has been waiting all night long.

title: poem in tercets|a garden after the gardener has died
text:
I. The Unlatched Gate

The hinge has learned a new, slow speech.
No hand to still its swinging arc,
it grieves in rust against the latch.

II. What the Roses Keep

They bloom regardless, flush and deep,
remembering the pruning knife
in every thorn they raise to keep.

III. The Watering Can

Tin throat turned skyward, dry and dumb,
it waits beside the silent spout
for footsteps that will never come.

title: blank verse meditation|commuting on a crowded subway
text:
Subway Psalm

The doors seal shut and we are borne along  
into the dark, a hundred breathing souls  
pressed close enough to hear the quiet shift  
of weight from foot to foot, the rustle low  
of coats, the private weather of each face.  
A woman reads; her thumb against the page  
turns slow, deliberate, as if she counts  
the minutes of her life. A young man sleeps  
against the glass, his forehead pale and smooth,  
and dreams of somewhere sunlight reaches through  
the tunnel's length. I hold the cold steel pole  
and sway with every lurch, and feel the press  
of strangers' shoulders, warm and unaware,  
as though we were a single animal  
that breathes in unison and does not speak.  
Between the stations there is such a hush—  
the roaring hush of motion—that I think  
of all the cities underneath the earth,  
of all the tired and the waking ones  
who ride this way each morning, carrying  
their unread letters and their grocery lists,  
their griefs wrapped neatly in their coat pockets.  
The lights go out a moment, flicker back,  
and no one gasps; we know the dark too well.  
We surface into evening, one by one  
unfolding toward our separate doors, and yet  
some thread of us remains down there, still joined,  
still swaying in the hollow of the earth,  
a congregation of the ordinary  
that prays by going home. The escalator  
lifts me toward the street, and I ascend  
into the wide and indifferent air, and carry  
the silence of the crowd within my chest  
like something almost holy, almost mine.

title: prose poem|an abandoned railway station
text: The ticket window’s glass holds a diorama of dust. A wasp, long dead, is a jeweled pin in the lapel of a curtain. The schedule board is a palimpsest of ghosts: a smudge of chalk, a phantom time. Someone has propped a bicycle with no wheels against the bench, a skeleton of intention. In the waiting room, the floorboards have memorized the weight of a thousand impatient shoes and now they just breathe, a slow, splintered respiration. A single, unpaired glove rests on the sill, thumb cocked, pointing at the tracks. The tracks themselves are two rusted zippers, half-open, spilling a cargo of weeds and sunlight. A signal, its eye gone dark, still leans toward the horizon, a blind man listening for a heartbeat in the iron. The only departure is a slow one, a drift of dandelion seeds catching the draft from a broken pane, heading out, out, past the water tower’s rusted chalice, into the wide, forgetful field.

title: blank verse meditation|first snow in a hospital parking lot
text:
The radio said flurries, so of course
it's six inches and the plows are somewhere
on 1-95, and I am standing in the far row
of the parking lot with a coffee going cold
in my fist, because my father is inside
getting his third liter of fluid drained
and the nurse said give us an hour.

The first flakes came down slow and separate,
each one a small event against the asphalt,
and I watched them die there, one by one,
the way he used to stub his cigarettes
on the porch rail, patient, in no hurry.
Then the sky let go and now the lines
are gone, the yellow lines, the arrows,
the number I was supposed to remember.

The lot is filling up. A woman in scrubs
runs past with a cardboard tray of coffees,
her sneakers squeaking on the wet black,
and somewhere behind me a car alarm
is going off and nobody cares.
The snow is not clean here. It falls
on the dumpster and the cigarette butts
and the spot where somebody's transmission
bled a rainbow on the concrete all summer.

I think about his hands, how they've gone
thin as the veins they keep stabbing,
how he said this morning, looking past me
at the window, that it looked like snow,
and I said no, not yet, and he said
I know what snow looks like.

The wipers on the empty cars are up
like a field of antennae, like they're listening
for something. Mine are down. I never
remember. I finish the coffee. I count
the plows on the road, which is to say
I count nothing. The snow keeps coming.
It doesn't mean anything. It's just water
remembering a different shape.

title: villanelle|an old piano left on the curb
text:
The Old Piano on the Curb

The rain has stained its ivory to bone.
Its pedals rust in grass grown up between
the broken keys that no one plays alone.

Some child once practiced scales in monotone
beneath a window's warm and lamplit screen—
the rain has stained its ivory to bone.

The neighbors pass and leave it to atone
for every song it held, now dulled and mean,
its broken keys that no one plays alone.

A mover's chalk still marks it like a stone
upon the curb, a hulk of black marine.
The rain has stained its ivory to bone.

Somewhere a house is quiet, overthrown
by silence where the music once had been—
its broken keys that no one plays alone.

Tonight the moon will make its lid a throne,
and dew will fill the hollows like a screen.
The rain has stained its ivory to bone,
its broken keys that no one plays alone.

title: ode|drought on a family farm
text:
I. The Cracks Remember Rain

The field spreads its palms like a beggar,
each furrow a line on a weathered face.
My father walks it, boots raising dust
that settles on his shoulders like a coat
he cannot take off. The corn stands
in thin confession, stalks like pencils
writing nothing. I remember when mud
was a language we cursed and loved—
now the earth opens its mouth
and we have no words to fill it.

II. The Cistern's Throat

The well hums a drier song each week,
its bucket knocking hollow on the stone.
My mother measures out the day in cups,
waters the tomatoes like they're children
running fevers. The rain barrel leans,
a drunkard emptied of his最后 drink.
At supper we pass the water pitcher
slowly, and no one says the word
that hovers like a hawk above the barn—
*drought*—we chew our bread
and listen to the sky not speaking.

III. What We Carry Forward

Tonight the horizon stacks its clouds
like promises, and still they pass us by,
gray caravans heading somewhere greener.
My grandfather's hands, mapped with years
of dust, fold around a coffee cup
and he says: *We are made of waiting.*
The dogs sleep in the shade of the truck
and dream of puddles. Somewhere beneath
this cracked and patient ground,
the roots hold on—small fists
that have not yet learned to let go.

title: ballad in quatrains|fishing with an uncle who never talks
text:
The Silent Uncle’s Line

The lake lay still beneath the gray,
The boat slid from the shore,
My uncle baited hooks that day
And spoke no word the more.

He handed me the tangled reel,
He showed me how to cast,
He did not say just how to feel
When ripples hurried past.

The dragonflies came skimming low,
The sun climbed up the sky,
He watched the water’s ebb and flow
With neither wave nor sigh.

I asked him if the fish would bite—
He only nodded slow,
And pointed where the shallows light
Began to gleam and glow.

The shadows stretched across the pine,
The bobber dipped and spun,
He gripped my shoulder once—a sign—
And whispered, “Pull, my son.”

The bass came flashing, broad and bright,
He netted it with care,
And in the fading afternoon light
He smiled, and left it there.

We rowed for home without a word,
The oars made steady sound,
The only talking that I heard
Was water all around.

But something in that quiet space
Had told me all I know—
He’d taught me patience, love, and grace
Without a voice, and so

I keep that silence in my chest,
That lake, that light, that line,
And know the lessons I love best
Were never spoke—but mine.

title: blank verse meditation|a city bus at 2 a.m.
text:
The diesel idles like a dull ache in the jaw.
The driver, a man with a face like a folded map,
stares through the windshield at the nothing ahead.
The fluorescent tubes inside are a cold, even light
that makes the empty seats look like a row of teeth
in a jaw that has forgotten how to close.

A woman boards, her coat a burst pillow of down.
She pays, sits, and unpacks a small, foil-wrapped meal
from a purse the size of a hardcover book.
The smell of it—vinegar and old grease—blooms
in the recycled air. She eats with the precision
of a watchmaker, then folds the foil into a bird.

We lurch past a laundromat, its windows black mirrors.
Past a man asleep on a bench, a cairn of coats.
The streetlights are sodium-orange, a color
that belongs to no natural hour. They tick past
like the beads of an abacus counting out the dark.

The woman gets off. The driver sighs, a sound
like a tire losing its last breath of air.
He pulls the handle. The doors fold shut with a gasp.
The bus is a lung. The city is a body.
We are the slow, deep breath it takes
before it has to speak again.

title: prose poem|a lighthouse keeper's last night on duty
text:
The Last Watch

Tonight the lamp burns as it has for forty years, and I have trimmed the wick for the final time. The glass still turns its slow and patient circle, throwing its long white finger out across the water, and I think how it has pointed at nothing and everything—at ships that never saw it, at storms that swallowed the light, at the small dark waves that come and go like breath. The logbook lies open on the desk, its pages full of weather and the names of vessels, and I write the last entry slowly, as though the ink itself might refuse to dry. Outside, the sea is doing what the sea always does, indifferent and enormous, and the wind presses its soft mouth against the windows. I have lived so long with this light that I no longer know which of us is keeping watch. Tomorrow another man will climb these stairs, and the lamp will burn for him as it burned for me, and the sea will not notice the difference. But tonight the beam goes out across the dark water one last time, and I stand in its turning, and I let it pass through me, and I do not move.

title: free verse poem|moving out of a childhood home
text:
The light switch in the hall
still clicks twice—
once for on, once for the ghost
of every hand that ever reached for it.

I am packing the house into boxes
but the house keeps unpacking itself:
a pencil mark on the doorframe
says I was once this tall,
the kitchen window holds a tree
that has grown three feet since spring.

In the corner of my bedroom
a shadow shaped like a desk
where I learned the word "forever"
and practiced it on the wall
in letters I could reach.

The stairs still know my weight.
They creak in the same place
they did when I was ten
and trying to be invisible.

I carry the last box to the car.
Behind me, the door
does not close so much as
fold into a page
of a book I've read so many times
I know it by heart.

I drive away with the house
still in my hands—
a small, warm thing
that will not stop glowing.

title: ghazal|a city bus at 2 a.m.
text:
I. The Last Route

The driver's hands are maps of routes the night has worn,
and every stop's a word in sentences the night has worn.
The fluorescent light hums low, a tired hymn of wires,
while seats hold shapes of absent men the night has worn.
Outside, the storefronts blink like eyes that cannot close,
their neon bleeding into rain the night has worn.
The city sheds its daytime skin of horns and haste;
the bus becomes a moving room the night has worn.
A newspaper dissolves to pulp beneath a passenger's shoe—
old headlines turn to unread rain the night has worn.

II. Passengers

A nurse who smells of antiseptic, sleep, and rain
sits counting stations like a rosary of rain.
A janitor folds his cap and dreams of open fields
where dust is sweet and not the gray that falls like rain.
Two lovers share one earbud, split a single song,
and let the chorus fill the space between them—rain
against the glass becomes the drum their silence keeps,
the driver humming harmony to falling rain.
A man who lost his keys, his job, his argument,
stares through his own reflection stitched with rain.
The bus exhales; the doors accordion the dark;
each rider holds a private weather, private rain.

III. Terminal

The depot glows like something left awake too long,
a lighthouse for the stranded, burning late, too long.
The driver counts his coins and lets the engine rest;
the clock above the platform argues with the dark too long.
Somewhere a kettle whistles in a break-room dawn,
and steam writes fading cursive on the window, late too long.
The seats are empty now, but still they seem to hold
the warmth of everyone who rode this late, too long.
The route folds back into itself, a sleeping snake;
the city turns its other cheek to morning—late, too long.
By four the first commuters gather at the glass,
and ride the ghost of two a.m. awake too long.

title: ghazal|a library on a Sunday afternoon
text:
Sunday Ghazal in the Stacks

The sun through tall windows lies gold on the floor,
and dust motes drift slow in the cold on the floor.

A clock in the hallway keeps measuring noon—
each tick a small stone that is tolled on the floor.

The world and its errands are locked out and gone;
the hush is a coat that is folded on the floor.

A girl in the corner turns pages like wings,
her shadow a bird that has rolled on the floor.

The shelves hold their voices in spines of old leather—
centuries breathing, controlled, on the floor.

I read one line twice, and the afternoon deepens;
the light, growing long, has been strolled on the floor.

Outside, someone’s Sunday goes driving and calling,
but here it is kept, and it’s cajoled on the floor.

O keeper of silence, O lamplit and still—
let the world wait; let it be told on the floor.

title: blank verse meditation|a wedding seen from the kitchen staff's view
text:
The plates arrive like tide-wrack. We stack them
in the steel sink’s dark, a chipped mosaic
of butter hardened into cairns, the bones
of lemon sole picked clean. Out there, the band
has started up—a horn’s brash, silver laugh
that rattles through the pass-through’s swinging door.
We see the bride’s hem smudge the parquet floor,
a glass of something red begin to tilt,
a groomsman’s hand correct it. We don’t cheer.

The pastry chef is torching crème brûlée,
the little blue flames jumping like a pulse.
She works the sugar into glass and says
the marriage is a kind of caramel:
you have to burn it just to make it sweet,
and then you can’t un-burn it. In the walk-in,
the flowers for the morning-after brunch
breathe out their wet, green breath. The dishwasher
hums its one long note. We are the hum.
We are the scrape of steel on bone, the hiss
of water finding every dirty crevice.

Someone’s new wife is crying by the coat check,
but not from sadness. Someone’s new husband
is telling a joke that no one hears the end of.
The kitchen clock has hands like spatulas.
It is almost time to serve the coffee
in cups so small they look like thimbles, black
and bottomless. We move among the tables
like shadows with a purpose, clearing space
for what comes next: the tipping of the chairs,
the sweeping up of rice, the ordinary
morning that will arrive like a clean plate.

title: Shakespearean sonnet|a lost glove on a fence post
text:
The Glove Upon the Fence

A single glove upon a fence post placed,
Its fingers pointing upward to the gray
And indifferent sky, by wind and weather effaced,
Waiting for hands that wandered far away.
Perhaps a child who ran through autumn leaves
And never noticed what her fingers shed,
Or one who loved and lost, and still believes
The wind will bring it home to warmth instead.
It clings to splintered wood through frost and rain,
A small abandoned ghost of woven thread,
Till snow shall bury it and sun shall stain
The wool with gold, and all its warmth be dead.
   Yet still it waits, as patient as the stone,
   For hands that will not come to claim their own.

title: villanelle|the night shift at a diner
text:
The hash browns hiss like something out of spite.
My name tag’s pinned on crooked, says “MARGE,”
and someone’s left a twenty for the night.

The truckers come in reeking of the light
they drove through, black coffee, eggs done hard.
The hash browns hiss like something out of spite.

The jukebox eats a dollar, plays “Tonight’s
the Night” for the fourth time. Len from the yard
tips his hat and leaves. It’s not the night

for talking much. The kid who does the fryer’s white
as flour, says his girlfriend’s due in March.
The hash browns hiss. Like something out of spite

the clock above the grill won’t move. I wipe
the same clean counter. Once, a man in scars
sat here till dawn and left. Not quite the night

I’d choose. The window shows my face just right—
tired, a little mean, a little far.
The hash browns hiss like something out of spite.
The sun comes up. I turn off half the lights.

title: pantoum|watching a parent grow old
text:
I. The Hands That Held

The hands that held me now hold still.
A window frames the fading light.
I watch the slow and gentle will
of afternoon becoming night.

A window frames the fading light.
He folds the paper, sets it down.
Of afternoon becoming night,
the room is quiet, soft, and brown.

He folds the paper, sets it down.
I bring the tea. He says my name.
The room is quiet, soft, and brown.
The kettle whispers, just the same.

I bring the tea. He says my name.
The hands that held me now hold still.
The kettle whispers, just the same.
I watch the slow and gentle will.

II. The Long Hallway

He walks the hallway, slow and sure.
Each step a small negotiation.
The photographs along the door
keep watch with silent patience.

Each step a small negotiation.
I offer him my arm. He smiles.
Keep watch with silent patience,
and measure out the extra miles.

I offer him my arm. He smiles
at something only he can see.
And measure out the extra miles
between the man he was and me.

At something only he can see,
the photographs along the door
between the man he was and me
he walks the hallway, slow and sure.

III. What I Will Keep

The coat still hangs beside the door.
I cannot bring myself to move it.
He wore it walking to the store,
and every season knew it.

I cannot bring myself to move it.
The pockets hold a folded glove.
And every season knew it—
the coat still carries all his love.

The pockets hold a folded glove.
I press my face against the wool.
The coat still carries all his love.
The house is quiet, beautiful.

I press my face against the wool.
He wore it walking to the store.
The house is quiet, beautiful.
The coat still hangs beside the door.

title: free verse poem|the sound of a train at night
text:
Night Freight

A low growl first,
more felt than heard,
shivering the window glass
like a moth against a lamp.

Then the horn—
two long, one short—
a lonely animal calling
across the dark pasture,
asking nothing, telling everything.

The rails begin their humming,
a steel-string thrum
that gathers in the floorboards,
in the marrow of the sleeping house.

Clack and clack, the coupling's pulse,
a heartbeat dragging its long tail
of boxcars through the valley,
each one ticking off the miles
like a metronome for no one.

The whistle again, farther now,
worn thin by distance,
a thread pulled through the needle
of the night—

and then the fading,
the slow unwinding
of that iron lullaby,
until the only sound remaining
is the silence it has taught
to breathe.

title: elegy|a city bus at 2 a.m.
text:
The driver is a man shaped like a question mark,
his spine a curve of weariness. He pilots
the last whale through a reef of streetlights.
The doors exhale their pneumatic sigh
for no one. The plastic seats, orange as processed cheese,
hold the ghosts of commuters: a woman’s perfume
turned to a smell like burnt sugar, the ghost
of a wet dog, the ghost of a man who whispered
a whole argument into his phone.

We are a container for the city’s held breath.
A dropped transfer ticket on the floor
is a moth with a broken wing.
The fluorescent lights hum a hymn
to the Church of the Late Shift. Outside,
a rat drags a pizza crust like a fallen banner
across the wet asphalt. The driver’s coffee
is a cold, black mirror in its styrofoam cup.
He doesn’t look at it. He looks at the route,
a litany of empty intersections, a string
of unpronounceable saints.

This is the liturgy of the empty vessel.
The route is a loop of tape, played
until the magnetic ribbon is transparent.
It carries the weight of all it has carried:
the drunk’s confession, the nurse’s fatigue,
the student’s blank stare at a glowing rectangle.
It is a lung that breathes for the sleeping city,
a slow, mechanical respiration.
At the final stop, it will fold its doors
like hands, and wait for the dawn
to break its bread.

title: Shakespearean sonnet|the first heartbreak
text:
First Break

The heart once whole now learns the weight of stone,
A hollow drum where joyful rhythms died.
I walked the halls of light yet felt alone,
With nothing left but echoes I could hide.
Your name, a splinter working through the vein,
Still whispers warmth that I must learn to spurn.
Love's early frost has left a silver stain
On everything the spring has yet to turn.
Yet in this ruin something small takes root—
A quieter pulse, a breath that steadies slow.
The wound will close, though scarred beneath the suit
Of days I wear, and still, somehow, I grow.
So let the first cut teach what time will prove:
The heart breaks open to make room for love.

title: ghazal|a jazz club in the rain
text:
The rain taps out a broken beat on the awning.
Tuesday. The trio's late. My beer goes flat. I don't mind.

The bass player's girl is crying in the coat check,
mascara going soft. He plays like he don't mind.

Some nights the horn just quits—halfway through "Naima,"
just stops, like the thought's gone bad. The regulars don't mind.

The owner waters the gin. The piano's missing a key
somewhere up top. Nobody's fooled. The tune don't mind.

Last week a man in a wet suit asked me for a light,
then told me his whole life. I smoked it slow. I didn't mind.

The window fogs. The streetlight bleeds. Somebody's umbrella
turns inside out down the block. The rain don't mind.

title: prose poem|a nurse finishing a twelve-hour shift
text: The hallway at 6 a.m. is a country no one else has visited. She walks through it with the slow gravity of the moon, her shoes making the soft percussion of a sentence finally reaching its period. In the break room, the fluorescent light is a pale anaesthetic, and she sits, unwinding the stethoscope from her neck like a rosary she no longer needs to count. Her hands still remember the fever of a stranger's wrist, the papery weight of an old man's cough. Somewhere behind her, the night's small emergencies are already becoming stories—the code blue that resolved into a single held breath, the child who slept at last. She pours coffee that is more shadow than substance, watches the steam rise and vanish like a last confession. Outside, the city is a patient just waking, its morning pulse a faint blue line across the monitor of the sky. She thinks of her own bed, how it waits like a promise she has kept a thousand times. The shift is over. The shift is never over. She carries it home in the hollow of her shoulder, a quiet ache shaped like everyone she touched.

title: elegy|a small-town Friday football game
text:
Friday Night Lights, Extinguished

The stadium hums beneath a bruised November sky,
a bowl of light carved from the darkening fields.
The bleachers fill with fathers, mothers, girls
who wear their letters like a second skin,
and boys who pace the sidelines, waiting for their turn
that never comes, or comes too soon, or comes at last.

The band inflates the anthem, brass and drum,
and all the town stands up, and all the town
believes, for one more hour, in something clean:
the snap, the handoff, the collision and the gain,
the forward pass that hangs like a held breath
before it finds a pair of outstretched hands.

I think of how the grass remembers everything—
the scuffed-up cleats, the sweat, the shouted plays,
the coach who paced this same white line for years
and now sits in the stands with folded arms,
his whistle silent on a shelf at home.
The goalposts stand like gallows for the sun.

The seniors play their final home game now,
and something in their shoulders knows the truth:
that this is it, the last time down the field,
the last bright Friday of their given lives.
They hit the line as if to break it open,
as if the whole town's hope were in their pads.

And when the clock runs out, the lights go down
in sections, like a sentence losing words,
and cars pull out along the county road,
their taillights smearing red across the cold.
The field goes dark. The grass grows still. The town
turns off its porch lights, one by one, and sleeps,
and dreams of autumn, and of boys who run
forever toward a end zone made of light.

title: short lyric poem|the smell of a grandmother's kitchen
text:
Yeast lifts its slow balloon
under a dish towel. The radiator
ticks like a cooled pistol.
On the sill, a jar of buttons—
horn, bone, the pearled
grief of a cardigan—
keeps its own weather.

Something with cloves
is losing its argument
with something with vinegar.
The pilot light
breathes its blue bud.
A fly rehearses
the window's dead chord.

And the whole house leans
toward the oven's small sun,
where the pie's crimped lip
gathers the light
like a scar that has learned
to hold something sweet.

title: villanelle|autumn leaves in a cemetery
text:
Autumn Leaves in a Cemetery

The autumn leaves drift down among the stones,
in burnished gold and crimson, softly cast;
a quiet choir in melancholic tones.

The wind through empty branches sighs and moans,
and gathers what the fading year amassed—
the autumn leaves drift down among the stones.

Each marker bears a name the moss disowns,
where memories and marble both hold fast
a quiet choir in melancholic tones.

The maple bleeds its fire, then atones,
and scatters flame where shadowed grasses mast;
the autumn leaves drift down among the stones.

Beneath the yew, in consecrated zones,
the sleepers keep a silence that will last—
a quiet choir in melancholic tones.

So seasons fall in rhythmic, slow cyclones,
and beauty settles where the grief was vast:
the autumn leaves drift down among the stones,
a quiet choir in melancholic tones.

title: free verse poem|migrating geese over a frozen lake
text:
The V of them pulls a seam in the gray sky
over Miller's pond, which froze shut Tuesday
with the suddenness of a slammed door.
I'm out here with the dog, who doesn't look up,
just noses a beer can someone left
half-buried in the cattails.

They're late this year. My father would have said
that means a hard one coming. He said that
every year. He's been dead six winters now
and I still hear him say it, the way you hear
a phone ring in a house that's empty.

The lead bird breaks and reforms the point,
breaks and reforms it. Like a man
pacing a waiting room. Like my mother
rearranging the same three photographs
on the mantel, every day, for no one.

The ice ticks and settles. The dog finds something
frozen in the mud and worries it loose.
I should call her in. The light's going.
Somewhere under all that stillness
a fish is turning over, slow as a dial.

The geese don't land. They never do here.
They just keep going, stitching their one
crooked line across the water's white eye,
and I stand here with my hands in my pockets
until they're a smudge, until they're a thought
I can't quite hold, until the dog
barks once at nothing and I turn
and we walk back up the hill together.

title: short lyric poem|the moon over a refugee camp
text:
A quarter moon, a bent tin spoon
doles out the dark in measured scoops.
The tents below are folded sighs.
A child holds up one palm. The moon
stays there—a small, unclaimed white stone
she keeps because the sky forgets.

title: elegy|a garden after the gardener has died
text:
I. The Secateurs

They hang on their hook by the shed,
their jaws half-open, as if
about to speak a word
that only roses understand.

The hinge has seized. No hand
comes to work the small rust loose.
The dead heads gather on the stems
like unread letters.

II. The Rows

The beans have woven past their poles
and fallen into one another's arms,
unsure which way is up
now that the tutoring stopped.

The parsley has gone to seed—
tall, pale, extravagant,
spending itself on air.
The weeds keep no schedule but their own.

III. The Gate

It swings a little in the wind,
unlatched, the way he left it
meaning to come back before dark.

The path remembers his weight
in its worn stones. The roses
bloom anyway, and do not know
they are a eulogy.

title: villanelle|a wedding seen from the kitchen staff's view
text:
The plate warmers hum. We are the engine room.
Through the pass, a lens-flare of a hundred phones
catches the bride’s dress, a whipped merengue bloom.

The groom’s uncle has cornered the waitstaff for a boom
of a story, spittle-flecked, about his loans.
The plate warmers hum. We are the engine room.
