A busboy scrapes a mountain of uneaten groom-
cake into the bin. The band’s off-key trombone
catches the bride’s dress, a whipped merengue bloom.

The florist’s peonies, dyed the shade of a deep bruise, loom
in their vases, dropping petals like soft, pink stones.
The plate warmers hum. We are the engine room.

The mother of the bride, a perfume-cloud of doom,
hisses at the caterer in clipped, low tones.
The plate warmers hum. We are the engine room.

We polish flutes and stack them in the gloom,
a stainless-steel and sweating-skinnedUnknown.
The plate warmers hum. We are the engine room.
The bride’s dress, a whipped merengue bloom.

title: ode|autumn leaves in a cemetery
text:
Ode to Autumn Leaves in a Cemetery

O gold against the granite gray,
O crimson drift where sleepers lie,
You fall in slow, unhurried play
Beneath the mute and marble sky.
The wind, a sexton, sweeps the ground,
And piles you where the headstones stand,
As if to soften every mound
With beauty from a careless hand.

You settle on the nameless stone,
You cover up the date, the name,
And make the forgotten dead your own
In flares of momentary flame.
What sermon does your silence preach?
What liturgy of rust and red?
The branches lean, and seem to teach
A gospel for the buried dead:

That all things bright must let go,
That glory is a letting-down,
That summer's green and winter's snow
Are one in you, O falling crown.
The yew tree keeps its ancient watch,
The angel folds its mossy wing,
And you, without a fear to match,
Go down to meet the coming spring.

O leaves, O ephemeral gold,
O scripture written on the air,
You make the cemetery bold
With something softer than despair.
For where you fall, the ground is warm,
And where you rest, the dark is kind—
A bright, brief, beautifully sworn
Reminder left for those behind.

title: prose poem|a mother's hands
text: She keeps a rubber band around her left wrist, the thick one from a broccoli bunch, and snaps it when she's counting under her breath—plates, pills, the minutes until the kettle clicks. Her right thumbnail has a ridge in it from the time the car door bit her in the Price Chopper lot, 1998, and she never let it heal straight, kept picking at the split like a scab she was saving. The knuckles go wide in winter. She rubs them with the same lotion she's used since I was small, the pink one that smells like a doctor's office trying to be a garden, and the smell gets into the dish towel, into the birthday cards, into the hair of anyone she holds too long. There's a burn scar shaped like a comma on the soft part between thumb and finger. She got it reaching over a flame for a spoon she didn't need to reach for. She does that. Reaches over the fire for the wrong thing. I have watched those hands fold a fitted sheet into a rectangle that shouldn't exist, watched them hover over a phone that wouldn't ring, watched them in the rearview passing me a sandwich wrapped in foil so tight it took me the whole ride to get into it.

title: pantoum|an old piano left on the curb
text:
The Old Piano on the Curb

Its bench is gone. The curbstone is its bed.
Two legs are broken, and the lid won't close.
A maple carcass, lacquer peeling red,
it leans into the rain the way it knows.

Two legs are broken, and the lid won't close.
Some child has chalked a flower on its side.
It leans into the rain the way it knows—
a hundred thousand practice scales have died.

Some child has chalked a flower on its side.
The pedals rust in grass the mower missed.
A hundred thousand practice scales have died;
the sounding board still holds what they insist.

The pedals rust in grass the mower missed.
Tonight the trash truck takes what curbs allow.
The sounding board still holds what they insist—
a hymn, a quarrel, someone's scales just now.

Tonight the trash truck takes what curbs allow.
A maple carcass, lacquer peeling red,
still humming what the neighbors won't allow.
Its bench is gone. The curbstone is its bed.

title: villanelle|hope after a long illness
text:
I. The Dark Room

The blinds are drawn against the morning's flare;
my hands have memorized the ceiling's grain.
I hold the fragile thread of hope in there.

The clock dissolves the hours into air,
and every breath arrives with subtle pain.
The blinds are drawn against the morning's flare.

I dream of gardens I could never share,
of running barefoot through the silver rain.
I hold the fragile thread of hope in there.

The visitors speak softly on the stair,
their voices fading, distant and in vain.
The blinds are drawn against the morning's flare.

But something in the silence learns to bear,
a quiet seed that answers to no chain.
I hold the fragile thread of hope in there.

One day the light will find me unaware,
and I will rise and dress and walk again.
The blinds are drawn against the morning's flare;
I hold the fragile thread of hope in there.

II. The Turning

The window opens, and the air is new;
a sparrow argues on the dripping eave.
I find the strength to see the season through.

The cup is warm; the simple act will do—
to lift it, drink, and let the body believe.
The window opens, and the air is new.

The mirror shows a stranger passing through,
a paler ghost that I must not deceive.
I find the strength to see the season through.

The physio counts the steps I must pursue,
and though I tremble, still I do not leave.
The window opens, and the air is new.

The doctor's words are measured, kind, and few;
he says the worst is past, and I may grieve.
I find the strength to see the season through.

The sun returns to paint the room in hue,
and in my chest, a loosening of the weave.
The window opens, and the air is new;
I find the strength to see the season through.

III. The Garden

The gate is wide, the path is overgrown;
I step into the green and breathing light.
The long dark winter leaves me not alone.

The roses that I planted, now my own,
have climbed the fence and blossomed out of sight.
The gate is wide, the path is overgrown.

I kneel and press my palms against the stone,
and feel the warming earth, and know it's right.
The long dark winter leaves me not alone.

The friends I feared were lost have not been flown;
they gather near, and hold me, and recite
how wide the gate, how far the path has grown.

The child I was, the one who dreamed and shone,
returns to me across the lawn in white.
The long dark winter leaves me not alone.

I stand and face the sun I've always known,
and hope, the quiet seed, becomes the light.
The gate is wide, the path is overgrown;
the long dark winter leaves me not alone.

title: ballad in quatrains|a forest fire seen from far away
text:
The Distant Burning

From off the ridge we saw the glow
Across the valley's darkened space,
A crown of fire, burning slow,
Upon the mountain's wooded face.

The evening sky was smeared with red,
The stars stood back and hid their light;
A river of flame, overhead,
Ran down the canyons of the night.

The pine trees flared like tapers tall,
The oak became a burning brand;
We watched the fiery curtains fall
Across the skyline of the land.

We could not hear the crashing limb,
The hiss of sap, the creatures' flight;
The smoke rose like a seraph's hymn
Against the temple of the night.

The wind would shift, the embers leap,
A thousand sparks would take the air,
Then settle down to smolder deep
In hollows past our seeing there.

At dawn the glow was faded gray,
The mountain stood in ashen shroud;
The sun came up to meet the day
Beneath a thin and bitter cloud.

And still we stood and could not turn
From where the silent scar was laid,
As if some old and distant burn
Within ourselves had been displayed.

title: blank verse meditation|teenage summer jobs
text:
First Paycheck

The summer asphalt breathes its tar-black heat
against the sneakers of the newly hired.
I count the register’s slow arithmetic,
the coins that smell of strangers’ hands and gum,
and learn how hours pool into a wage.
The manager’s voice drifts from somewhere near—
a script of napkins, straws, and closing tasks.
I stack the chairs and watch the parking lot
give up its glare to evening’s gradual blue.
Somewhere a screen door slams, a bicycle
ticks down the block, and all the older kids
who never worked are laughing by the fence.
I fold my apron with a kind of pride
that has no witness but the humming lights.
The first cash pressed into my palm feels thin
as paper, yet it weighs a different day—
one I have made, and no one gave to me.

title: blank verse meditation|the moon over a refugee camp
text:
Tonight the moon is doing that thing again—
the way it did over the camp in ’86,
propped like a dented hubcap on the wire.
My mother called it “God’s fingernail,”
said it scraped the dark down to the bone.
You could read a newspaper by it, she said,
though no one had a newspaper.
Just the same three letters chalked on a board,
a list of names that grew shorter each week.

I remember a man from the next tent
who kept a mirror lashed to a pole,
angled at the moon, and swore
he could see his village in it.
He’d hum a song about a river
that I never learned the words to.
The water here tastes like rust and patience.
The moon doesn’t care. It pours itself
over the tarps, over the latrine ditch,
over the children drawing houses in the dust
with sticks they’ll burn for fire by morning.

Someone’s radio coughs out a song
from a country that no longer exists.
The moon leans in, a nosy neighbor,
and I think how it’s the same moon
that hangs over a parking lot in Ohio,
over a woman I almost married,
who is probably asleep now, probably fine.
It is not a symbol. It is a rock.
It is a bald bulb burning through the tent flap.
It is the light by which we count what’s left—
three cans of beans, one shoe, a photograph
curled at the corners like a leaf in fall.

Tomorrow they say the trucks will come.
Tonight the moon is a cold coin
pressed into my palm. I close my fist.
I do not spend it.

title: ghazal|grief after a dog dies
text:
The Leash Still Swings

The leash still swings from the hook by the door—grief.
Your bowl holds a moon of water on the floor—grief.

I wake to the click of nails on the hallway wood,
then remember. The dark learns my pace once more—grief.

Your name is a burr in my throat I cannot spit out;
each syllable scratches the same throat sore—grief.

The park path remembers your zigzag arithmetic,
the squirrels you tallied, the trees you scored—grief.

I fold your blanket into a smaller square,
then unfold it. I kneel on the kitchen floor—grief.

The house keeps your shape the way a coat keeps shoulders.
I wear the empty air you wore—grief.

Let the last light ladder the window and climb the wall.
Let the bowl stay full. Let the leash swing. Let it pour—grief.

title: Shakespearean sonnet|watching a parent grow old
text:
I. The Hands

I watch his hands, which once could lift the world,
now tremble at the simple task of tea;
the steady fingers, casually unfurled,
that built my childhood frame and cradled me.
I see the spotted map of years inscribed
on skin that held me safe from every fall,
and all the stories that those hands described
are fading now behind a weaker wall.
He waves away my help with quiet pride,
as if to say the failing is not his,
and something in my chest is set aside,
a grief that only watching a parent gives.
   These hands that taught my own to hold and make
   now teach me how to watch, and how to ache.

II. The Stories

He tells the tale again, the selfsame one,
of how he met her on a summer's day,
and though I know the ending has begun
before he speaks, I let him have his say.
The names arrive a little out of place,
the order of the seasons goes astray,
but still the wonder settles on his face
as if he's meeting her again today.
I used to count the errors, keep the score,
and gently turn the record to its start;
but now I let the turning be his door,
and hold the repetition to my heart.
   For what is memory but love held fast,
   and I would hear his morning till the last.

III. The Light

He sits beside the window in the sun
and lets the afternoon pour over him,
and though his wandering gaze has come undone,
the light still finds the edges, gold and dim.
I bring the blanket, tuck it at his side,
and he, surprised, says thank you, soft and low,
as if I were a stranger who had tried
to warm a passing man before I go.
And yet I stay, and watch the falling day
make slow amber of his silvered head,
and find no words that I could ever say
to pay the debt of all the love he shed.
   So let the evening lengthen, let it keep;
   I hold the light for him, and then I weep.

title: sequence of haiku|watching a parent grow old
text:
The Quiet Turning

Strong hands lift the world,
now they tremble at the task
of a simple button.

The stories repeat,
same beginning, middle, end—
I learn them by heart.

Slow steps to the door,
a journey that once took秒,
now a morning's work.

He calls me his child,
for a moment in the fog,
then the fog returns.

I bring him water,
watching his reflection drink,
older than the glass.

title: dramatic monologue|tide pools and hermit crabs
text:
The moon’s a bored cashier, making change
in silver. The water’s left its post,
a slick of kelp like a discarded receipt.
I’m the only one here to audit the loss.

The anemone’s a fist of wet flannel,
a flower that forgot how to be picked.
And here’s the tenant, the hermit crab,
dragging his leased shell like a U-Haul
hitched to a nervous man. He’s all
elbows and suspicion, a tiny, armored
landlord with a squatter’s rights.

He doesn’t scuttle. He *considers*.
He tests the air with a periscope eye,
a wet comma on a stalk, then makes
his move—a sudden, clattering
repossession. He flips the old shell,
a calcium eviction notice, and shoves
his soft, pink, vulnerable ass
into the spiral staircase of a new one.

It’s not a home. It’s a borrowed coat.
It’s a used car with a dicey transmission.
He’s a connoisseur of vacancy,
a collector of foreclosures.
He tries on a whelk, a moon snail, a limpet,
each one a different kind of cramped.
He’s looking for the perfect fit,
the one that feels like a lie he can live in.

The tide’s a slow, dumb animal
coming back to lick its wounds.
It will fill this whole stone auditorium
with a cold, green applause.
And he’ll be ready. He’ll be tucked in,
a fist in a pocket, a secret
the ocean keeps from itself.
He’s the small, hard fact
at the center of the soft, shifting story.
He’s the punchline. He’s the pearl.

title: prose poem|the sound of a train at night
text: The 2:14 to Albany doesn't so much arrive as unzip the dark. First the rails, that high thin whine like a wet finger on a wineglass rim, then the horn — two longs, a short, a long — though I've never once counted them the same way twice. My grandmother called it the lonesome whistle, which embarrassed me at twelve and doesn't now. From the back porch you can hear the whole thing happen: the engine's held breath, the slow exhale of couplings, a sound like someone dragging a chair across a floor upstairs. Then the long freight of it, boxcars ticking past, the click-clack going soft and softer, a deck of cards being shuffled back into its box. My father used to say you could set your watch by it, but he never did, and neither do I. Somewhere past the crossing the horn goes thin as a thread and then it's just the crickets again, and the dog's tags, and the refrigerator humming its one note, and the night zipped shut behind it.

title: dramatic monologue|the smell of a grandmother's kitchen
text:
The Kitchen Keeps Its Own Religion

No one has cooked here since the funeral,
yet every afternoon at four the air
remembers cardamom — a ghost of steam
that climbs the wallpaper like a vine
and finds me at the table, waiting.

She kept the windows shut in winter.
The stove breathed out; the walls breathed in.
I'd sit beneath the hanging copper pots
and watch her hands do what her hands knew —
the dough turned over like a whispered word,
the knife that rocked, the onions going glass.

The house has forgotten how to hold its breath.
The pilot light is out. The burner grates
are cold as pews. But still, at four o'clock,
that smell comes back — not memory, but weather —
a low pressure of cumin, bay, and time,
and I am eight years old and in the way,

and she is saying *move*, and I am moving,
but not enough, not ever far enough
to lose the warmth that rises from the pot —
the way a blessing rises without sound.

I have her spoon. I have her crooked pan.
I have the recipe in her slanted hand
that I can't read. What I can read is this:
the kitchen keeps its own religion — steam
for incense, and for scripture, the burned ring
of a kettle on the wood, and for a god,
the smell of something cooking that will feed
a person who is not yet in the room.

title: ghazal|a nurse finishing a twelve-hour shift
text:
I. Handoff

The hallway hushes; night shift leans against the wall.
She counts the breaths she charted, leans against the wall.

Twelve hours pooled in her shoes like rain. The med cart’s wheel
still ticks its small refrain against the wall.

She signs her name where another’s begins—two hands,
one ledger, passing light against the wall.

II. Clocking Out

The badge-swipe beeps; the door exhales her into cold.
Her coat still smells of antiseptic, into cold.

A patient’s “thank you” follows her like a small lamp
down the parking lot, a thread of warmth into cold.

She is so tired her shadow lags, then catches up—
two silhouettes walking home into the cold.

III. First Light

Coffee steams; the kitchen window turns to gold.
She lets her shoulders drop, and the room turns gold.

Somewhere a call bell rings in someone else’s hands.
She is not needed now. The morning turns to gold.

She sleeps like a tide going out—and the day,
unwatched, keeps its own vigil, turning gold.

title: Shakespearean sonnet|grief after a dog dies
text:
The Silent Leash

The leash hangs idle by the quiet door,
And morning comes without its eager bark.
No clicking claws upon the kitchen floor,
No joyful shadow racing through the park.
The bowl sits full, the blanket lies unstirred,
Where once a breathing warmth would curl and keep
Its faithful vigil, never speaking word,
But guarding all my sleeping and my sleep.
O little heart that beat so true and fast,
You asked no more of life than just to be
Beside me, and the years too quickly passed—
Now silence keeps a mournful company.
   Yet grief is but the price of love so deep,
   And what I loved, I would not fail to weep.

title: short lyric poem|the stars seen from a desert
text:
The sky's a black tarp snapped tight over the lot.
Someone shook out a box of tacks and nails.
A few are crooked. One is burning out,
a cigarette coal in the wind's teeth.

My shadow's a dry well I keep dropping coins in.
The tacks don't care. The nails hold down
a map of nowhere, and the nowhere's mine—
I lie on the hood, warm metal ticking,

and count the ones that fall. The desert breathes
through a hole in its throat. A jackrabbit
writes its name in dust and erases it.
The tacks hold. The tacks hold. The dark's a sieve.

title: ode|a soldier writing home
text:
Ode to a Soldier Writing Home

The candle gutters in the tent,
its flame a small, uncertain guest
that leans across the paper, bent
on reading what I have not guessed—
the words a tired hand will trace
to bridge the miles of dust and stone,
to find, beyond this foreign place,
a kitchen chair, a voice, a home.

The ink runs slow. The night is deep.
The guns have quieted their throats,
and in the hush the shadows creep
like friends who read my unfinished notes.
I write of rain, of bread, of boots,
of little things that keep me sane—
the way a sparrow's whistle suits
the morning, though it sounds like rain.

I do not write of what I saw.
I do not write of what I fear.
I fold the darkness into law
and send the daylight, thin and clear,
to where she keeps the kettle warm
and sets a place she will not fill,
and reads my lines against the storm
and loves me, though I love her still.

O paper, carry what I cannot say—
the ache that has no rank or name,
the ordinary, holy day
I miss, and miss, and miss the same.
O ink, be gentler than the shell.
O words, be braver than the gun.
Go home. Go home. Go home, and tell
her that the morning has begun.

title: Petrarchan sonnet|fishing with an uncle who never talks
text:
The lake is glass. He cuts the Evinrude.
I watch his shoulders, welded into place,
the way his right hand, weather-stained and rude,
reels out the line with neither speed nor grace.
The bobber sits. The dragonflies patrol.
He does not speak. The silence is a kind
of net he drags through water, slow and full
of everything he's chosen not to find.
Then—ripple. Slack goes tight. He sets the hook
with one wrist's flick, and something in me stirs:
the fish, a flash of chrome, the way he took
my childhood silence and made it his. The whirr
of reel is all our language. Dusk comes down.
He rows. I hold the oars. We make no sound.

title: dramatic monologue|hope after a long illness
text:
I. The Dark Room

Three hundred days I watched that crack
travel the ceiling like a slow river.
I learned the grammar of waiting—
the clock's dry cough, the lamp's dim stutter,
the way a spoon of broth could be
a whole day's weather.

I do not recommend it. Still,
I found the floorboards' grain by heart,
and when the fever left its wet handprint
on the window, I could name
each finger of the frost.

II. First Light

Today the curtain moved without me.
Just air—but air that came from somewhere
past the gate, and it had been
in the world, and it came back
to tell me.

I stood. My legs were two strangers
I agreed to trust. The mirror showed
a person I would have to meet again,
and I said, Hello. I said it twice.

III. The Garden

The crocus does not ask
who forgot it. It simply keeps
the appointment it made with the dark
last October, and arrives—

purple, absurd, undeterred.
I kneel down in the wet grass
like a man returned from a long war
who finds his house still standing,
his key still turning the lock,
and the table set, and the bread
still warm.

title: blank verse meditation|a phone call from a long-lost brother
text:
The Call

The phone rang once, then twice, and I just stared—
a number with no name, a hollow sound
that cut the quiet of the afternoon.
I almost let it go, but something pulled
my hand toward the receiver, and I said
hello the way you say it to a stranger,
guarded and thin. Then came the pause, the breath,
and then the voice I knew before the words:
my brother, gone these seven years, who spoke
my name as though it were a door he'd knocked on
late at night, uncertain of his welcome.

We talked of nothing much—the weather, work,
the way the old house settled in the cold.
He did not say where he had been, and I
did not ask. Some rooms you leave unlit.
But in his voice I heard the gravel road
we walked as boys, the creek that took my shoe,
the kitchen light our mother left on late.
He laughed, and it was strange how much a laugh
can carry of a summer long since burned.

He said he had to go. I said I knew.
We hung up, and the silence afterward
was not the silence that had come before—
it had a shape now, edges, something warm
and unfinished, like a sentence left
to hang between two people who have learned
that love is mostly standing in the door
and letting in the cold, and letting out
the ache you thought had hardened into stone.

title: ballad in quatrains|tide pools and hermit crabs
text:
The moon’s a dropped contact lens in a sink of cloud.
The tide pulls back like a lip from a bad tooth,
and the whole shore’s a rummage sale of kelp and stone.
Here’s a pool, a pocket of the ocean’s held breath.

A periwinkle wears its shell like a hard hat.
An anemone’s a fist of wet chrysanthemums
that closes when my shadow falls across the water.
The hermit crab drags its borrowed house—a moon snail’s

spiral, a whelk’s cone—across the corrugated floor.
It’s a squatter in a foreclosure, a tenant
with one eye on the market. I watch it test
a vacant shell the way you’d thumb a used car’s

fender for Bondo. It flips the thing, walks in
ass-first, then hauls the old place out like a moving van
leaving a curb. The sun’s a cigarette butt
stubbed out on the horizon. The tide comes back

to reclaim the furniture. The crab tucks in,
a fist in a glove, a key in a lock. The pool
fills up with cold, green light, and the whole coast
is a landlord changing the locks.

title: ghazal|insomnia and the refrigerator hum
text:
The Refrigerator's Ghazal

The moon glares through the blinds; I count its cold degrees.
The kitchen hums a single note—insomnia's slow disease.

That motor's drone, a metronome that ticks against the dark,
rewrites the silence line by line, a psalm on bended knees.

I press my ear against the wall: the compressor's tired heart
pumps freon through the veins of night, a pulse that will not cease.

The icebox opens like a mouth. The light spills out too white.
I stare into the frozen waste and wait for some release.

The yogurt cups, the wilted greens, the leftovers of noon—
they keep their vigil, row on row, in frigid, humming peace.

Outside, a dog barks once, then stops. The world forgets to breathe.
The refrigerator holds the floor, its sermon without cease.

O sleepless one, what do you seek? The hum has no reply.
It only offers endless night, and cold, and no surcease.

title: elegy|a forest fire seen from far away
text:
From the ridge road we pulled over, my brother
and I, because the whole north face
was doing something we had no word for—
not burning exactly, more like breathing,
a slow orange pulse under the pines
you could count, if you wanted, like a heart.
The smoke went up straight first
and then bent east, and I thought of the kite string
we lost in that same tree line, August, 1989,
how it stayed up there a week, white against the green,
until my father said leave it, it's the tree's now.
We watched until the light went strange
and the deer came down past the fence line,
not running. Just walking out, one after
another, their coats gone dull with ash.
My brother said something about the wind
and I said something back and neither of us
moved. Somewhere under all that
a creek I'd fished as a kid was going
over its stones as if nothing,
the way a name keeps being said
in a room the person's left.
The fire never reached us. It rained
on the third day and the news moved on
to other counties. But I still see it
when the stove catches wrong,
that pulse, that patient orange arithmetic,
and the deer, and the string still up there,
holding whatever it held.

title: sequence of haiku|a soldier writing home
text:
I. Ink and Dust

Dust on the letter—
his hand shakes as he writes home
under foreign stars.

II. Words Unsaid

Words crossed out and torn—
he cannot tell her the truth
of the distant guns.

III. The Sealed Word

Sealed with trembling thumb,
carried far from muddy boots—
she will read his heart.

title: Shakespearean sonnet|a city bus at 2 a.m.
text:
The Midnight Bus

The city sleeps beneath a sodium moon,
And empty streets like ribbon'd shadows lie;
The bus, a weary whale, hums out its tune
And cuts the darkness with a heavy sigh.
Its windows hold a scattering of souls—
The nurse who worked the ward, the baker's man,
A dreamer clutching close his midnight goals—
All bound within the metal caravan.
The driver, silent sentinel of night,
Steers through the stoplights' solitary red,
While overhead the stars lend borrowed light
To weary travelers and the homeward-led.
   So journeys on through dark and quiet deep,
   A steel-born shepherd guarding those who weep.

title: ballad in quatrains|coffee at dawn before anyone wakes
text:
The streetlamp's still a guttering yellow coal.
The kitchen clock's a single, ticking spark.
I measure grounds, and watch the water roll
to darkness in the kettle's copper dark.

The first drop hits the carafe and makes a sound
like someone tapping on a windowpane.
The smell comes up—wet earth and something browned,
a ghost of rain held over fields of grain.

The grinder's whir has stopped. The house is still.
I hear the furnace cycle with a click.
The coffee drips its black into the chill,
a slow, deliberate, and patient tick.

Steam lifts and smears the window's greasy glass.
A shape goes by—a raccoon or a cat.
I hold the warm mug's handle, let time pass,
and watch the night drain from the welcome mat.

The first sip is a wire pulled too tight.
The second is the slackening of the same.
The sky goes from a bruise to a pale light.
The coffee cools. I say the morning's name.

title: blank verse meditation|the smell of a grandmother's kitchen
text:
The Smell of a Grandmother’s Kitchen

There is a room that time has not consumed,  
though years have passed since last I stood within  
its warmth and watched the afternoon arrive  
through curtains thin as breath against the glass.  
The air was never still. It moved with steam  
and settled on the shoulders like a shawl  
of something older than the house itself.  

I speak of what the senses keep when all  
the rest has gone to photograph and dust.  
The smell was not a single thing but lay  
in layers, each one patient on the last:  
the bread that rose before the sun had found  
the sill, the coffee dark and slow to wake,  
the onions sighing in the pan, the faint  
and clinging sweetness of a cinnamon  
that lived in drawers and never left the wood.  

It was a language spoken without words,  
a grammar of the ordinary made  
eternal by the hands that stirred and shaped.  
Flour on the counter, a white drift  
of something like a snow that would not melt.  
The oven's breath, a steady, patient heat  
that pressed against the cheek and called the child  
to peer through glass at wonders turning gold.  

I think the soul is made of such as this—  
the residue of kitchens, not of creeds.  
A scent can open what the mind had sealed,  
and suddenly the dead are at the stove,  
and I am small again, and hunger is  
a kind of love, and love a kind of bread  
still warm, still waiting on the counter's edge.  

The room is gone, or else the room remains  
but I have changed, and cannot find the door.  
Yet when the evening settles in my house  
and I have lit the burner, poured the oil,  
a ghost of that old fragrance rises up—  
not mine, not hers, but something in between,  
a bridge of breath across the quiet years.  

And I am fed by what I cannot hold.

title: short lyric poem|the night shift at a diner
text:
The fry cook's name is Earl, and he's been dead
for seven years, but he still comes in
to scrape the flat-top clean at 3 a.m.,
his spatula a slow, arthritic bird.
The waitress, Marla, keeps his coffee cup
behind the register, though no one drinks from it.

The jukebox only plays the B-side now.
The neon sign outside has lost a letter—
it hums "DIN" into the wet black street.
A trucker with a tattoo of a hawk
that's mostly scar by now stirs sugar in
his decaf, asks if we're still serving pie.

We are. The crust is cardboard, cherries canned.
He eats it anyway. The clock above
the door is seven minutes fast, and has been
since '09, when the power flickered out
and something in its guts just gave up trying.

Marla wipes a table no one sat at.
Earl scrapes. The hawk man pays. The rain
starts up again, soft as a cough.
The pie case glows. The coffee turns to tar.
The morning is a rumor we don't trust.

title: ballad in quatrains|a father teaching his daughter to drive
text:
The keys are cold within her hand; he sits
Where sunlight through the windshield makes a haze.
The radio is off. The engine fits
Its idle to the quiet of his gaze.

He shows her how the mirror frames the road—
A silver river narrowing behind.
She adjusts it, nervous, and the load
Of all her watching settles in her mind.

Her foot is hesitant upon the gas;
The car creeps forward like a held-in breath.
He says, *Just ease it,* and the moments pass
As slow as shadows, steadying her death-

Grip on the wheel. The driveway opens wide.
He points: *Now signal. Check your blind spot. Turn.*
She does, and something in her chest and pride
Learns the small language only drivers learn.

The curb approaches. Brakes. A sudden lurch.
He laughs—the first time all day—and she does too.
The maple leans above them like a church
Of green, and all the ordinary blue

Of sky pours through the windows as she tries
Again, and gets it right. He does not say
*Good job*—he simply watches, and his eyes
Are soft with something that has no display.

Backing up, she sees him in the mirror:
A man grown quiet in the passenger seat,
His hands at rest, his teaching drawing nearer
To what cannot be taught—the slow retreat

Of all the miles he'll let her drive alone.
The sun goes down the street. The headlights come
On, pale against the dusk. She drives them home
While he sits back and listens to the hum.

title: spoken-word poem|a mother's hands
text:
The Cartography of Her Hands

I have memorized the map of my mother’s hands.
Not the lines a palm reader would trace,
but the riverbeds of a life lived in service.
I know the topography of her knuckles,
the small, swollen hills that rise with the weather,
the valleys between her fingers, worn smooth
by the constant flow of work and worry.

Her hands are not soft.
They are not the hands of a lady in a portrait,
folded and still.
They are the hands that taught me how to tie my shoes,
her fingers a patient, fumbling knot over my own.
They are the hands that braided my hair,
a gentle, insistent tug that meant *be still, I love you.*

They are the hands that held a thermometer to my lips,
that smoothed a cool cloth across a fevered brow,
that mixed the dough for a thousand loaves of bread,
punching it down, a quiet, rhythmic violence
that turned flour and water into the staff of our lives.

I have seen those hands bleed.
A slip of a knife while dicing onions for a stew
no one would thank her for.
A burn from a hot pan, a splinter from a fence,
a hundred small, unrecorded wars fought for us.
She would suck the wound, wrap it in a cloth,
and go back to the stove.

Her hands are a library of silent stories.
The scar on her thumb from the screen door that slammed in ’89.
The callus on her palm from the handle of a grocery bag,
heavy with the weight of our needs.
The thin, papery skin, now, that bruises at a touch,
a map of fragility I am not ready to read.

These are the hands that held me first.
The hands that formed my world before my eyes could focus.
And now, when I hold them,
they feel smaller than they used to.
They feel like a bird, resting in my own.
I trace the lines, the rivers, the roads,
and I try to memorize the feel of them,
the geography of a love so deep
it carved itself into bone.

I am learning the map by heart.
I am learning the map by heart.

title: pantoum|a lost glove on a fence post
text:
The glove is a flattened starfish on the fence post,
its five splayed fingers stiff with last night's frost.
A vinyl palm turned up as if to check for rain,
the cuff a bracelet of mouse-grey ice.

Its five splayed fingers stiff with last night's frost,
the thumb's a hitchhiker going nowhere, heading west.
The cuff, a bracelet of mouse-grey ice,
holds the blue ghost of a wrist that pulled it off.

The thumb's a hitchhiker going nowhere, heading west,
past the dead corn's paper skeletons, the ditch's tinny creek.
It holds the blue ghost of a wrist that pulled it off
to fish a phone from a pocket, or point at a hawk.

Past the dead corn's paper skeletons, the ditch's tinny creek,
a school bus groans its gears and does not stop.
To fish a phone from a pocket, or point at a hawk—
the reason's gone, dissolved like breath in the cold.

A school bus groans its gears and does not stop.
The glove is a flattened starfish on the fence post,
the reason gone, dissolved like breath in the cold,
a vinyl palm turned up as if to check for rain.

title: Petrarchan sonnet|a phone call from a long-lost brother
text:
The Long-Distance Call

The phone rang sharp against the quiet night,
a number strange, unknown to my routine;
I answered, and a voice came through the line—
half-recognized, then blazing into light.
Five years of silence vanished in that slight
and trembling breath, that hesitant design
of words held back too long. "It's me. I'm fine."
The kitchen tilted, everything too bright.

We spoke of nothing much—the rain, the cold,
a town he'd left, the coffee going stale—
and all the while the years we never told
lay stacked between us, fragile, thin, and pale.
He said he'd call again. I heard him go.
The dial tone hummed the things I didn't know.

title: poem in tercets|a mother's hands
text:
She kept a paring knife in the glove box
for peaches from the stand off Route 9,
wiped the blade on her jeans, said the fuzz

gets everywhere. Her knuckles went white
gripping the wheel through the construction
the summer they rerouted everything downtown.

There's a scar like a comma under her thumb
from the screen door that slammed on the Fourth,
and she'd hold my chin to dab the Bactine,

thumb pressed to my lip to keep me still.
She could find a splinter in bad light,
work it loose with a needle she'd singe first,

tell me not to be a baby. The nails
were always short. She bit them at red lights.
She'd fold her hands in her lap at the doctor's

and I watched them there, two animals
she'd brought along and taught to sit.
Now they shake a little pouring the coffee,

and she hides it, turns toward the window,
says the pills make her tired, says
the tree by the fence needs cutting back.

title: villanelle|a soldier writing home
text:
The candle gutters; ink runs thin and slow.
He prints each word with care upon the page.
The distant guns thud out their status quo.

He tells her of the mud, the rain, the snow,
the sergeant’s cough, the rations, and the rage.
The candle gutters; ink runs thin and slow.

He does not write the things she must not know:
the field of boots, the boy who was his age.
The distant guns thud out their status quo.

He draws a crooked heart, a bird, a bow,
a house, a sun, a garden and a cage.
The candle gutters; ink runs thin and slow.

Outside, the wire hums. The searchlights glow.
A rat goes nosing through the equipage.
The distant guns thud out their status quo.

He signs his name. The dawn is coming. Oh,
he folds the letter once, and takes the stage
of mud and wire. Ink runs thin and slow.
The distant guns thud out their status quo.

title: elegy|a beekeeper in winter
text:
I. The Hives at Dusk

The hives sit like small coffins in the snow,
each entrance stopped with wire and breath of straw.
He walks the row and lays a gloved hand low
against the boards, and feels no hum, no thaw—
just wind that worries at the lid,
and all the summer's golden roar gone dead.
He counts them twice, as if he always did,
and turns for home with nothing in his head
but smoke and clover, and the weight of comb.

II. The Kettle

Indoors, he boils the water, holds his cup,
and hears, or thinks he hears, a distant drone
inside the pipes—the house remembering, grown
strange with winter. Once he kept them up
past dark, the lantern warm, the frames alive
with thirty thousand small machineries.
Now snow ticks at the glass, and nothing thrives
but steam, and the slow arithmetic of bees
he reckons in his chair: the cluster's heat,
the queen at center, turning in her sleep.

III. First Thaw

By March he's at the apiary before
the ice has left the ditches, prying lids,
and finds them—some—still clinging to the floor,
a fist of bees gone cold beneath the skids.
He brushes out the dead with careful hands,
sets sugar cakes, and waits on warmer days,
and does not say what every keeper understands:
the ones that live will carry on the ways
of all small kingdoms—hive and hum and loss—
and he will keep them, though he counts the cost.

title: poem in tercets|drought on a family farm
text:
The cenotaph of the combine’s shadow
stretches a full half-mile by noon.
It is a sundial for the end of the world.

My father checks the rain gauge again,
a polished brass collection of emptiness.
He taps the glass like a thermometer.

The creek is a rumor the cows repeat
in their lowing, a story of water
they tell each other in the shade of the pump house.

The well coughs up its last coin:
a single, brown salamander
who blinks at the language of light.

We eat supper with the windows open
so the house can listen for thunder.
The plates are cool against our wrists.

title: short lyric poem|a lighthouse keeper's last night on duty
text:
The Last Light

The lamp still turns its patient eye
across the dark, unanswering sea.
Tomorrow they will come, and I
will hand the keys, and I'll be free.

For forty years the salt has worn
my hands, my window, and my name.
Tonight I keep the light reborn
and hold its small, familiar flame.

No ship to save, no storm to brave—
just fog, and stars, and one long beam
that sweeps the water like a wave
and folds my lifetime into dream.

title: villanelle|first snow in a hospital parking lot
text:
The flake came down like a lost pill, then another,
on the windshield of my father’s Corolla.
First snow, and the lot hummed with the generator.

I’d parked in Row C, near the dripping gutter,
holding his glasses case and his blue umbrella.
The flake came down like a lost pill, then another.

A nurse in scrubs smoked fast, cupping the weather,
her lighter sputtering. She said, *This’ll be over
by noon.* First snow, and the lot hummed with the generator.

I scraped a circle clear with a credit card’s edge—later
I’d find the card cracked, the numbers smeared to blur.
The flake came down like a lost pill, then another.

My father slept inside, tethered to a monitor.
His room smelled of wet wool and hand sanitizer.
First snow, and the lot hummed with the generator.

The salt truck idled. Someone’s radio played a low, slurred
jazz. I watched the white erase the yellow lines, the tire
tracks. The flake came down like a lost pill, then another.
First snow, and the lot hummed with the generator.

title: villanelle|drought on a family farm
text:
The creek bed's a scar of cracked clay,
The tractor sits rusting in dust.
My father walks the fields each day.

The corn rows have nothing to say—
Stalks like bent wires, black and unjust.
The creek bed's a scar of cracked clay.

My mother scans a sky of gray,
Her garden a socket of trust.
My father walks the fields each day.

The well coughs its last, they say;
The windmill's blades grind rust.
The creek bed's a scar of cracked clay.

The mortgage letter comes to stay.
The bank's voice is thin as dust.
My father walks the fields each day.

At dusk the swallows drift away.
The porch light gathers rust.
The creek bed's a scar of cracked clay.
My father walks the fields each day.

title: spoken-word poem|moving out of a childhood home
text:
Part I: The Inventory of Ghosts

I am walking through these rooms like a museum after hours,
my footsteps the only sound against the hardwood floors that taught me how to dance.
I’m tracing the grooves in the doorframe where my height was a climbing vine,
stretching towards a sky I thought I’d never reach.
Every scuff on the wall is a fossil of a tantrum,
every stain on the carpet is a map of a spill I swore I’d clean.
I am packing up the echoes,
folding the laughter into cardboard boxes,
wrapping the shouting in newspaper.
It’s strange how a house holds your history in its bones,
how the plaster breathes out your childhood
and the windows hold the reflection of every version of you that ever looked out.
I am taking the pictures off the hooks,
leaving behind perfect, sun-bleached squares of paint—
little portals to the past that I can’t take with me.

Part II: The Weight of Boxes

Cardboard is heavier than it looks.
It’s not the books or the plates or the winter coats,
it’s the gravity of the memories packed tight inside.
I’m taping up the flaps on a decade of my life,
sealing it with the screech of the dispenser.
My hands are paper-cut and tired,
lifting the sum total of my existence into a rental truck.
I find a toy under the radiator, dust-covered and forgotten,
and I hold it like a relic, a shard of a time when the world was small enough to fit in this room.
We are stripping the beds,
leaving the mattresses bare like blank pages,
and the silence in the hallway is deafening.
It’s the sound of a chapter closing,
the heavy, hollow thud of a door pulling shut.
I am carrying my home in my arms,
but it feels lighter than it should,
because the home was never just the wood and the nails,
it was the people,
and they are scattering like seeds in the wind.

Part III: The Key and the Horizon

I stand on the porch with the key in my palm,
a small, cold piece of metal that no longer belongs to me.
I turn it one last time in the lock,
listening to the click that sounds like a gunshot in the quiet afternoon.
This is the place where I learned to ride a bike,
where I cried over broken hearts,
where I dreamed of a future that looked exactly like this moment—
standing on the edge of the unknown.
I slip the key under the mat for the next stranger,
the next family who will fill these walls with their own noise.
I walk down the driveway, and I don’t look back.
The horizon is wide and terrifying and bright.
I am leaving the safety of the known,
stepping out of the frame of the photograph,
and becoming the person I was always meant to be,
somewhere else.

title: elegy|tide pools and hermit crabs
text:
The Small Kingdoms

The tides have gone and left their dead—
a shard of shell, a weed of red,
the bladderwrack's forgotten thread
        among the stones.

Here in the hollows, cool and clear,
the hermit crabs convene, and steer
their borrowed houses, nothing near
        to call their own.

How patient, in the ebbing light,
they drag their armor through the night
of pooled seawater, taking flight
        from stone to stone.

They trade their dwellings, shell for shell,
each spiral a brief citadel,
a kingdom where the breakers fell
        and left them peace.

But tide will turn and tide will take
the little walls the waters make,
and every small and scuttling wake
        will find release.

O pilgrims in a borrowed coat,
who drag your houses, rock to float,
who ask no more than just to note
        the water's grace—

the pools will dry, the moon will pull,
the sea come back and make them full,
and find each wanderer, beautiful,
        in his small place.

title: elegy|first snow in a hospital parking lot
text:
First Snow in a Hospital Parking Lot

The flakes came down like tiny, unread notes
dropped from a sky that had no one to tell.
They settled on the windshields, on the roofs
of cars that had been waiting since first light,
and on the wheelchair ramp their thin white fell
as if to soften what the building keeps.

Beneath the sodium lamps the snow turned slow,
each flake a small delay of gravity,
and in the lot the painted arrows drowned
under a gentleness no one had asked.
A nurse stood smoking by the ER door;
her breath and the snow exchanged a brief hello.

Somewhere inside, a monitor kept time.
Somewhere outside, the plows would come by dawn.
But for an hour the world forgot its rush
and let the falling be the only sound—
as if the lot, the lamps, the idling dark
were granted one white page to start again.

I watched a single flake land on a scar
of asphalt where the ambulances turn,
and thought how snow is just the sky's attempt
to lay a hand on everything at once.
It does not last. It does not mean to stay.
It only means to say: I was here too.

title: dramatic monologue|the four seasons of an orchard
text:
My grandfather planted these trees the year the well went dry.
He said, "We'll eat apples or we'll eat dust,"
and my grandmother just looked at him
the way she looked at weather she couldn't argue with.

Spring comes in like a cough through the house—
the buds break and I think of his hands,
knuckle-cracked, wrapping twine around a whip-thin trunk.
I still find his coffee cups behind the barn.
I don't move them. The rain doesn't either.
The bees come back. They don't remember me.

Summer, the orchard is a green roar,
and the heat sits on the rows like something alive.
My daughter was born in July. I carried her out here
before she had a name, and the light through the leaves
made stripes across her face like a small convict
of this place, this dirt, this stubborn row of trees.
She's twelve now. She hates the picking.
She says the apples smell like rot. She's not wrong.

Then the yellow, and the ladders, and the cold hands.
The cider press squeals like a pig and I let it.
My back is a map of every season I've stood here.
The deer come down at dusk and take what they take.
I don't begrudge them. I've taken too.

Winter, and the orchard is a skeleton I know by heart.
I walk the rows and count the ones that split in the ice.
Three this year. I'll cut them in the spring.
The snow makes everything look forgiven.
It doesn't mean it is.

My grandmother died in February. She never liked the trees.
She said they took too long to say anything.
I'm standing in the cold now, listening.
They're still not saying anything.
I'm still here.

title: poem in tercets|fishing with an uncle who never talks
text:
The lake is a flattened coin of light.
He rows. The oarlocks keep their slow complaint.
A dragonfly sews shut the afternoon.

*

My rod is borrowed. Still, the line goes down
through tea-brown water, past the sunken leaves,
to where the perch hold their cold positions.

*

He clips a sinker with his thumbnail, spits,
and hands me back the rig. That’s the whole lesson.
His silence has a grain to it, like wood.

*

Across the bay a loon repeats one note
until the hills agree. He does not turn.
The cigarette between his fingers burns

*

a slow inch toward the knuckle. Once, a fish
broke water like a struck match, and I swear
his shadow almost smiled. The shadow knows

*

how to keep still. The dock comes back in view
the way a word comes back when you’ve forgot
you’ve been forgetting it. He ships the oars.

*

The minnows stitch their silver into rings.
He ties the boat. He does not say a thing.
The whole lake settles in him like a stone.

title: spoken-word poem|a nurse finishing a twelve-hour shift
text:
I. Handover

The clock hands crawl to seven,
and I hand over the worst of it—
bed four’s blood pressure, still a stubborn secret,
bed nine’s daughter, who cries louder than her mother,
the man in twelve who calls me “angel” and means “wait.”
I give my clipboard the weight of a small life.
I give the next shift my tired, practiced smile.
The hallway exhales.
The fluorescent lights stop humming my name.

II. Scrubs

I peel the day off in the bathroom,
scrubs stiff with coffee and courage.
There’s a stain on the sleeve I can’t name,
so I name it “Tuesday.”
The mirror shows a woman with creases
where her face used to be smooth,
hair escaping like it’s been running
from something twelve hours long.
I wash my hands one more time—
not for hygiene now, just for the ritual,
the warm water a small forgiveness.

III. Bus Stop

The streetlight blinks like a monitor
I’m no longer watching.
I sit on the bench and let the night
give me back to myself,
one breath at a time.
Somewhere behind me, the hospital
keeps its vigil without me—
and that’s the whole job, isn’t it:
to hold, and then to let go,
to walk home under a sky
that doesn’t need my charting.
The bus comes. I board. I am, for now,
nobody’s emergency.

title: free verse poem|a lighthouse keeper's last night on duty
text:
The Last Light

The lamp hums its old familiar hymn,
a sound he’s known for forty years,
since he was young and storms were just
a reason to stand watch.

Tonight the sea is calm,
a liar’s calm, he thinks,
flat as a table of dark glass.
The beam sweeps out its patient arm
and finds no one to warn.

He climbs the spiral one last time,
his hand on the cold iron rail
that knows the shape of his grip.
Each step a word in a sentence ending.
At the top, the great lens turns,
slow as a planet,
throwing its white blade over the water
and pulling it back.

He thinks of all the ships he never saw,
the ones the light saved
without a single witness,
the ones it didn’t.
He thinks of the logbook’s blank last page
and the pen he’ll leave beside it.

Tomorrow a new keeper comes,
younger, with steadier hands,
and the light will go on turning
as if nothing has been lost.
But tonight it is his.
The salt on the glass, the smell of oil,
the whole dark Atlantic waiting
for the one thing he has to give.

He watches the beam go out
and come back, out and back,
a heartbeat over black water,
and he lets it beat
until the gray line of morning
opens like a door.

Then he turns the switch.
The great eye closes.
The silence that rushes in
is the loudest thing he’s ever heard.

title: pantoum|a phone call from a long-lost brother
text:
The screen lit up: a number I didn't know,
some area code from a state I'd never been.
I let it ring twice more. The ice machine
down the hall shuddered, then went slow.

Some area code from a state I'd never been—
I answered standing up, a dumb reflex.
Down the hall the ice machine shuddered, then
went quiet. His voice came through the static, vexed

and older. I answered standing up—a dumb reflex
I blamed on my knees. He said my name like a test.
Went quiet. His voice came through the static, vexed
by twenty years of nothing. The window's west

light bled across the counter. He said my name like a test,
then talked about a boat he'd almost bought,
by twenty years of nothing. The window's west
face held a truck's red taillight, caught

then gone. He talked about a boat. He'd almost bought
a house near water where the paper mill
still runs. A truck's red taillight caught
in the glass and dragged its color down the sill.

A house near water. Where the paper mill
spat steam all night, he said. I heard him draw
a breath and hold it. The light slid down the sill.
I said the word for him I barely knew:

spat steam. All night. I heard him draw
a breath like hauling anchor. Somewhere a door
slammed twice. I said the name I barely knew,
and he repeated it—a knock, a hinge, the floor

giving beneath us both. Somewhere a door.
I let the silence do its slow arithmetic.
He repeated my name—a knock, a hinge. The floor
was cold. Outside, one star, thin and sick.

I let the silence do its slow arithmetic.
He said he had to go. The ice machine
kicked on. Outside, one star, thin and sick.
The screen went dark. I stood there, seventeen

again, and told the window he had to go.
The ice machine settled. Then it, too, went slow.

title: dramatic monologue|migrating geese over a frozen lake
text:
The ice came early that year. I remember
because my father was still in the hospital in Duluth
and I was driving back and forth on 35,
and the lake by the casino was already locked up,
gray as a nickel, and the geese kept circling.
They kept circling. That's what I remember.
Fifty of them maybe, bugling that broken horn sound,
coming down and finding nothing but a hard shine,
a floor that wouldn't take them, and going up again,
and coming down, and up. For an hour.
My wipers were shot, streaking the glass,
and I just sat there at the boat launch with the engine off
and the cold coming through the door seals,
watching them try. My father used to hunt them.
He had a call he could make with his throat.
He'd say, *listen, they're asking the water a question.*
The water never answered for him either,
not the way he wanted. Toward dusk
the flock gave up and went on south
or maybe just to the open channel by the power plant—
you never know where they end up.
I drove to the hospital. He was asleep.
The TV was on with the sound off.
I didn't wake him. There was a smell of green Jell-O
and something under it, something like copper.
I sat in the chair that doesn't pull out to a bed
and watched his chest go up and down, up and down,
and thought how a lake freezes from the top down,
so the fish are down there in the dark
all winter, just hanging in it, slow as old men,
and I ate his Jell-O. I did. I ate it.
I was hungry and he wasn't eating.
That's the whole thing, I guess. The ice
takes what it takes and the rest of us
drive home in the dark with the heat on high.

title: free verse poem|teenage summer jobs
text:
The summer I turned sixteen, I worked
the early shift at Miller's Garden Center,
seven to noon, before the heat came down
like a lid on the greenhouse.

I learned the weight of water—
how a full can pulls your shoulder
from its socket, how the hose
writhes like something alive
and you have to hold it like a snake.

The petunias didn't care
that I was tired. They opened
their pink mouths anyway,
demanding. I respected that.

At noon I'd walk home
with dirt in the creases of my hands,
my shirt stuck to my back,
the smell of fertilizer and gasoline
following me like a second self.

My mother would say, *You smell
like a farm*, and I'd stand in the shower
until the water ran cold,
watching the soil spiral down the drain
like something I was supposed to keep.

I made ninety dollars a week
and spent it on gas and a used guitar
I never learned to play well.
But I learned the weight of things—
a flat of marigolds, a bag of mulch,
the long afternoon before the rain came,
the way the world asks you to carry
what it gives you, even when
your arms are full.

title: ghazal|learning a second language as an adult
text:
I. First Lessons

The tongue I borrow stumbles on the loan.
Each word a stranger, met but not yet known.

I conjugate by lamplight, tense by tense,
and hear my mother's language overthrown.

A noun arrives without its gender, lost
like luggage on a carousel alone.

The teacher says the accent lives in breath—
I breathe, and hear the old world in my own.

II. The Marketplace

I barter grammar for a loaf of bread.
The baker frowns; my sentence goes unfed.

At night the dictionary keeps me warm,
its pages whispering what I should have said.

A child corrects me at the bus stop, kind
as only children are. My face goes red.

Somewhere between the verb I meant and spoke,
a second self is quietly being bred.

III. Second Nature

One morning I awoke and dreamed in it—
the borrowed river deepening its bed.

I catch myself mid-thought, no longer translating,
the way a scar forgets that it once bled.

Two languages now quarrel in my mouth
like sisters sharing one ancestral bed.

I am not fluent; fluent is a shore
the swimmer never reaches. Still I tread.

title: prose poem|a father teaching his daughter to drive
text:
The Lesson

The car is a second classroom, and my father is the teacher again, though the subject has changed from long division to the language of the road. He sits beside me, a calm navigator in the passenger seat, his hands resting on his knees as if in prayer, though I know he is praying for the brakes. The cul-de-sac becomes our practice field, a loop of asphalt where I learn the weight of the wheel, the tentative pressure of the gas pedal, the way a car breathes when you let it. He speaks in a low, even voice, a metronome of instruction: *easy now... look ahead... feel where you want to go.* I am all elbows and apologies, jerking the wheel, overcorrecting, a colt on ice. But he never flinches, only says, *try again,* as if the world has endless second chances. And in that small, contained space, I feel the strange intimacy of this transfer of power—his foot hovering over the invisible brake on his side, my foot learning the courage of the other. He is teaching me to move forward, and I am learning to leave him, one slow revolution of the cul-de-sac at a time.

title: blank verse meditation|tide pools and hermit crabs
text:
The water pulls back from the shelf of stone
and leaves a world of small, specific hungers.
A pool the size of a cereal bowl holds
a violet urchin, a fist of mussels, and the husk
of a crab, its legs still jointed, still articulate
in the cool air. The hermit crab is a tenant
in a spiral condominium, a scavenger
who drags his borrowed architecture over the grit.
He tests the lip of a periwinkle shell,
his body a soft, pale comma of need.
The tide is a landlord who will return.
For now, the anemone’s tentacles are furled,
a crown of wet petals closed against the sun.
A sculpin holds its ground in a seam of water,
its eye a bead of oil. The light is a blade
that pares the surface. Everything here
is a negotiation: the snail’s rasp on the glass,
the barnacle’s glue, the starfish’s slow, patient arm
prying the world open. I watch the crab
reverse himself, haul his house across a ridge
of coralline algae, and disappear
into a crevice. The pool ticks and settles.
It is a small, salt-stung economy
of take and hold. The ocean is a mumble
at the edge of hearing, a promise
it will keep. I leave the crab to his fierce
domesticity, his hinge of fear and want,
and the pool to its brief, brilliant argument
with the air. The sun climbs. The water
begins its slow retreat from the rock,
leaving a rind of salt, a silvered edge.

title: ode|a beekeeper in winter
text:
Ode to the Beekeeper in Winter

The hives stand hushed beneath a shroud of snow,
like little monasteries locked in prayer.
You walk among them, booted, breathing slow,
and listen for the hum that isn't there—
or is it? Faint as memory below
the frost-locked lid, a clustered warmth somewhere
that dreams of clover fields and summer's glow
while winter whittles everything to bare.

You mend the frames, you patch the wind's assault,
you bank the straw against the bitter chill.
You read the quiet like a sacred text,
and count the losses, and forgive the rest.
The smoke-cold air has taught you what comes next:
to tend the dark, and wait, and trust the small.

title: elegy|learning a second language as an adult
text:
The Noun Cases of Snow

Tonight the window is a textbook I can’t close.
Each flake declines itself against the glass—
a language I have studied for ten years
and still pronounce like something breaking.

In the kitchen, my mother’s tongue
sits in a jar of brine, unopened.
I hold my mouth the way one holds a key
to a house already sold. The radiators knock
in iambs I was never taught to hear.

Somewhere a child is conjugating snow
without effort, the way birds
do not practice migration. I watch her
through the double pane—her mittened hand
catching what I only name.

The grammar of belonging is a cold room.
I have learned the future tense of leaving:
*I will have gone. I will have spoken.*
But the past is a village under snow,
its smoke still rising in my throat.

By morning, the plow will erase the street.
I will stand at the sink, rinsing a cup,
and practice the word for *home*
until it means the shape of my own breath
fogging the glass—a small, imperfect noun
I keep declining, declining, declining.

title: ghazal|autumn leaves in a cemetery
text:
I. Falling

The maples shed their copper coins on stone—
a currency the wind will spend alone.
Each name engraved is softened by the drift
of rust and ochre settling bone by bone.
The mourners come and go; the leaves remain,
a congregation gathering unknown.
What falls is not forgotten, only changed—
the cemetery keeps what it has sown.

II. Interment

Between the headstones, leaf on leaf is laid
like letters in a language undecayed.
The caretaker's rake gathers them in rows,
an alphabet of amber, unafraid.
Rain presses them like seals against the ground;
the earth receives the tithe that autumn paid.
Beneath the frost, a slow and patient ink
rewrites the names the granite has portrayed.

III. Rite

The last leaf lets go—a small, unsponsored prayer
that finds no heaven, only open air.
It settles where the yew tree keeps its shade
and joins the others sleeping unaware.
Who grieves the leaf? The season does, and moves
on to the next, and next, with patient care.
The gate swings shut. The wind resumes its psalm.
The stones stand vigil. Nothing is elsewhere.

title: pantoum|time and memory
text:
The Hourglass We Carry

The clock forgets what it has said.
The hours fall like grains of sand.
A voice still whispers in my head
of things I no longer understand.

The hours fall like grains of sand;
the past is never truly gone.
Of things I no longer understand,
a faded photograph lives on.

The past is never truly gone—
it hums beneath the present's floor.
A faded photograph lives on
behind a locked and painted door.

It hums beneath the present's floor,
a voice still whispering in my head.
Behind a locked and painted door,
the clock forgets what it has said.

title: poem in tercets|an old piano left on the curb
text:
The bench is gone. Someone has propped a clay pot
where the sheet music used to lean, holding a dead
geranium. The lid, propped open, is a black mouth

full of broken teeth. When the wind moves,
it doesn't make a sound. It's not that kind of ghost.
A sticker on the fallboard says *Free*, the ink

bled to a blue bruise by last week's rain.
My neighbor, Mrs. K, says she heard it played
once, through a wall, in 1982. A hymn, she thinks.

The middle-C key is a yellow tooth.
The pedals are two tarnished coins
no one will ever spend. I think of my own hands,

how they've forgotten the shape of a scale,
how they only know how to hold a phone, a mug, a leash.
A boy walks by and hits one low note with his palm.

The sound is a cough from a basement.
It hangs in the air, a dust mote, then is gone.
The streetlight will come on soon and make it a monument

to nothing. To the space between a hand and a key.
To the long, slow weather of being left behind.
I don't take it. I just stand here, listening

to the silence it has become, a heavy, carved thing
on the curb, waiting for the truck, for the men
who will grunt it into the back and drive it away.

title: blank verse meditation|a forest fire seen from far away
text:
From a Distant Ridge

The evening holds a smudge of orange light
above the tree line, far enough that I
can watch it without turning in my bed.
The smoke climbs slow and leans against the sky
like something tired, unwilling to let go.
I think of all the small and nameless lives
that go unsung in any chronicle—
the beetle working underneath the bark,
the owl whose eyes have never known a word,
the seed that waited years to open up.
The fire takes them without taking note,
and yet the forest will come back, they say,
in time, in green, in unremembered springs.
I stand here on this ridge and do not move.
The distance makes a kindness of the sight,
and I accept it, knowing what it costs.

title: ballad in quatrains|a lighthouse keeper's last night on duty
text:
The coffee's cold. The kettle's dry.
The window shows a quarter moon.
I've walked these stairs so many times
I know which step is loose.

The brass rail's polished where my hand
has worn it, thirty years.
The logbook's got a coffee ring
from 1982.

The light goes round. The light goes round.
The ships go by. The ships go by.
I've seen a thousand hulls slide past
and never learned one name.

My wife is dead. My son's in Perth.
The dog is getting old.
I wrote the roster for the spring
in pencil, in the dark.

The foghorn test at four a.m.
still makes me flinch. The gulls
have learned my habits, or I've learned
to read their squabbling.

Last week a tanker lost its power
and drifted past the Point.
I watched the lifeboat putt-putt out
and did the thing I do.

The light goes round. The light goes round.
The coffee's cold again.
I'll leave the logbook as it is.
The kettle's stayed dry all night.

By six the relief will come up the path,
young fellow, new boots, doesn't know
the loose step. Let him find it.
I'll hand him the brass key and go.

title: prose poem|the smell of a grandmother's kitchen
text:
I. Yeast

Before I reach the door, the air has already opened its arms: warm flour, damp and breathing, a sweetness that rises like a slow tide. The oven clicks and ticks, keeping time with something older than clocks. I am small again on the linoleum, waiting for the dough to forgive me for wanting it too soon.

II. Smoke and Onion

Later the kitchen turns honest—bacon fat spitting its gossip, onions going soft and gold in the pan, a whisper of vinegar sharp enough to make my eyes remember her hands. She hums off-key and stirs, and the smell wraps around me like a coat I've outgrown but refuse to give away.

III. Sugar Dust

And at the end, the sweet hush: cinnamon settled into the curtains, vanilla lingering in the corners like a secret, powdered sugar drifting down over everything—her apron, the counter, my hair. Years from now, in some other kitchen, one breath of it will bring this room back whole, and she will still be here, humming, dusted in light.

title: ballad in quatrains|commuting on a crowded subway
text:
The Underground Tide

The platform hums a hollow tune,
The clock above is running late;
We stand beneath the sodium moon
And for the opening iron wait.

The doors slide back with grinding groan,
A wave of shoulders, coats, and knees;
We pack the car and claim our own
Small space with practiced expertise.

The train begins its lurching flight,
A hundred faces, blank and worn;
We sway together through the night
Like reeds by unseen currents torn.

A stranger's elbow finds my side,
A briefcase pressed against my spine;
We ride the dark, relentless tide
And never once give up our line.

The speaker crackles out a name,
A few slip free and disappear;
The rest of us remain the same,
Still pressed and patient, year by year.

At last my station's signal glows,
I squeeze and stumble toward the light;
The metal serpent sighs and goes,
And leaves me to the breathing night.

title: elegy|a lost glove on a fence post
text:
Not laundered, not buried, but posted here
like a notice for a dog that never learned
its name. Five fingers of wet wool
gone stiff as a starfish in the cold,
a mitten’s cousin, the left one, the one
that always knew the combination lock
of my pocket. Somewhere a hand
is making a fist around nothing,
a coin slot of a hand, a hand that pats
its own thigh in the checkout line
like a man checking for his heart.
The fence wire hums its one note.
The glove points nowhere, thumb up,
a tiny hitchhiker from a country
where the roads are all sleeves.
It has forgotten the oven door,
the steering wheel, the small warm neck
of a beer. It is becoming weather.
By spring it will be a husk of salt,
a rumor of lint. But tonight
the porch light finds it and mistakes it
for a hand waving goodbye, and waves back.

title: pantoum|a small-town Friday football game
text:
Friday Night in a Small Town

The stadium lights hum low above the field,
and folding chairs are gathered on the grass.
The autumn air is warm, the stands are filled—
a Friday night that seems too good to pass.

And folding chairs are gathered on the grass,
the marching band rehearsing in the cold.
A Friday night that seems too good to pass,
as cheerleaders shake their silver and gold.

The marching band rehearsing in the cold,
the popcorn stand is busy with a line.
As cheerleaders shake their silver and gold,
the hometown crowd is doing fine.

The popcorn stand is busy with a line,
the quarterback is nervous in the huddle.
The hometown crowd is doing fine
beneath the lights, a warm and rowdy huddle.

The quarterback is nervous in the huddle,
the coach is pacing, shouting out a play.
Beneath the lights, a warm and rowdy huddle,
the score is tied with seconds left to play.

The coach is pacing, shouting out a play,
the autumn air is warm, the stands are filled.
The score is tied with seconds left to play—
the stadium lights hum low above the field.

title: spoken-word poem|a library on a Sunday afternoon
text:
The radiator’s ticking like a cooled-down engine.
Someone’s left a nectarine pit
on the windowsill by the large-print westerns.
I know because I sit here every Sunday,
third carrel from the reference desk,
where the light comes through the grille
and makes a zebra of my arm.

A boy in a too-big hoodie
is reading about volcanoes
and breathing through his mouth.
His mother mouths the words
of a picture book to his sister—
*the bear went over the mountain*—
and the sister says, *again*,
and the mother says, *in a minute*,
and doesn’t.

Down the aisle, a man with a laptop
is crying very quietly
at a spreadsheet.
I pretend not to see.
The clock above the biographies
has been eight minutes slow since April.
Nobody fixes it. It’s a kind of agreement.

I came here to write a letter
to my father, who is dead,
but instead I’m reading the same paragraph
about the mating habits of the caddisfly
over and over, and thinking
about the sandwich in my bag,
the way the mustard has probably
soaked through the bread by now,
the way my mother used to cut them
on the diagonal, said it made them
taste better, and it did.

The radiator ticks.
The boy turns a page.
The nectarine pit dries in the sun.
Outside, a car door slams,
and someone laughs at something
I will never know,
and the slow clock holds its breath,
and the caddisfly, in its little case of sticks,
goes on building toward nothing
in particular, which is, I think,
the whole trick of it.

title: free verse poem|a factory town after the plant closed
text:
The last whistle hangs in the air like a struck bell
no one has the strength to ring again.
Windows along the main street hold their breath—
glass eyes that watched the gates swing shut
and memorized the shape of leaving.

The water tower still spells the company name
in letters the rust is slowly eating.
At dusk it leans its shadow across the roofs
like a hand withdrawn too late.

In the lot where trucks once idled, gravel
grows a thin beard of weeds.
Someone's father's lunchbox, dented, blue,
turns up in a drawer, still smelling faintly
of bologna and machine oil.

The river keeps its old habit, going
the only way it knows.
Herons stand in the shallows like unpaid debts,
patient, unmoving, waiting for a fish
that learned to swim in darker water.

On the porch, a woman waters geraniums
she planted the spring the layoffs came.
She waters them every evening,
the way some people pray—
not expecting an answer,
just needing the sound of water
falling on something still alive.

title: ode|time and memory
text:
Ode to the Keepers of the Hour

O Time, unseen and ceaseless architect,
who lays the cornerstone of every day,
who bids the moment rise and then defect
on silent feet that never lose their way—
you carve the world with patient, passing hands,
yet leave behind, upon the shifting sands,
a gift more durable than stone or steel:
the memory, which makes the fleeting real.

For what is time but motion without trace,
a river running nameless to the sea,
until the mind, in some still, sacred place,
lifts up the past and bids it stay with me?
O Memory, twin sister, keeper dear,
who gathers what the hours scatter far,
you hold the laughter of a vanished year
and keep it bright, a small and steadfast star.

Together, Time and Memory, you weave
the fabric of the self, the thread of years;
the moment that we lose, you both retrieve,
and make of passing days a thing that cheers.
The scent of rain on summer's long-ago,
the cadence of a voice no longer near—
you grant them life, and in their living show
that nothing truly loved is lost to fear.

So let the clock advance, the seasons turn,
and let the hair grow silver with the frost;
the heart has lessons it will always learn
from holding dear the things it counted lost.
O Time, who takes, and Memory, who gives,
I praise you both, who make me what I am—
for in the mind, the vanished moment lives,
and in the living, time becomes a psalm.

title: elegy|fishing with an uncle who never talks
text:
The tackle box is a reliquary
of hooks, each in its own
compartment, like the teeth
of a small, patient animal.
He opens it with a click
that is the only sound
he makes for hours.

The lake is a flat, gray eye
that doesn't blink. My uncle
is a man made of elbows and silence,
his line a single, taut nerve
sent down into the dark.
He reels in nothing, casts again.
The lure, a plastic minnow,
wobbles its lie through the water.

I am learning the grammar
of the unsaid. The way a grunt
can mean *pass the pliers*.
The way a long exhale
through the nose means *no*.
The bobber is a red and white
punctuation mark, a period
at the end of a long, watery sentence.

Once, he caught a boot.
Once, a turtle, which he freed
with a quiet, practiced violence.
The sun bakes the mud.
The dragonflies are tiny, electric
blueprints for a machine
that only hovers.

This is the inheritance:
a dented aluminum boat,
the smell of gasoline and scales,
and this quiet that is not empty
but full, like a jar
of pond water held to the light,
swarming with a life
you can't name, that doesn't need you
to speak its name to go on living.

title: pantoum|a factory town after the plant closed
text:
The Quiet Lot

The factory town forgets the sound of steel.
Its windows hold the gray of empty days.
The whistle's ghost has nothing left to feel.
The streets repeat their slow, unwinding ways.

Its windows hold the gray of empty days.
The diner's stools are turned toward the door.
The streets repeat their slow, unwinding ways.
The river carries what it carried before.

The diner's stools are turned toward the door.
A lunch pail rusts where grass has come to stay.
The river carries what it carried before.
The smoke has thinned and drifted far away.

A lunch pail rusts where grass has come to stay.
The whistle's ghost has nothing left to feel.
The smoke has thinned and drifted far away.
The factory town forgets the sound of steel.

title: sequence of haiku|a jazz club in the rain
text:
Rain on the awning—
the doorman lets me in
without checking my hand.

Third stool from the end.
Wet coat steaming on the back.
The piano starts late.

Her left hand, I swear,
finds the note the radiator
was already humming.

Somebody's umbrella
drips a slow counterpoint
under "Body and Soul."

Two drinks in,
I can't tell the bass from
the pipes in the wall.

The drummer sweats through
his shirt. The window sweats through
its one neon word.

She plays the wrong chord,
once, on purpose, and grins
at no one I can see.

Last call. The rain
hasn't quit. Neither has
the ride home I'm not taking.

title: sequence of haiku|a factory town after the plant closed
text:
Shuttered windows gleam—
the gate chain's orange rust blooms
where shifts once entered.

Empty parking lot,
a single crow lifts and lands
on the "HIRING" sign.

Smokestack silhouette
learning the shape of silence—
first snow fills its mouth.

The company store
still spells its name in peeled paint;
someone's wiped the dust
from one small window
to watch the street go nowhere—
dusk, then the streetlights.

title: villanelle|a small-town Friday football game
text:
I. The Field at Dusk

The field at dusk is lined with chalk and light,
and cars arrive in rows of dust and chrome.
Small-town Friday holds its breath tonight.

The band files in beneath the falling white
of stadium lamps that call the faithful home.
The field at dusk is lined with chalk and light.

The cheerleaders rehearse their silver flight,
the popcorn warms, the bleachers fill with home-
town voices: Friday holds its breath tonight.

The quarterback, still small beneath the height
of stands, looks up and finds the crowd his own.
The field at dusk is lined with chalk and light.

A father points, a child holds on too tight,
and strangers nod like neighbors they have known.
Small-town Friday holds its breath tonight.

The whistle waits. The grass is trimmed and right.
The whole town leans into the great unknown.
The field at dusk is lined with chalk and light.
Small-town Friday holds its breath tonight.

II. The Kick

The kick goes up against the darkening sky,
a spinning moon the whole town stops to watch.
The season turns on how the ball will fly.

The linemen lean, the linebackers apply
their shoulders low, their helmets in a clutch.
The kick goes up against the darkening sky.
