A mother's hand finds out another's; why
do small towns tremble at a leather touch?
The season turns on how the ball will fly.

The runner finds a seam and lets it lie
behind him, past the paint, beyond the crutch
of fear. The kick went up against the darkening sky.

The referee spreads arms. The crowd's reply
is thunder rolled from bleachers, low and much.
The season turns on how the ball will fly.

The band erupts. The old men start to cry
or swear or hug. The night is double Dutch
of joy. The kick went up against the darkening sky.
The season turns on how the ball will fly.

III. The Lights Go Out

The lights go out above the emptied field.
The bleachers cool. The popcorn bags are gone.
The town goes home to let its Friday yield.

The quarterback, his helmet unrevealed,
walks past the gate and finds his mother's lawn.
The lights go out above the emptied field.

A scoreboard hums its number, softly sealed
in shadow, and the chalk lines carry on.
The town goes home to let its Friday yield.

Somewhere a radio replays the yield
of fourth-and-long, the pass that everyone
saw. Lights go out above the emptied field.

The diner stays awake. The booths are filled
with boys who lost and boys who almost won.
The town goes home to let its Friday yield.

And Monday will restore what Friday steeled:
the grind, the bell, the ordinary sun.
The lights go out above the emptied field.
The town goes home to let its Friday yield.

title: spoken-word poem|the four seasons of an orchard
text:
Spring: the bud-swell breaks like a knuckle crack,
and the bees come in their fuzz, drunk
on the first sweet nothing. I walk the rows
with a coffee gone cold, counting the green
knobs on the branches—each one a small
closed fist of sugar. The mower coughs,
spits a stone. The air smells like wet
cardboard and possibility. Nothing is promised
but the graft holds. The graft holds.

Summer: the canopy is a held breath,
a green room where the wasps patrol.
I drag the hose like a stubborn thought.
The fruit hangs heavy as a bad decision
you keep making. You can hear the apples
thickening—a low electrical hum
if you press your ear to the bark.
The sun is a boss who never leaves.
At dusk the deer come, delicate thieves,
and take what they take. I let them.
What's one more mouth in this loud green world?

Fall: the ladder's aluminum teeth
bite the trunk. I climb into the crown
and the whole tree shifts its weight.
The picker's bag fills with dull thuds—
Galas, Honeycrisps, the occasional
rotten heart I toss to the grass.
The cider press groans like an old man
getting up. The wasps are slow now,
drunk on the leavings. Yellow jackets
in the fallen fruit, a slow gold fever.
The light goes long and slanted. Everything
smells like vinegar and farewell.

Winter: the orchard is a skeleton
in a bad coat. I walk the rows
and the snow squeaks like new shoes.
The trees are black lines drawn on white,
their pruning wounds like little mouths.
I sharpen the shears. I oil the gate.
The deer have eaten the last windfall
and left their tracks—a delicate script
I can't read. The cold is a clean knife.
Under the snow, the roots are doing
their slow arithmetic. I wait.
I am good at waiting. The graft holds.
The graft holds.

title: ode|the four seasons of an orchard
text:
Ode to the Four Seasons of an Orchard

I. Spring
Now blush the boughs with petal-light,
and bees hum low in the warming air;
the orchard wakes from winter's night,
and every branch puts on its prayer.
The dew, a glass to morning's face,
holds budding promises in place,
and hope, unspoken, fills the space
where fruit shall come to bear.

II. Summer
O green cathedral, roofed with leaves,
where sunlight sifts in golden threads!
The swelling fruit no longer grieves
for blossom-time, but quietly spreads
its weight against the patient bough.
The wind walks softly, whispering now
of sweetness that the months allow —
a choir the orchard sheds.

III. Autumn
Come, russet hour, and let it fall —
the apple, pear, the heavy plum!
The ladder leans against the wall,
the baskets wait, the pickers come.
What spring once promised, summer fed,
now ripens into gold and red,
and every gathered, fragrant bed
sings harvest's gladness home.

IV. Winter
Then silence: bare and silver-gray,
the orchard stands in frosty sleep.
The snow keeps watch till lengthening day
shall wake the roots the earth holds deep.
Yet in the dark, beneath the cold,
the old oath and the seed take hold —
for every winter, too, is told
a promise it must keep.

V. Envoi
So turns the orchard's faithful year —
in bloom, in leaf, in fruit, in rest —
and each season, drawing near,
proves every ending blest.
What falls shall rise, what sleeps shall wake;
the bough remembers, for our sake,
the circle it was born to make
from winter's quiet breast.

title: Shakespearean sonnet|the four seasons of an orchard
text:
The plum trees by the fence I never fixed
go white in April, then the bees come through
like something out of a bad dream—too many, too
thick in the air, and me out there at six
with coffee, watching. Summer's just a trick
of light through leaves, the green a deeper hue
each week, the hard little knots that grew
to fruit I bagged and lost to rot, or picked.
October: ladder, bucket, a wasp inside
my sleeve, my father's voice about the crop
not worth the water. Now the cold has stripped
the branches bare, and every year I've tried
to prune them right. I stand here and I stop.
The wind comes off the hill. The boughs are tipped
with nothing, and the dog won't come inside.

title: Shakespearean sonnet|an old piano left on the curb
text:
The rain has lacquered all its ivory
to dun and yellow, and the pedals rust.
Some child has propped the lid to let it be
a cave for spiders, and the settling dust
has made a second silence of the keys.
Who hauled it here, and why, I do not ask.
It leans against the curb as if to seize
one final breath of air, and drops the mask
of being furniture. Last night I heard,
or thought I heard, through all the wind and rain,
a slow chord wander like a wintering bird
that would not leave the eaves. I passed again
at dawn. The street was empty. Only where
it stood, a dry square waited on the air.

title: villanelle|coffee at dawn before anyone wakes
text:
I. First Light

The house is still, the blinds are drawn,
and nothing stirs but steam and me.
I drink my coffee at the dawn.

The kettle's whisper now is gone;
the clock ticks slow and endlessly.
The house is still, the blinds are drawn.

A single bird begins its song
outside the dark and silent tree.
I drink my coffee at the dawn.

The day's demands will come anon,
but not before the clock strikes three.
The house is still, the blinds are drawn.

I hold the warm and heavy stone
of mug, and let the quiet be.
I drink my coffee at the dawn.

Before the world has fully yawned,
I keep this hour awake with me.
The house is still, the blinds are drawn.
I drink my coffee at the dawn.

II. The Only Sound

The only sound is spoon on cup,
a small and silver, ringing chime.
The sleeping world is waking up.

I watch the dark begin to sup
on lighter air, and mark the time.
The only sound is spoon on cup.

The shadows, folded, now fold up;
the window wears a paler rime.
The sleeping world is waking up.

I will not go and wake them up—
my wife, my son—not yet. The climb
of sun is slow. The spoon on cup

is all my company. I sip
and let the bitter, warming lime
of morning steep. They're waking up

in dreams, still far from this. I keep
the quiet like a secret. I'm
the only sound—the spoon, the cup.
The sleeping world is waking up.

III. Before the Names

Before the names, before the day,
before the footsteps on the stair,
I have this hour to give away.

The steam curls up and drifts astray,
a ghost that lingers in the air.
Before the names, before the day,

I do not need a thing to say.
I only need to sit and stare
and have this hour to give away.

The light is thin and far and gray;
the floor is cold; the room is bare.
Before the names, before the day,

the coffee's dark and bitter stay
is all the comfort I can bear.
I have this hour to give away.

And when I hear the first "Good day!"
I'll turn and smile, and I will share
the names, the day, the light, the stair—
but keep this hour I gave away.

title: pantoum|insomnia and the refrigerator hum
text:
The Appliance Sings

The refrigerator hums its steady note,
a drone beneath the ceiling's blank despair.
I lie awake and count the hours I float,
and find no rest in any midnight air.

A drone beneath the ceiling's blank despair,
the clock ticks on with cold and even breath.
And find no rest in any midnight air—
the dark rehearses everything but death.

The clock ticks on with cold and even breath;
the sheets are twisted into winding rope.
The dark rehearses everything but death,
and morning waits beyond the far-off slope.

The sheets are twisted into winding rope.
I lie awake and count the hours I float,
and morning waits beyond the far-off slope—
the refrigerator hums its steady note.

title: poem in tercets|a beekeeper in winter
text:
The Beekeeper in Winter

The hives stand silent in the snow,
a row of kingdoms under frost,
where none may come and none may go.

He lifts the lid, and counts the cost
of cold, and hears the clustered hum
of lives that wait, and are not lost.

His smoke is cold, his hands are numb,
he sets the sugar cake and seal,
and prays the thaw will sooner come.

The winter wind is sharp as steel,
but in his chest a summer burns—
he keeps the faith the bees will feel.

He walks the frozen path, and turns
to hear, beneath the quiet white,
the sound of spring that still returns.

title: dramatic monologue|drought on a family farm
text:
The pump’s been coughing up nothing but air since Tuesday.
Dad just stands there, staring down the well,
like he’s waiting for it to apologize.
The dirt in the east forty is starting to look like the surface of the moon,
all ash and powder. Even the crows have quit.
I found a deer skull in the creek bed yesterday,
bleached white as a dinner plate, and I thought,
*well, at least something’s clean.*

Mom keeps the good china in the hutch,
the ones with the little blue flowers,
and she dusts it every Sunday like a prayer.
She says, “We’ll use them when it rains.”
She says it like a fact. Like a law of physics.
Last night I heard her on the phone with my aunt,
her voice all tight and quiet, saying,
“I don’t know, Linda. I just don’t know.”

The bank sent another letter.
Dad put it under the sugar bowl.
He thinks I don’t see him looking at the sky,
squinting at it like he’s trying to read a language
he used to know.
The dog won’t come out from under the porch.
Smart dog.

I remember when the creek was a creek,
when the back pasture was a sea of green you could get lost in,
when the air smelled like wet earth and not this—
this hot, flat nothing.
I remember my grandfather’s hands,
cracked and brown as the dirt he worked,
and how he’d say, “The land always pays you back.”
He’s dead now.
The land isn’t paying anything back.

I’m supposed to go back to school in three weeks.
I haven’t packed a thing.
I just sit on the porch step and watch the horizon,
waiting for a cloud that never comes,
listening to the silence,
which is louder than any storm I’ve ever heard.

title: free verse poem|the moon over a refugee camp
text:
A curl of smoke, a thread of light—
the moon is a coin worn thin
by too many hands.

It hangs above the tarpaulin roofs,
above the rows of shoes outside the tents,
above the child who counts the stars
and finds one missing.

The moon does not choose sides.
It pours its milk
on the barbed wire,
on the water queue,
on the old man’s open palm
where a photograph has softened to a ghost.

Somewhere a radio coughs.
A woman hums a song
from a country that no longer answers.
The moon listens, pale as an ear
pressed to a wall.

It is the same moon
that hung over the orchard,
over the kitchen window,
over the bed where someone
once slept without counting.

Now it is a bowl
turned upside down.
Now it is a key
that fits no lock.
Now it is only light,
stupid and generous,
falling on everything equally—
the dust, the wound, the small hand
reaching up
as if to switch it off.

title: poem in tercets|the moon over a refugee camp
text:
I. Arrival

A coin of light slips through the wire,
counting the tents like a quiet teller,
keeping a ledger no one asked for.

II. Ration

It pours its pale and even measure
on tin and tarpaulin, child and elder—
the only thing divided fair.

III. Lullaby

Above the fence it hangs, unclaimed,
a lantern no border will extinguish,
rocking the sleepless with borrowed flame.

title: sequence of haiku|the first heartbreak
text:
First Break

New moon, empty room—
your laughter still in the walls,
then the door clicks shut.

I read your last words
the way one reads a map home
to a burned-down house.

Cold coffee at noon.
The cup you gave me still warm
with a ghost of hands.

Spring comes anyway.
Cherry blossoms don't ask why
I'm crying in June.

I learn to sleep straight,
to take up the whole mattress,
to forgive the dark.

One day I notice
the ache has grown quiet—like
snow melting to grass.

title: villanelle|time and memory
text:
The clock above the laundromat is stuck at nine.
My mother's voice is folded in a drawer.
The past is just a tenant who won't sign.

A dog barks at the mailman down the line.
The future is a key without a door.
The clock above the laundromat is stuck at nine.

I find a ticket stub, a valentine,
a photograph of someone on a shore.
The past is just a tenant who won't sign.

The dryer tumbles quarters, lint, and wine-
dark socks. The fluorescent lights all hum and pour.
The clock above the laundromat is stuck at nine.

I dial a number, hear the empty whine
of static, let it ring and ring once more.
The past is just a tenant who won't sign.

Some nights I think the whole street's doing fine
without me. Then I hear the corner store
bell ring. The clock is stuck. It's always nine.
The past is just a tenant. I won't sign.

title: elegy|coffee at dawn before anyone wakes
text:
The grinder's a cold lump. I leave it.
The kettle, though—I set it on the burner
out of habit, and it ticks like a slow insect
while the window goes from black to that grey
that isn't quite a color. Tuesday's mug,
the one with the chip I never fixed,
sits where you left it, upside down,
a small monument to unfinished things.

I measure the grounds by feel. Two scoops.
A little more. The smell comes up anyway,
even before the water, that dark dust,
and I'm back in the kitchen on Vernon Street
where the linoleum curled at the corner
and you'd stand in your coat, not speaking,
waiting for the pot to finish its argument
with the percolator. You always said
the first cup was the only honest one.

The drip starts. I watch it
like it's a clock I don't trust.
Outside, a car passes, and the dog
lifts his head, then doesn't.
The light is doing what light does—
getting bolder, taking the room.
I pour. The steam fogs my glasses.
I drink it standing up, too hot,
and it's bitter, and it's mine.

title: pantoum|migrating geese over a frozen lake
text:
The lake has locked its thousand eyes in glass.
Above, the geese stitch southward through the gray,
their wings a row of commas drawn in ice.
The reeds stand frozen, waiting for the day.

Above, the geese stitch southward through the gray;
their calls fall down like pebbles through the cold.
The reeds stand frozen, waiting for the day.
The water keeps its memories in its hold.

Their calls fall down like pebbles through the cold—
each honk a small departure, sharp and plain.
The water keeps its memories in its hold,
a sky beneath the sky, a frozen vein.

Each honk a small departure, sharp and plain.
I count them as they vanish into mist.
A sky beneath the sky, a frozen vein—
the lake holds what the winter can't resist.

I count them as they vanish into mist,
their wings a row of commas drawn in ice.
The lake holds what the winter can't resist.
The lake has locked its thousand eyes in glass.

title: poem in tercets|a phone call from a long-lost brother
text:
I. The Ringing

The phone shakes dust from decades on the sill.
A voice I knew before the world went gray
says my name like a key it never lost.

II. The Static

We trade the weather, work, the price of bread—
each syllable a stone across a creek
too wide to see the other side of, yet.

III. The Promise

He says *I'll call again*, and I say *soon*,
two men who learned to hold the door ajar
against the closing dark, and mean it now.

title: pantoum|a library on a Sunday afternoon
text:
Sunday Hours at the Library

The Sunday light falls soft and slow,
Between the shelves of sleepy books.
A quiet hum, a sunlit glow,
In every whispered corner's nooks.

Between the shelves of sleepy books,
The dust motes drift in golden air.
In every whispered corner's nooks,
A reader breathes a silent prayer.

The dust motes drift in golden air,
A child turns a page with care.
A reader breathes a silent prayer,
While afternoon suspends them there.

A child turns a page with care,
The clock hands circle, unconcerned.
While afternoon suspends them there,
A hundred quiet lessons learned.

The clock hands circle, unconcerned,
A quiet hum, a sunlit glow.
A hundred quiet lessons learned—
The Sunday light falls soft and slow.

title: prose poem|learning a second language as an adult
text: The tongue is a stubborn animal. It wants the old pasture. In the new language, every vowel is a door I have to shoulder open. I practice in the car at red lights, the words for *refrigerator*, *dawn*, *elbow*, and the woman in the lane beside me is singing to her steering wheel, and I am jealous of her fluency in joy. At the kitchen table, the subjunctive arrives like a wasp in the screen door—I trap it under a glass, admire the furious architecture of its wings. My tutor says *think in it*, but my brain is a house with one lit window. I dream in the grammar of my first mouth: a river that never asked permission. In the morning I make coffee and say the word for *ashes* and the word for *slow* and they taste like pennies and honey. The cat blinks at me from the sill. He has no opinions about my accent. I love him for that. I love the woman at the bakery who corrects my *r* by curling her own tongue, unashamed, as if showing me a trick with a coin. There is a country inside me I am trying to immigrate to. The border is a sentence. The passport is a sound I make over and over, a small bell I ring until the bell is my hand and the hand is a door and the door is a mouth and the mouth is open, open, open.

title: dramatic monologue|the night shift at a diner
text:
The Night Shift at a Diner

The coffee’s burned since midnight. I don’t care.
The clock above the pie case ticks too loud.
I wipe the counter where the truckers stare
into their cups like they’re confessing proud
and unforgivable things. The neon hums
a hymn for no one. Booth four’s cracked vinyl
still holds the shape of someone’s absent thumbs.
I refill decaf. Outside, something final
scrapes wind against the glass. A waitress learns
to love the hour when no one needs a name—
just eggs, just toast, just one more chance. It burns
behind my ribs: this counter, this small flame
of being seen at three a.m. and staying.
The door chimes. Someone’s leaving. Someone’s staying.

title: brief healing poem-and-prose reflection addressed to 'you'|a beekeeper in winter
text:
The Keeper in Winter

You leave the hives their silence,
a season's hush of honey sealed in wax.
No smoke, no velvet hum—
just the slow arithmetic of waiting,
and the weight of little lives
you carry like a warmth in your two hands.

You have learned the art of doing nothing well:
to stand at the cold edge of the orchard
and trust the cluster in the dark,
the way the whole world holds its breath
around a heart not visible.

May your patience be its own sweet harvest.
May the quiet keep you, too.

title: poem in tercets|the ocean during a storm
text:
The buoys start their lying, a false calm
in the green room of the swell. Then the first slab
lands like a foreclosure notice on the sand.

The jetty’s a row of broken knuckles.
Somewhere a gate is slamming in the deep—
a sound you feel behind your sternum.

The gulls have vanished into the cloud’s bruise.
The ocean flips its mattress of cold salt,
tossing the furniture of wrecks.

Rain doesn’t fall so much as travel sideways,
a scatter of needles looking for a vein.
The lighthouse does its one trick, over and over.

By three a.m. the whole coast is a cough
that won’t clear. The tide drags its wet
bedsheet back, then slaps it down again.

title: short lyric poem|learning a second language as an adult
text:
The Late Lexicon

A tongue I knew before I knew the words,
now strange with rules I trace like weary birds
that circle, land, and lift again in doubt—
each sentence something I must build without

the easy ear of childhood. Still I try:
a noun takes root, a verb learns how to fly
across my sleep. My accent keeps its scar.
I am a stranger here—and yet, how far

the small lights go, the ones I start to name.
The world grows wider, syllable by flame.

title: free verse poem|the stars seen from a desert
text:
Tonight the sky is doing that thing
where it goes on too long.
I'm on the tailgate of a truck that isn't mine,
borrowed coat, someone's thermos going cold
beside my hip, and the sand
has already gotten into everything.

There's a trick to looking up out here.
You have to let your eyes go soft,
stop trying to pin anything down.
Then the faint ones come out,
the ones the city ate years ago,
a scurf of light, a spill across the dark
like salt across a wet table.

I keep finding the Dipper.
I don't even mean to. It's like a word
you learned as a kid and can't forget.
My father showed it to me once, badly,
pointing at the wrong patch of sky,
and I never corrected him.
He's been dead six years now
and I still look where he pointed.

Somewhere a dog is barking at nothing.
The fire's down to its last orange nerve.
Mars is up there, red as a bad decision,
and the whole Milky Way is just
a smear, a thumbprint, a scar
that never quite healed over.

I don't know what I'm supposed to feel.
Mostly I feel the cold coming through
the canvas of my shoes,
and how small a person gets
before they get honest.
Tomorrow I'll drive back to the interstate
and the stars will fold themselves away
like they were never there at all.

But right now there's a satellite
moving steady as a thought
across the whole indifferent business,
and I watch it until it's gone,
and then I watch the place it was.

title: pantoum|moving out of a childhood home
text:
The keys I hold are cold and newly mine.
The hallway light is just a yellow stain.
I leave the porch bulb burning for the blind
who never come, and would not know my name.

The hallway light is just a yellow stain
on wallpaper where height-marks used to climb.
Who never come, and would not know my name—
I sweep the dust of twenty years of time.

On wallpaper where height-marks used to climb,
a faded square still guards the mirror's place.
I sweep the dust of twenty years of time
and find my childhood pressed against the base.

A faded square still guards the mirror's place.
The floorboards creak in sentences I know.
I find my childhood pressed against the base—
the house still speaks, but has no voice to show.

The floorboards creak in sentences I know.
I leave the porch bulb burning for the blind.
The house still speaks, but has no voice to show.
The keys I hold are cold and newly mine.

title: sequence of haiku|grief after a dog dies
text:
The Collar

Still by the back door,
your leash hangs in the silence—
I can't move it yet.

The Bowl

I fill it by rote,
then set it down in the dark.
The floor stays untouched.

The Window

Your nose-print fades
from the glass where you waited.
I press my palm there.

title: spoken-word poem|a city bus at 2 a.m.
text:
The driver’s a deacon of the empty lane,
his hands two pale birds resting on the wheel.
The fluorescent light’s a dentist’s hum.
We are a rolling specimen jar.

A woman in a sequined top
clutches a box of donuts like a relic,
her reflection smeared across the glass
in streaks of neon and exhaustion.

Somewhere a man is folding his whole life
into a paper crane. He sits three rows back.
I know this because I hear the crease
of every single year he’s letting go.

The map above the door’s a constellation
no one believes in anymore. The stops
are just suggestions. We lurch between them
like a thought that keeps forgetting its own point.

A kid in headphones leaks a tinny beat
that sounds like someone tapping on a pipe
in a basement where the water’s rising slow.
He doesn’t blink. He’s building something huge
behind his eyes, and we are not allowed to see it.

The deacon brakes for nothing. Red light, green,
it’s all the same cathedral to him now.
He’s been driving this route so long
he knows the potholes by their first names.

I watch a moth collide with the ad for liposuction,
slide down the plastic, stunned but still alive.
It’s the most hopeful thing I’ve seen all week.

We are not going anywhere important.
We are just a rumor of a city
moving through the city’s sleep.
The exhaust is a ghost that follows us,
and the moon is a streetlamp that someone forgot to turn off.

At the last stop, the deacon opens the door
and the night comes in like a stray dog
that’s been waiting for exactly this.
He doesn’t shoo it. He just nods,
and we all ride a little further
into the dark, together, pretending
we have somewhere to be.

title: prose poem that reads like an English translation of a French Symbolist poem|a nurse finishing a twelve-hour shift
text:
The Hour of Mercury

She moves through the corridor as through a nave of greenish glass, where the lamps have the pallor of drowned moons. Her shadow, trailing behind her, is a long black veil that the dawn will soon devour. Twelve hours have fallen from her shoulders like petals from a dying rose, one by one, each with its own faint sigh.

In the hollow of her palm, the last thermometer glimmers like a small silver fish, exhausted by the fever of the world. She lays it down as one lays down a weapon after a war that no one won. The antiseptic air clings to her skin, a perfume of invisible wounds, of whispers swallowed by white linen.

Outside, the streetlights dissolve into the gray of morning, and the city exhales its first cold breath. She thinks of her bed as of a distant country, its pillows white as the snows of an imagined north. Her eyelids are heavy with the weight of all those sleepless vigils, with the slow drip of saline, with the quiet arithmetic of survival.

The clock at the nurses' station ticks like a heart that has forgotten whom it beats for. She removes her cap, and her hair falls like dark water released from a dam. In the mirror of the elevator, she sees a woman who is also a ghost, a vessel emptied of its twelve hours, drifting toward the pale harbor of sleep.

And the morning, indifferent and luminous, begins to fill the ward with its cruel, beautiful light.

title: prose poem that reads like an English translation of a French Symbolist poem|migrating geese over a frozen lake
text: The geese go over in that broken script I can never read—black syllables against the tin sky, and the lake below them holding its breath under a lid of ice. My father would have called this weather “between two soups.” He said it in '89, the year the boiler died and we ate lentils for a week. The geese don't care about lentils. They carry their hunger south like a suitcase they refuse to check. I watched them from the jetty, the one the council never fixed, its boards soft as bread. A dog barked somewhere behind the reeds and then thought better of it. The ice made that sound ice makes—a tuning fork struck once, far off, in a room you'll never find. I thought about the letter I haven't answered, the one from my sister in Rouen, and how she always underlines the word “please.” The geese kept going. They have no interest in my sister. They have no interest in Rouen, though they might pass near it, high up, a flicker of wings over the cathedral. The lake will stay frozen another month, then go gray, then green. The geese will not come back this way. Or they will, and I'll be somewhere else, standing on a different shore, misreading a different sky.

title: Shakespearean sonnet|a jazz club in the rain
text:
The neon bleeds across the wet asphalt,
A scarlet whisper on the midnight street.
The rain taps out a syncopated halt
To every passing cab’s retreat.
Inside, the smoke has married to the bass,
A blue note hangs suspended in the air.
The piano drops a chord of empty space,
And someone’s laughter dissolves into prayer.
The drummer’s brushes sweep the window’s tears,
The trumpet climbs the staircase of the storm.
A woman hums away her wasted years,
And folds the darkness into something warm.
    The rain will wash the sidewalk’s silver scars,
    But not the ghost that lingers in the bars.

title: ghazal|the stars seen from a desert
text:
I. The First Night

The sky unfolds its ledger, counting stars.
Sand grains rehearse the numbers, counting stars.

A nomad reads the dark like scripture margins—
each constellation letters, counting stars.

The cold descends; my breath becomes a small cloud.
The desert teaches patience, counting stars.

II. The Long Watch

By midnight, half the heaven's lamps are lit—
the other half still kindling, stars on stars.

The dunes shift softly, jealous of the heights.
I lie below them, dwindling, stars on stars.

A meteor scratches out one line of fire,
then silence—ink resettling, stars on stars.

III. Before Dawn

The east turns gray; the brightest few hold on,
stubborn as embers, fading stars to stars.

The Milky Way dissolves into the light—
a river running backward, stars to stars.

I fold my blanket, carry morning home,
and keep the desert's darkness: stars to stars.

title: spoken-word poem|fishing with an uncle who never talks
text:
The Language of Water

We leave before the sun has found its voice,
boots crunching gravel like a whisper we agree not to say out loud.
My uncle carries two rods and no words,
has carried them this way for thirty years,
and I have learned to read the silence
the way other people read the sky.

He hands me a coffee. It is too sweet.
That is his first sentence of the day.

The lake is a flat gray page
we have come to write on with our lines.
He shows me how to thread the worm—
his hands do all the talking,
calloused, certain, older than the lake itself.
*This is how you hold a thing gently
and still let it go.*

We sit. The boat rocks its slow arithmetic.
He does not tell me about his father,
or the war, or the year the mill closed,
or why he comes here every Sunday
like a man keeping an appointment with something holy.
He doesn't have to.
The water says it all in ripples.

When the line goes taut, he nods—
one small dip of the chin, the whole dictionary
of his approval. I reel it in.
A perch, silver as a coin, flashing its brief opinion.
He unhooks it, turns it in his palm like a question,
then lets it fall back to the only home it knows.
*That is what you do with small things that surprise you:
you hold them, briefly, and you let them live.*

By noon the sun has climbed his shoulders
and the silence between us has grown comfortable,
worn smooth like the handle of a rod.
I ask him nothing. He answers everything.
The loons call across the water—
the only ones here who talk more than us.

On the drive home, radio off,
he says, out of nowhere, "Good day,"
and it lands in the truck cab like a fish in a bucket,
flopping, alive, the most he has said in hours.

And I understand, finally:
the man has been talking to me all along.
The lake was his mouth.
The silence was the sentence.
And I—I was the listening
he had been waiting for.

title: spoken-word poem|time and memory
text:
The Clockmaker’s Drawer

Time is not a river.
I know, because I’ve tried to drown in it.
It’s a drawer. A wooden drawer that sticks in summer,
full of things that almost fit.

Memory is the thief who lives inside.
She doesn’t steal. She rearranges.
Moves your mother’s laugh to a Tuesday in October
when you swear it happened in June.
Puts a stranger’s face behind the wheel of your first car.
Folds a whole decade into the smell of rain on hot pavement.

I asked Time for a receipt.
He said, *I don’t do returns.*
I asked Memory for a witness.
She said, *I only do versions.*

So here’s what I’ve learned, standing in this hallway
with the light switch I can never find:
You don’t own the past. You rent it.
And the landlord keeps the key.

But once—once I opened the drawer
and found a note in my own handwriting:
*You were happy here. Don’t ask when.*
I keep it in my pocket.
It’s the only proof I need.

title: children's picture-book folktale told in simple rhythmic prose|an abandoned railway station
text:
The station stood at Miller's Bend
where the tracks just stop and the gravel ends.
Painted pine, gone silver-grey.
The ticket window's cracked but the sign still says
HALFWAY (population: gone away).

Old Man Peabody swept it clean
every Tuesday, though no train was seen
since '62, the year the line
ran out of money and out of time.
He swept the platform. He wound the clock.
He kept the key in a coffee tin lock.

A girl named Ruth from the farm next door
left a marble once by the waiting-room door.
A boy left a whistle. A dog left hair.
A woman left a hatpin there.
Nobody knows why. They just did.
The station kept them. The station hid
them under the bench, behind the stove,
in the dusty light of the pigeon cove.

The trains went by on a different track—
far off, a rumble, a rumble back—
and the station leaned its ear that way
like a grandpa listening to what you say
when you're too small to say it loud.
The station nodded. The station bowed
its crooked roof to the passing sound
and swept its dust across the ground.

Peabody died in '84.
The broom's still there, against the door.
The clock ran down on a Wednesday night.
Ruth's grown up. The marble's white.
And sometimes, when the wind is right,
you hear a whistle—thin and bright—
though nothing's coming, nothing's due,
and the sign says HALFWAY, which is true.

title: Petrarchan sonnet|a father teaching his daughter to drive
text:
I. The Parking Lot

This empty lot of asphalt, gray and wide,
becomes our classroom on this Sunday clear.
I sit beside you, hiding every fear,
and watch your knuckles whiten on the guide.
The engine hums; you let the brake slip slide,
then jerk to stop. I say, "There's nothing near.
Just ease it." Patiently I volunteer
the rules of distance, signaled turns, and pride.
You bite your lip and concentrate your gaze,
and in your furrowed brow I glimpse the child
who once rode tricycles in summer haze.
The wheel is yours; the morning sun is mild.
We circle slow through these uncluttered ways,
where every small correction is compiled.

II. The First Road

The side street opens to the broader lane,
and suddenly the world is not so kind.
A truck looms up; I feel my stomach bind,
yet keep my voice a level, calm refrain.
"Check mirrors, signal, brake—now start again."
You hesitantly pull, and leave behind
the safety of the curb, and I remind
myself that trust is stronger than the rein.
The center line unspools beneath the tires;
your shoulders loosen as the speed aligns.
I watch you learn the language of desires—
the measured throttle, and the careful signs.
A father's heart, though anxious, never tires
of watching how a fledgling skill refines.

III. The Open Highway

At last the ramp, the merge, the open road—
you press the gas and find a steady speed.
The wheat fields blur; the sky is vast, agreed
to hold us in its afternoon bestowed.
I lean my head against the window, owed
this quiet moment, watching you proceed
with confidence I did not know you need
to show me, as the miles are overflowed.
Somewhere behind us, parking lots and fears
recede like exit signs we've passed unseen.
I see the woman in you, through these years,
though still my girl behind the wheel, serene.
The highway hums; the future volunteer
of distance takes us home, and in between.

title: short untitled lowercase poem in the style of modern Instagram poetry books|teenage summer jobs
text:
the summer i worked at the car wash
on route 9
i learned that a hose has a mind of its own
and that mr. delaney
who owned the place
kept a radio on the same oldies station
all day every day
so now i can't hear "brown eyed girl"
without smelling tire shine
there was a kid named dev
who quit after two weeks
said the heat was melting his brain
and honestly he wasn't wrong
we used to eat gas station taquitos
on the curb behind the bay doors
and watch the sun bleach the asphalt
nobody ever told us we were building character
or anything like that
we just got paid fridays
in envelopes
and drove around with the windows down
until the gas ran out.

title: spoken-word poem|a lighthouse keeper's last night on duty
text:
The lamp is lit. The wick is trimmed.
The brass rail gleams where my hand has been.
Forty years of salt have etched my skin,
and the sea keeps coming in.

The foghorn coughs its old refrain,
a sound I've learned to wear like rain.
The ships go by. They do not know
the light they pass was tended slow,
that someone counted every turn
of the great lens, and watched it burn
against the dark that wants to win.
The sea keeps coming in.

I climb the stairs. I know each one —
the seventh creaks, the twelfth is done
in shadow where a moth once died.
I sweep the glass. I step outside.
The wind is sharp. The stars are thin.
The sea keeps coming in.

Tomorrow, someone else will tend
this flame. A stranger's hand will send
the beam across the water's face.
I'll be a name, a time, a place.
But tonight the light is mine to keep —
I'll hold it while the world's asleep,
and let the dark come close, and then
I'll let it go. The sea comes in.

title: brief healing poem-and-prose reflection addressed to 'you'|insomnia and the refrigerator hum
text:
I. The Hour That Won't Dissolve

You lie awake and count the hum
the way others count sheep—
a low, patient drone
that holds the dark together.

Nothing is required of you tonight.
Not sleep. Not answers.
Just this: the fridge breathing in the kitchen,
keeping the milk cold,
keeping watch.

---

II. Small Consolations, Running

You think of the light inside it,
how it waits all night
for someone to open the door
and need something.

Maybe that is a kind of prayer—
to stay lit and ready,
to hum your one note
into the empty hours
and call it faithfulness.

---

III. Toward Morning

You will not remember falling asleep.
That is how it goes—
the hum keeps going,
the dark lets go,
and somewhere between one thought
and the next, you are carried.

You did not have to earn this rest.
It comes, like the light in the fridge,
simply because you are still here,
still warm, still wanted
by the quiet morning.

title: short lyric poem|a wedding seen from the kitchen staff's view
text:
The Table Set for Two

We hear the clatter, not the vows,
the sharp command, the clinking glass.
We see the love, but not the how,
as through the swinging doors they pass.

The soup is plated, hot and pure,
the roast is carved, the sauces gleam.
A world of taste we must procure
to match the fragment of their dream.

We wash the crystal, scrape the bone,
and stack the chairs when they have fled.
A quiet kitchen, ours alone,
with phantom music in our head.

title: brief healing poem-and-prose reflection addressed to 'you'|the sound of a train at night
text:
You, with your ear against the dark—

think of the train not as a horn but as a finger
dragged along the spine of a sleeping animal,
the whole valley shivering once and going still.

Somewhere a conductor lifts a thermos to his teeth
and the coffee inside has gone the color of pennies.
The rail ticks like a cooling stove. A moth

folds itself into the porchlight's fist.
Whatever you broke today, the freight is carrying it
in a boxcar with no address, hauling it

past the water tower, past the gravel plant's
lit-up emptiness, past the field where the deer
stand like fenceposts with their eyes on fire.

You don't have to forgive the noise.
Just let it pass through you the way it passes
through the trestle—loud, then less, then

a small ache in the floorboards, then the dog
sighing back down into its fur. Listen:
the night is not empty. It is full of things

leaving, and the leaving is a kind of company.

title: ballad in quatrains|the ocean during a storm
text:
The Ocean During a Storm

The sky turns black, the wind grows shrill,
The waves rise up like walls of gray;
The ocean heaves with angry will,
And tears the quiet shore away.

The thunder rolls across the deep,
The lightning splits the drowning air;
The waters wake from restless sleep,
And cast their white foam everywhere.

The sailors pray beneath the mast,
The timbers groan, the sails are torn;
Each rolling surge more fierce than last,
Since night began and hope was born.

At dawn the fury starts to fade,
The sea forgets its wild complaint;
The sun across the waves is laid,
And all the world is calm and faint.

title: Shakespearean sonnet|a father teaching his daughter to drive
text:
The keys are cold within her novice hand;
he sits beside her like a held-in breath.
The wheel is huge, the road a pale demand,
and every curb is intimate with death.
He teaches her the language of the brake—
the measured pressure, and the yielding turn—
how patience is a thing one has to make,
how even fear is something one can learn.
She pulls into the traffic, slow and straight,
her knuckles white, her jaw a quiet line,
and he recalls how once, beside a gate,
she wobbled on a bike and called it fine.
He says nothing. The mirror holds his face—
a man who taught her how to leave a place.

title: elegy|the stars seen from a desert
text:
I. First Light

The stars come out like animals to drink,
and I, a shadow learning how to think,
kneel in the sand and let the silence sink.

II. The Long Watch

The desert holds the sky the way a bowl
holds water meant for no one. I am whole
enough to name what burns and not the cold.

III. What Remains

By dawn the stars are grains the wind will take.
I keep their small deaths for the morning's sake —
a handful of cold fire I cannot wake.

title: children's picture-book folktale told in simple rhythmic prose|grief after a dog dies
text:
The Little Lantern

When Old Dog lay down in the snow,
the little lantern lost its glow.
It flickered once. It flickered low.
It whispered, “Friend, I have to go.”

The house grew quiet, room by room.
The little lantern dimmed with gloom.
It would not shine. It would not bloom.
It hid its light in sleepy doom.

“Come back,” it cried. “Come back and play!
Who’ll lick my hand at end of day?
Who’ll chase the sticks I throw away?”
The lantern had no words to say.

Then Grandma came and sat beside.
“Grief is a tide,” she gently sighed.
“It rolls and rolls, both deep and wide.
It’s love with nowhere left to hide.”

She lit a candle, small and true.
“Old Dog still shines, and so do you.
The love you gave, the games you knew —
that light is yours. It shines right through.”

The little lantern, day by day,
found one small spark, then two, then gray,
then gold — like sunrise on the bay.
It learned to glow a softer way.

It did not dim. It did not fade.
It kept the warmth that Old Dog made.
And in its light, the children played —
and love stayed lit, and love stayed stayed.

title: long free-verse catalogue poem with sweeping lists and anaphora|the night shift at a diner
text:
The Night Shift at a Diner

At the hour when the streetlights give up their halos to the fog,
when the last bus has coughed its diesel sigh and gone to sleep in the depot,
when the neon OPEN hums like a tired insect against the glass,
we take our places.

I have wiped the counter until it holds the ceiling lights like a still lake,
I have stacked the napkins into a paper cathedral,
I have filled the ketchup, the salt, the sugar, the toothpicks in their little glass coffin,
I have brewed the coffee that will outlive us all.

Here comes the trucker with his logbook and his loneliness,
here comes the nurse off the late shift, still smelling of antiseptic and other people's grief,
here comes the student with her highlighter and her third refill,
here comes the man who orders pie and never eats it,
here comes the woman who talks to no one and tips like a confession,
here comes the cop, the cabbie, the couple who will not stop touching each other's hands,
here comes the ghost of every regular who ever slid into booth four.

I have heard the jukebox choose the same sad song eleven times,
I have heard the fryer hiss its small green curses,
I have heard the screen door bang like a metronome of the sleepless,
I have heard the silence between two people who have run out of things to say and are grateful for it.

I have scraped the grill until my arms remembered their own weight,
I have flipped the eggs like small suns over a black horizon,
I have burned my wrist on the edge of the oven and worn the scar like a badge,
I have watched the clock drag its hands through syrup,
I have watched the window turn from ink to graphite to a thin gray promise,
I have watched the first bird stitch the dark together with its thread of song.

And I have poured the coffee, and I have poured the coffee,
and I have asked *how you doing tonight* like a prayer I learned by heart,
and I have said *take your time* to the ones who have nowhere to be,
and I have slid the check face-down like a small white flag,
and I have wiped the counter again,
and I have wiped the counter again,
and I have wiped the counter again.

This is the liturgy of the almost-morning,
this is the congregation of the wide-awake and the nearly-asleep,
this is the kingdom of laminate and fluorescent light,
this is the long slow hymn of the night shift,
and we are its choir, and we are its choir,
and we are singing.

title: sequence of haiku|migrating geese over a frozen lake
text:
The ice groans like a door—
my father's field glasses, chipped,
hang from my cold neck.

V formations, then
one straggler pulling the dark
behind it like thread.

I count them badly.
The dog barks at nothing, twice,
then gives up, sits down.

Somewhere out past
the sandbar where we lost the oars,
wings keep going, wings.

title: short nature essay in lyrical prose (about 300 words)|moving out of a childhood home
text:
The House We Leave Behind

The house will keep what we cannot carry. The lilac by the porch will go on breathing its purple breath into May, though no one will cut it now for the kitchen table. The maple out back will keep its slow counting of the years, ring by patient ring, and the wind will still find the loose board on the fence and worry it like a held thought.

We walk the rooms one last time. Morning leans through the windows, laying its pale hands on the floors we wore smooth with running. How strange, to love a thing by leaving it. The walls hold the faint warmth of our voices the way a coat holds the shape of shoulders.

Outside, the yard is doing what it has always done—the clover threading its small green stars through the grass, the sparrows stitching the air with their quick, ordinary joy. Nothing here knows how to say goodbye. The earth simply continues, generous and indifferent, and I find I love it more for that.

I take a single stone from the garden, gray and river-smooth, warm from the sun. A small weight for my pocket. Something to remind me that home was never the walls at all, but the way the light came in, and the way we let it.

title: meditative lyric that reads like a translation of a German poem|a city bus at 2 a.m.
text:
The bus is a lit room that hates its furniture.
Orange plastic, the color of processed cheese.
The driver is a man paid to outlast the dark,
his face a closed transaction.

Outside, the traffic lights conduct their empty business
with no one. A red, a green, a red.
The streetlamps are tall, thin men
who’ve forgotten what they came outside to say.

The engine is a low, constant vowel.
It is the sound of a refrigerator in a house
where everyone is finally asleep.
It is the sound of a large, tired animal

dreaming of a field it has never seen.
A man in the back seat is folding his hands,
over and over, as if practicing
for a future he can’t afford.

The windows are blackboards wiped clean.
The city is a lesson no one has to learn.
We are a cargo of warm, breathing parcels.
We are a sentence that has lost its verb.

title: prose poem that reads like an English translation of a French Symbolist poem|hope after a long illness
text:
The Lamp Renewed

Illness had made of the room a aquarium of pale hours, where the light came filtered through the thick glass of fever, and every object wore the slow halo of things long submerged. I lay among the drowned furniture, counting the respirations of the clock, while hope—that small, obstinate fish—swam in circles behind my ribs, its scales dimmed to the color of old tin.

But today the window has opened its blue eye, and the curtain stirs like a veil lifted from a face. The air carries the scent of wet stone and distant lilacs, and I hear, beyond the courtyard, a sparrow rehearsing its single note with the patience of a monk copying a manuscript. The sun, that old alchemist, transmutes the dust motes into a slow gold snow.

O season of convalescence, you are a corridor of mirrors where the body relearns its own outline! The hand, so long a stranger, touches the table and believes again in the solidity of wood. The blood remembers its river-mouth, its delta of small joys. And hope—no longer the anxious fish—becomes a lamp carried through the corridors of the house, its flame leaning forward as if to greet the morning, though the wick is still short, and the glass still bears the fingerprint of the dark.

title: Petrarchan sonnet|first snow in a hospital parking lot
text:
The First Snow in the Hospital Parking Lot

The nurses’ cars wear white, and every space
is hushed beneath a slow, unbroken fall.
A wheelchair track is penciled down the hall
of open asphalt, filling in, erasing.
The ambulances idle, and the ceiling
of cloud lets down its soft, forgiving pall.
Somewhere a daughter steadies in the squall
of flurried light, and will not let her mother fall.

Across the lot, a windshield’s warming glow
makes one small room of light where someone waits—
a father with the engine running low,
his breath a fog against the frozen gates
of glass. The snow keeps coming, soft and slow,
and settles on the roofs, and hesitates.

title: prose poem|teenage summer jobs
text:
The Summer We Were Paid in Sunlight

We were fifteen and immortal, or at least minimum wage, which felt like the same thing. The pool concession stand smelled of chlorine and melted popsicle sticks, and we counted tips in nickels while the radio played the same three songs until they became the soundtrack of our invincibility. Later it was the grocery store, where I bagged peaches at dawn and learned the weight of things—a watermelon, a customer's silence, the long Saturday hours that stretched like taffy. My friend mowed lawns in the heat until his skin turned the color of the dirt he worked in, and he'd show up at my register with grass in his hair like a crown. We spent our first paychecks on gas and CDs and the kind of freedom that doesn't require a destination. The manager at the car wash taught me to fold towels the right way; the lifeguard taught me to whistle loud enough to stop a heart. We were learning everything except how to be still. The summer job is a country we visited once, where the alarm clock was a tyrant and the break room was a parliament of the bored and beautiful, where we first suspected that money was real and time was not. We punched the clock and the clock punched back, and somehow we grew a little taller in the space between. Years later I still catch the smell of sunscreen and hear the register's ding, and I am fifteen again, counting nickels into a jar, rich beyond measure, paid in sunlight, spending it all.

title: short untitled lowercase poem in the style of modern Instagram poetry books|time and memory
text:
the clock in the kitchen
is three minutes fast
and has been for years
so we live slightly ahead
of ourselves

last night i found
a grocery list in your handwriting
from a store that closed
in the spring
and the milk was already expired
when you wrote it

i keep meaning to change the battery
but there's something honest
about a hand that drags
a little behind the actual hour
like a voice
calling from the next room
just as you're leaving

title: elegy|an abandoned railway station
text:
The Silent Platform

The rails have rusted into earth,
where dandelions push their heads
between the ties that hold no trains,
and dust accumulates like years
upon the bench where no one waits.

The timetable, a yellowed ghost,
still promises a 7:15
to somewhere no one goes anymore.
Its glass is cracked; the wind slips through
and reads the names of vanished towns.

The signal light, unlit for decades,
leans like a tired sentry
watching a horizon that forgot
what it was waiting for.
Ivy climbs the ticket booth,
counting coins of sunlight on the floor.

Here, the echo of a whistle
is a rumor told by walls.
The platform stretches into meadow,
its concrete fingers losing hold
of the straight and certain line
that once divided here from there.

No one will arrive today.
No one has arrived for years.
But the swallows still return
to nest beneath the canopy,
and the rain still falls on schedule,
and the moon still waits upon the platform
for a train that will not come—
faithful as the silence
that keeps this station standing
in the long, slow dusk of things.

title: free verse poem|an abandoned railway station
text:
The ticket window's glass is crazed but holds.
Someone scratched a heart there with a key,
initials soft as soap now. I used to wait
by the third bench, the one with the split slat,
for the 5:12 that always coughed in late
and smelled of diesel and wet wool.
My mother packed me sandwiches with the crusts on
because I liked them, which she never understood.

The timetable's a palimpsest of rain.
Blackpool. The races, Saturdays. A dog
that ran the platform once and wasn't caught
till Kirkham. Nobody's swept the leaves
since the year the roof got tired of the weight
and let a section go. The pigeons like it.
They've made a kind of tenement of the eaves
and argue about nothing, all day, all day.

There's a pram down by the buffer stop, rusted through,
wheels gone, one handle pointing at the sky
like it's asking something. I don't go close.
The waiting room still has its fireplace.
Somebody's chalked a word on the door that isn't kind.
The clock says ten past something, doesn't say what.
I sit on the split slat anyway. The light comes through
the broken place in the roof and makes a shape
that moves along the wall and doesn't mean
a single thing. I stay until it's gone.

title: pantoum|autumn leaves in a cemetery
text:
I. Falling

The leaves let go above the stones,
a slow confetti none will sweep.
The wind rehearses hollow tones
where marble beds lie fast asleep.

A slow confetti none will sweep
drifts down between the leaning names.
Where marble beds lie fast asleep,
the yew tree keeps its dark flames.

Drifts down between the leaning names—
each letter softened by the rain.
The yew tree keeps its dark flames;
the grass grows over what was plain.

Each letter softened by the rain,
the wind rehearses hollow tones.
The grass grows over what was plain.
The leaves let go above the stones.

II. Interment

They gather in the open graves,
a congregation gold and red.
The sexton wind no longer raves;
it tucks the season in its bed.

A congregation gold and red
lies down where no one comes to mourn.
It tucks the season in its bed
and waits for frost to be reborn.

Lies down where no one comes to mourn—
the acorn and the epitaph.
It waits for frost to be reborn
and settles into cenotaph.

The acorn and the epitaph
are covered by the falling crowd.
It settles into cenotaph:
a silence gathered, folded, bowed.

III. Vigil

The raking stops; the shadows climb.
A lantern sways on iron hooks.
The last leaf keeps its own slow time
and closes like a finished book.

A lantern sways on iron hooks;
the owl takes up the vacant shift.
The last leaf keeps its own slow time
and lets the quiet be its gift.

The owl takes up the vacant shift.
The wind rehearses hollow tones.
And lets the quiet be its gift—
the leaves let go above the stones.

title: prose poem that reads like an English translation of a French Symbolist poem|a mother's hands
text: The hands are two pale spiders that have forgotten how to spin. They rest on the tablecloth, exhausted cartographers of a country no one visits. My mother's hands. The knuckles are small, calcified moons. Between them, the skin is a map of river deltas that lead nowhere, tributaries of a lost language. I watch her fold a dish towel, and the motion is a ritual from a dead religion: the precise, useless folding, the smoothing of the fabric, the final, dismissive pat. Once, those hands pulled a splinter from my heel with the delicacy of a watchmaker. Now they tremble when she lifts her tea. The veins are blue threads in a faded chintz. She is talking about the price of grapes, and her hands are two birds, trapped in the amber of the afternoon light, beating their wings against the glass of a window that is not there.

title: ode|commuting on a crowded subway
text:
The 6:14 to Grand Central is a lung
that breathes me in with a hundred others,
a man's elbow a permanent fixture in my ribs,
the wet wool smell of someone's November coat.

I have memorized the constellation
of a woman's earrings, three stops running,
and the way the doors exhale us
onto platforms that all look like waiting rooms
for a dentist I hated as a child.

There is a boy who reads the same page
of a paperback every morning. I want to ask
if he's okay. I don't.
My coffee goes cold against my wrist.

Somewhere past 59th the lights stutter
and we are all just breathing in the dark together,
strangers with our faces in our phones,
our shoulders touching like we're learning
a language none of us will speak.

At my stop I step over a puddle
that is mostly someone else's spilled soda,
and I don't look back at the train,
and the train doesn't look back at me.

title: prose poem that reads like an English translation of a French Symbolist poem|the sound of a train at night
text: The train at night is a long vowel pronounced somewhere behind the hills. It draws the darkness taut, a thread through the needle of the valley, and the houses lean their sleeping heads against the sound. The rails are two cold rivers running without water; the wheels count the sleepers like a rosary of iron and wood, and the smoke—blue, almost violet—unfolds its slow scarf across the moon. Somewhere a window is a lit tooth in the jaw of the dark, and behind it a woman lifts her hand to the glass, not waving, only touching the cold. The whistle is a wound that does not bleed, a single note held until it becomes the color of distance. The night leans closer. The train passes like a word in a language we almost remember, leaving the silence more silent, and the fields exhale their long, dark grasses. The sound goes on without us, into the country of sleep, where the only light is the memory of a window, and the only motion is the slow, deliberate closing of the dark.

title: spoken-word poem|the first heartbreak
text:
The First Break

They told me it would feel like a storm,
like thunder cracking the porcelain sky,
like something loud and obvious.
But nobody told me it would be quiet.

Nobody told me it would be
the soft click of a door you didn't hear close,
the way a room empties without anyone leaving,
the pause before a sentence that never comes.

It was a Tuesday. It was ordinary.
The sun did not consult the sky for permission.
The bus was late. The coffee went cold.
And somewhere between the second and third ring,
I learned that a heart can break
without making a sound.

They say first love is a rehearsal,
but no one hands you the script for the morning after,
when his name is still a reflex in your thumb,
when you reach for a phone that has nothing to give you,
when the songs on the radio conspire like old friends
who've heard the punchline before you have.

First heartbreak is not a funeral.
There is no ceremony, no casserole dishes,
no one lowers their voice when they say his name.
It is just you, and a Tuesday,
and the terrible arithmetic of subtraction—
learning how to count what's left
when someone takes back the future
you'd already spent.

I didn't cry in the dramatic way.
I cried in the shower, so the water would take the blame.
I cried at a red light, and then drove on,
because the world does not pause for a breaking thing.
It just keeps handing you Tuesdays.

And here is the part they don't tell you—
the part I'm telling you now—
the first heartbreak is a door too,
not just the one that closed.
It is the long, slow, stubborn hinge
of learning you can survive your own weather,
that you are not the storm,
that you are the house.

So to the one who broke me first,
thank you for the quiet.
Thank you for the lesson
I would have paid anything to skip,
and would pay anything to have known.

I am still here.
The sun still does not ask permission.
And the heart, that foolish, faithful muscle,
keeps beating—
keeps beating—
keeps beating—

like it knows something
the rest of me
is still learning.

title: prose poem that reads like an English translation of a French Symbolist poem|first snow in a hospital parking lot
text: The first flake lands on the windshield of a Corolla like a rumor, and then another, and the lot begins its slow erasure—the yellow lines going under, the wheelchair ramp, the sign that says PATIENTS ONLY though nobody is a patient here, we are all just waiting. My mother is inside being scanned. I have been standing by the vending machine for forty minutes because the coffee is terrible and the waiting room smells of hand sanitizer and someone's wet wool coat. The snow does not care. It falls on the ambulance bay, on the cigarette butt frozen to the curb, on the plastic bag caught in the hawthorn bush since November. A woman in scrubs runs past with her hood up, laughing into her phone—*no, tell him the other thing, the thing about the—* and her voice is swallowed by the hush. I think of Verlaine, or maybe I don't, maybe I just think of the way my father used to say *regarde* when it snowed, how he'd stand at the kitchen window with his coffee going cold, and how that was the most he ever said about beauty. The flakes are getting bolder now, a white static over the parking meters. Somewhere a car alarm tries to sing and gives up. I should go back inside. I should check the board. But the snow is making everything temporary and I want to stand here a little longer in the cold that smells like iron and clean laundry, watching the world get quieter than a hospital at three a.m., watching the tire tracks fill in.

title: sequence of haiku|a forest fire seen from far away
text:
Orange line at dusk—
the ridge I knew as a child
breathes its last light out.

Smoke braids the far hills;
somewhere a name I still know
turns to ash and air.

Wind shifts on the plain—
I cup the small warmth I have
and do not go near.

title: long free-verse catalogue poem with sweeping lists and anaphora|watching a parent grow old
text:
I. The Inventory of Small Changes

First, the hands—the hands that could open any jar, any stubborn window, any stuck drawer in any house we ever lived in, the hands that tied my shoes and braided my hair and held the wheel at midnight on the long drive home—now they rest on the arm of the chair like two birds that have forgotten how to fly, and I notice the skin is thinner, the veins more visible, a map of rivers running to a sea I am not ready for.

Then the walk—the walk that crossed parking lots in three strides, that kept pace with me through airports and foreign cities and the corridors of hospitals where we waited for news—now it is a careful thing, a measuring thing, each step placed like a word in a language being relearned, and I find myself slowing, matching my stride to theirs, learning the grammar of patience.

Then the stories—the stories told twice, then three times, the same beginning, the same ending, the name of the neighbor's dog in 1974, the price of bread, the winter the pipes froze—and I listen as if for the first time, because for them it is the first time, or the last, or the only time that matters now, and I memorize the cadence, the pause before the punchline, the way the eyes still light.

Then the lists—the lists on the counter, the lists by the phone, the lists in the pocket of the coat that hangs by the door—milk, eggs, call the doctor, water the plants, remember, remember, remember—and I see my own lists multiply, a rehearsal for a future I push away, a future where I will write my own name at the top of the page and wonder why.

Then the sleep—the sleep that comes at odd hours, in the chair, mid-sentence, mid-thought, the head dropping like a stone into water—and I cover them with a blanket, turn down the television, stand in the doorway and watch the chest rise and fall, rise and fall, the oldest rhythm, the first song I ever knew.

Then the light—the light through the window in the late afternoon, the light that catches the silver in the hair, the lines around the eyes, the slight tremor in the hand that reaches for the glass—and I think: this is the light of a day that will not come again, and I stand in it, and I do not look away.

II. The Lessons I Did Not Ask For

You are teaching me how to be afraid—not the big fear, the fear of sirens and diagnoses, but the small fear, the fear of stairs, of curbs, of the space between the bed and the bathroom at 3 a.m.—and I am learning, though I did not enroll, though I would drop the class if I could.

You are teaching me how to repeat myself—how to say the same thing three times and mean it each time, how to laugh at the same joke, how to ask the same question and wait for the same answer—and I am learning the patience of the loop, the tenderness of the refrain.

You are teaching me how to lose things—keys, glasses, the thread of a thought, the name of a song, the face of a friend from forty years ago—and I am learning to find them, to retrace the steps, to search the pockets and the past, to say *it's here somewhere, we'll find it, don't worry.*

You are teaching me how to sit still—how to watch the birds at the feeder, how to count the cars on the street, how to let an hour pass without needing it to be anything—and I am learning, though my hands twitch for the phone, though my mind runs ahead, though I am not yet good at this.

You are teaching me how to say goodbye—not the big goodbye, not yet, but the small ones, the goodbye to the car keys, the goodbye to the garden, the goodbye to the stairs, the goodbye to the name of the street where you grew up—and I am learning to hold each goodbye like a stone, to turn it over, to feel its weight, to put it in my pocket and carry it.

You are teaching me how to be loved—how to receive it without earning it, how to sit in the chair while someone brings you tea, how to let your hand be held, how to say *thank you* and mean it, how to say *I'm sorry* and mean it, how to say *I love you* without adding *but* or *when* or *if*—and I am learning, I am learning, I am learning.

III. What I Will Remember

I will remember the hands, not the tremor but the tying of the shoes, not the veins but the braiding of the hair.

I will remember the walk, not the careful steps but the three strides across the parking lot, the hand on my shoulder in the crowd.

I will remember the stories, not the repetition but the first telling, the way the eyes lit, the way the voice rose, the way the past was a room we could enter together and close the door.

I will remember the lists, not the forgetting but the writing, the pen pressed to paper, the small act of hope that is a list.

I will remember the sleep, not the sudden dropping but the slow surrender, the blanket I spread, the television turned down, the rise and fall.

I will remember the light, the late light, the silver light, the light that catches and holds and does not let go.

I will remember the fear, and how we walked through it.

I will remember the loop, and how we sang it.

I will remember the losing, and how we found each other.

I will remember the stillness, and how we sat in it.

I will remember the goodbyes, and how we said them.

I will remember the love, and how it was not earned, and how it was not lost, and how it was not less than everything.

I will remember the light.

I will remember the light.

I will remember the light.

title: pantoum|a garden after the gardener has died
text:
The Unkept Garden

The gate swings loose upon its hinge,
and weeds have claimed the gravel walk.
The roses riot past the fence,
where none remain to hear them talk.

And weeds have claimed the gravel walk;
the trellis sags with untied vine.
Where none remain to hear them talk,
the poppies sow themselves in line.

The trellis sags with untied vine,
the watering can turns to rust.
The poppies sow themselves in line
across the beds he turned to dust.

The watering can turns to rust;
his gloves still wait upon the shelf.
Across the beds he turned to dust,
the garden tends itself, itself.

His gloves still wait upon the shelf.
The roses riot past the fence.
The garden tends itself, itself—
the gate swings loose upon its hinge.

title: villanelle|the sound of a train at night
text:
The trestle hums a single, stranded note
that stitches sleep to waking, stitch by stitch.
The train drags its long shadow through my throat.

A glass of water sweats. The clock’s hands float
above the dresser’s dust. The walls unhitch
the trestle’s hum, that single, stranded note.

The dog’s ears twitch. A moth against the screen
beats its small, paper heart out. I can’t switch
the train off, dragging shadows through my throat.

It’s not a whistle, not a horn’s dull bleat,
but the low grind of iron against a ditch
of air—the trestle’s hum, a stranded note

that combs the dark for tangles. Undercoat
of sound. The house’s bones begin to twitch.
The train drags its long shadow through my throat.

Somewhere a conductor’s thermos cools. Remote
as stars, the couplings knock. I scratch the itch
the trestle hums—that single, stranded note—
the train drags its long shadow through my throat.

title: short lyric poem|a garden after the gardener has died
text:
The secateurs are shut in the shed,
furred with a little rust. The roses
he trained against the south wall
have gone feral, thrown long green whips
over the path he laid, each slab
set level with a spirit-level's blink.

I find his gloves still in the barrow,
stiff as a hand he's left behind.
The hose lies coiled like something sleeping.
And the mint, which he cursed and cut
and cursed, has taken the whole bed,
and is moving, quietly, toward the gate.

title: villanelle|a lost glove on a fence post
text:
A single glove upon a fence post rides,
Its fingers stiffened by the wind and rain.
A small forsaken thing the frost abides.

Some hand once pulled it on with tugging strides,
Then left it there beside the farmer's lane—
A single glove upon a fence post rides.

The woolen thumb still points where nothing hides,
And every thread rehearses its small pain.
A small forsaken thing the frost abides.

The snow will come and blanket all the sides
Of pasture, fence, and the forgotten skein—
A single glove upon a fence post rides.

Whoever lost it walks where warmth resides,
And never looks behind them in the plain.
A small forsaken thing the frost abides.

Yet in the cold its empty shape confides
A hand's warm ghost that will not come again.
A single glove upon a fence post rides;
A small forsaken thing the frost abides.

title: blank verse meditation|an old piano left on the curb
text:
I. The Curb

The bench was taken first, or else it rotted;
either way the seat is gone, and so
the instrument sits angled like a ship
run aground on grass it never knew.
The legs have sunk an inch into the lawn.
Its lid, propped open once for parties, now
stands open to the weather, and the keys—
a yellowed jaw of teeth—hold still, hold still.

II. What the Rain Plays

The rain has learned the scale the owner left.
It falls in no particular degree,
just taps the sounding board until the wood
remembers being tree and gives it back
a low, unhurried resonance, a note
that has no name because the tuner's gone.
The hammers, swollen, will not strike; the strings
loosen their long held breath by half a tone
and call it music, and the evening calls
it nothing, moving on with its wet sleeves.

III. Inventory

Whoever takes it takes the missing bench,
the forty years of scales, the hymnbook's ghost
pressed flat against the rack, the pencil marks
of someone counting time. Whoever takes it
takes the winter coming, takes the way
the neighbors slow and do not stop, and takes
the small transaction of a thing that waits
to be a thing again—or else the truck,
the split of wood, the dump, the final rest
of all that patience in an unmarked field.

title: pantoum|a jazz club in the rain
text:
Blue Hour on Rue St. Claude

The rain comes down on the neon sign,
a saxophone bleeds through the door.
The sidewalk shines like a glass of wine,
and the night leans in for more.

A saxophone bleeds through the door,
the drummer's brushes sweep the floor.
And the night leans in for more—
the rain keeps time, and asks for more.

The drummer's brushes sweep the floor,
a trumpet mourns what came before.
The rain keeps time, and asks for more,
while smoke curls up from the corner store.

A trumpet mourns what came before—
the bass walks slow past the liquor store.
While smoke curls up from the corner store,
the rain comes down on the neon sign.

The bass walks slow past the liquor store,
the sidewalk shines like a glass of wine.
The rain comes down on the neon sign,
and the night leans in for more.

title: ghazal|the ocean during a storm
text:
The radar's green smear is a wound on the screen,
and the ocean is chewing the dock's splintered bone.

A gull, thrown like a glove, disappears in the gray;
the lighthouse keeps stuttering its one stuck tone.

Salt scours the paint from the shutters; a lawn chair
tumbles past like a thought you'd disown.

The buoy's bell clangs a warning no one can hear
over the diesel cough and the drone.

We tape the windows and fill the tub with clean water,
and the sea keeps dialing the shore's busy phone.

Tonight the horizon is just a rumor we tell
the dog, who paces and will not lie down.

Even the rain has forgotten what it was saying—
just static, just static, in a monotonous moan.

title: prose poem that reads like an English translation of a French Symbolist poem|commuting on a crowded subway
text:
The Underground Liturgy

At the hour when the lamps of the city are still hesitant, we descend—a slow procession of the sleepless, swallowed by the iron mouth of the stair. The turnstiles click like the teeth of some patient beast counting its congregation, and we are counted, one by one, into the fluorescent underworld.

The train arrives with a wind that smells of rain and other people's coats. Doors part with a sigh, and we press into the carriage as into a reliquary too small for its saints. Shoulder to shoulder, we sway—strangers bound in the accidental intimacy of the rush hour, our faces lit by the pale glow of small screens, each a private chapel of blue light.

Here a woman clutches her bag as though it held her soul; there a man's reflection floats in the black glass of the window, a ghost traveling backward through the tunnel. The wheels recite their litany—*clack, clack, clack*—a prayer in a language older than the city, and the overhead lights flicker like candles guttering before a storm.

We do not speak. We have learned the silence of the sardine, the reverence of the pressed. Between two stops, someone's elbow becomes a neighbor's pillow; someone's breath fogs the shoulder of a stranger's coat. We are a single organism now, breathing in unison, swaying as the train leans into the curve—a dark river bending through the veins of the earth.

At each station, the doors exhale a few souls and inhale others. The exchange is ritual, wordless. A beggar's voice rises and falls like incense, then fades beneath the wheels. A child laughs—brief, bright—and is swallowed by the murmur of the crowd.

And then, at last, the ascent: the stairs, the light, the sudden cold air of the street. We emerge blinking into the morning, scattered like seeds from a broken pod, each carrying the faint echo of the underground—the clatter, the sway, the shared and silent prayer of the pressed together—back into the bright and solitary day.

title: dramatic monologue|coffee at dawn before anyone wakes
text:
The house is still asleep. I hold the cup—
its warmth the only pulse besides my own—
and watch the window turn from black to blue,
the way a photograph develops slow
in chemicals I never learned to name.

Last night’s dishes lean in the dry rack
like parishioners who bowed and stayed.
The dog twitches once, deep in some dream
of rabbits, and the floorboards keep
their small opinions to themselves.

Steam lifts. It writes a word, then edits it.
Outside, a single bird is testing notes
as if the dark were something to be tuned.
I think of everyone I’ve loved, how each
is sleeping somewhere in this hour’s hush—
a wife, a friend, a father underground—
and how the coffee bitter on my tongue
is not a punishment but a proof:
the world is not yet asking anything of me.

This is the hour that belongs to no one.
Not to the bosses, not to the dead,
not even to the sun still under the rim.
Just this: a chair, a cup, a breathing man
who has not yet become a day’s appointment.

Soon the child will wake and need the light.
Soon the phone will start its small demands.
But now the dawn is doing what it does—
spreading like a rumor of forgiveness
across the lawn—and I am here to see it,
unshaven, quiet, drinking it all in.

title: prose poem|hope after a long illness
text:
The prednisone moon has finally waned. For months I lived in the swollen face of it, a stranger in the bathroom mirror, my own body a rented room I couldn’t evict. The world came to me in a slurry of pixels and the tinny voices of friends, a static I floated in. My main occupation was the ceiling, its archipelago of cracks, a geography I mapped with a feverish devotion.

Then, this morning, the first real thing: the smell of rain on hot concrete, sharp and mineral, a smell I’d forgotten had a color, a dark, wet slate. I stood on the porch and let it enter me. The neighbor’s dog barked and it wasn’t a spike in my skull, just a sound, a dumb, joyful noise. A single green shoot, a thug of a weed, has shoved its way through a crack in the walkway, and I didn’t see it as a problem to be solved. I saw it as a green fist.

Hope isn't a bird or a light. It’s this. The return of the specific. The knowledge that my hands, which trembled holding a glass of water, could maybe, soon, hold a trowel. That the ache in my joints might one day be the good ache of a long walk, a deliberate wearing-out. It is the taste of a peach, not the memory of a peach. It is the body, this treacherous, beloved country, slowly, slowly, opening its borders again.

title: Petrarchan sonnet|the first heartbreak
text:
First Break

The world was rewritten by your goodbye,
