and every street I knew forgot its name.
The sun still rose, but sunlight was not the same;
it touched my skin and taught me how to lie.
I kept the promises I could not keep,
I memorized the cadence of your voice,
and in the hollow where I had no choice
I planted sorrow and I watched it sleep.
Now I have learned the shape of empty rooms,
the weight of mornings no one comes to share,
the way a heartbeat stumbles, then resumes,
the little death of finding you not there.
And though the wound grows quiet, it still knows
the honest ache of everything it chose.

title: Petrarchan sonnet|the four seasons of an orchard
text:
The plum tree by the fence came down in March—
that ice storm, remember, took the gutter too.
My father’s ladder’s still leaned up against the porch,
and every spring I mean to cut it loose.

July: the cherries split before we picked.
The robins got the netting in a snarl.
I ate a peach still warm and sunsick
on the mower seat, and watched the wasps patrol.

October, and the cider press leaks rust
across the driveway. Someone’s jacket, blue,
hung on the branch since we don’t know whose—
the pears come down like fists, and turn to mush.

Now February, and the rows are bare
except one apple, wrinkled on the bough,
that no one climbed to reach. I leave it there.
The deer will find it. Let the deer see how.

title: Shakespearean sonnet|the stars seen from a desert
text:
I. First Night

The desert dark is such a heavy sea
that when the first star pierces through the deep
it seems a leak of light, too small to be
the trusted watch the wandering shepherds keep.
But then a second, and a hundred more,
the sky unbuttons like a coat of black,
and all the burning distances of yore
come crowding down the long and dusty track.
We lie upon the cooling sand and stare
at fires that were dead a thousand years—
the light still traveling, faithful through the air,
to find us here among the scrub and fears.
   The dunes are blind, the wind is deaf and dumb,
   yet overhead the ancient signals come.

II. The Map of Heaven

By midnight all the desert is a chart
of silver nails hammered into the night:
the Plough that drags its handle through the dark,
the Scorpion with its venom made of light.
We name the beasts and heroes as they climb
the ladder of the sky, and stake our claim
on every legend that outlasts all time
and every god who never learned his name.
The sand beneath us holds no mark or road,
no sign to tell the traveler where he's been,
but up above the burning map is stowed
with roads that every century has seen.
   We read the heavens like a borrowed book
   and never once escape its steadfast look.

III. Before the Dawn

At last the east grows gray, and one by one
the stars surrender to the coming day—
not vanished, only hidden from the sun,
still burning in their blind and patient way.
The desert will be cruel by afternoon,
a white and hammered anvil of the heat,
but we have memorized the silver rune
of night, and keep its cold against our feet.
What we have seen cannot be taken back:
the order and the wildness overhead,
the proof that darkness is not only black
but sown with fires that outlast the dead.
   We carry morning in our burning eyes,
   but keep the desert's stars, and all their skies.

title: short lyric poem|moving out of a childhood home
text:
The last box is taped, a sarcophagus
of my own making. The house exhales
a dust I never noticed. In the corner,
the ghost of a bookshelf is a lighter
rectangle on the wall, a sun-bleach tan line.
I pull a key from the lock and it’s warm
from the brass knob’s long habit.
Somewhere in the walls, a pipe knocks
twice, a code I’m no longer cleared for.
The fridge hums its final, flat note.
Outside, the lawn is a green buzzcut.
My whole life fits in a hatchback,
a cargo of odd-shaped, bubble-wrapped
organs. I am a surgeon of my own past,
closing a chest cavity. The streetlight
flickers on, though it’s only four,
a pale, early ghost of itself,
waiting for the dark to give it purpose.
I don’t look back. I just drive,
the rearview a small, bright theater
of an empty stage.

title: short untitled lowercase poem in the style of modern Instagram poetry books|the night shift at a diner
text:
untitled

the fluorescent lights hum
like they know something i don't
2 a.m. regulars
nurse their coffee
like a small religion
i refill cups
and keep my grief
behind the counter
the pie case glows
a tiny planet
of possible joy
someone tips a dollar
someone says thank you
the night almost forgives me

title: meditative lyric that reads like a translation of a German poem|a soldier writing home
text:
The candle stub’s too short to read by,
so I write by the smell of it.
Dear ones—the bread here tastes of chalk.
I think of the pear tree by the shed,
the one that leans. Has it borne?
My boots have separated from their soles
and I have learned to walk on that.
Yesterday a boy sold me an apple
for a button and a joke I can’t repeat.
The stars tonight are thick as lice.
Do not write to me of the garden.
Tell the dog I’m coming.

title: ballad in quatrains|time and memory
text:
The attic clock has stopped its sound,
its hands held fast in dust and gloom;
the sun through gauze makes slow profound
gold islands on the silent room.

A photograph with curled-white edge
holds laughter in a frozen place;
a child beneath the garden hedge,
a sun trapped in a freckled face.

The window glass remembers rain
in silver threads that will not dry;
the floorboards keep a faint disdain
for footsteps that have wandered by.

And when the final light has fled,
the house will hold what none can see:
a voice that sleeps inside a bed,
a name dissolved in memory.

title: children's picture-book folktale told in simple rhythmic prose|a city bus at 2 a.m.
text:
The Midnight Bus That Hummed

The city slept. The streets were bare.
The moon hung up without a care.
The lights blinked red. The lights blinked green.
The quietest streets you’ve ever seen.

But down the road, with a gentle hum,
A little bus said, “Here I come!”
With sleepy seats of velvet blue,
And one small light that warmly grew.

At 2 a.m., who waits to ride?
A cat with whiskers, deep and wide.
“Good evening,” said the bus. “Step in!”
The cat hopped on with a whiskery grin.

At 2 a.m., who else is there?
A pillow floating through the air!
It flopped inside and found a seat,
And sighed a sigh both soft and sweet.

Then came a shadow, tall and thin,
Who tipped his hat and climbed right in.
He hummed a tune. He tapped his shoe.
The little bus said, “I like you too.”

The bus rolled on through silver streets,
Past shuttered shops and quiet treats,
Past windows dark and lampposts bright,
Beneath the sleepy, watchful night.

It stopped for none. It stopped for all.
It answered every tiny call.
A yawn. A wave. A whispered “please.”
The bus rolled on with gentle ease.

At last the sky turned pink and gray.
The moon said, “Time to go. Good day.”
The cat stepped off. The pillow flew.
The shadow waved a soft “Adieu.”

And when the sun climbed up to see,
The streets were bare as bare could be.
But if you listen, soft and low,
You’ll hear a hum. You’ll see a glow.

For somewhere near, when night is deep,
While all the city’s fast asleep,
A little bus rolls through the blue—
And if you wave, it stops for you.

title: dramatic monologue|an abandoned railway station
text:
The ticket window’s a blind eye, glass gone milky
with a century of spit and weather.
I put my palm against the brick and feel
the old vibration—not a train, just a truck
downshifting on the county road, its air brake
a dry cough in the throat of the afternoon.

Somebody’s stenciled numbers on the platform,
a code for a town that no longer answers.
The bench is a rib cage. The timetable’s
a palimpsest of wasps, their paper nests
plugging the arrivals slot like a bad ear.

I think of the man who swept this floor at midnight,
his broom a metronome for no one. I think
of the woman who left a suitcase here in ’62
and walked into the field, and the field took her
into its ledger of green. The rails are rusted
to the color of dried blood on a mechanic’s rag,
and the switch is frozen mid-decision.

A crow lands on the signal arm and cleans
its beak on the metal, patient as a notary.
The wind comes through the broken window
and riffles an old newspaper—a headline
about the moon, a coupon for soap.
Everything’s a relic of the almost.

I sit on the rib cage. I wait for the crow
to finish. I am not waiting for a train.

title: sequence of haiku|fishing with an uncle who never talks
text:
The Quiet Uncle

Mist on the still lake—
two lines drop without a word,
ripples answer first

He hands me the net,
eyes fixed somewhere past the reeds—
I learn not to ask

Noon sun on our necks,
he grunts and passes the bait—
that is his sermon

A strike! Rod bends deep—
he leans, silent as the pines,
and I hold my breath

One fish, then silence,
the cooler lid clicks shut—
day measured in casts

Dusk stains the water,
he nods once toward the truck—
enough said, enough

title: dramatic monologue|a library on a Sunday afternoon
text:
The radiator clanks its one good knot of heat.
Mrs. Kowlski’s got the sports page spread
across the whole damn periodicals table again,
her glasses down her nose like she’s daring
the box scores to lie to her. They always do.

Over in Fiction, that kid is back —
the one with the army jacket, the cough
he tries to swallow. He’s got his forehead
against the shelf, mouthing the spine
of *Chekhov, Complete*, like a prayer
he’s embarrassed to be caught at.
I pretend not to see him wipe his nose
on his sleeve. I pretend to sort returns.

The light through the west windows is doing
that thing it does in October, that low
gold crawl across the floor, catching dust.
You could set your watch by how it hits
the globe. Somebody’s phone buzzes twice
in Non-Fiction and stops. Somebody sighs.

Down the far aisle a child is crying
very quietly, the way kids learn to.
The mother’s voice, a hush with teeth in it:
*I said one book. One.* The radiator knocks.
The kid in the jacket turns a page
and the sound is enormous, is a door
opening onto a field, onto a road,
onto some other Sunday, years from here,
where none of this will matter.

Mrs. Kowlski folds her paper. Looks at me.
*You’re out of toner,* she says. *The machine
ate my quarter in August.* I tell her
I’ll look into it. I will not look into it.
She nods like she knew, like she’s known
forty years, and goes back to the box scores,
to the small, reliable grief of the standings.

title: sequence of haiku|coffee at dawn before anyone wakes
text:
First light through the blinds—
a single cup steams alone
on the kitchen sill.

The house holds its breath.
Dark water learns the slow art
of becoming warm.

My hands cup the heat.
Outside, the world is still gray—
I drink the sunrise.

title: ghazal|the smell of a grandmother's kitchen
text:
I. The Threshold

The door breathes out a world before I knock—
cardamom and cumin braid the air, before I knock.
Turmeric stains the cutting board like sunlight,
and garlic’s ghost still lingers there, before I knock.
I am ten again, on tiptoe at the stove,
breathing in her patience, rare, before I knock.
The whole house wears a coat of simmering onions;
I shrug off the cold street’s stare before I knock.

II. The Alchemy

She measures love in pinches, not in spoons—
a cinnamon dusk, a saffron noon of spoons.
The pressure cooker hisses its old sermon
while fenugreek perfumes the afternoon of spoons.
Yeast blooms in a bowl like a slow secret;
dough rises under cloth, a moon of spoons.
I learned that hunger has a name and address,
and it was hers—the tune of spoons.

III. What Remains

The kitchen keeps her voice inside its steam—
clove smoke, burnt sugar, the dream inside its steam.
I cook her recipes and still I’m small,
reaching for a hem of steam.
Some scents are doors that never fully close;
I stand in the frame of steam.
The house is sold, the stove is cold, and yet
I breathe her name in steam.

title: prose poem that reads like an English translation of a French Symbolist poem|autumn leaves in a cemetery
text: The maples have let go their last copper coins and the wind, a bad accountant, scatters them among the headstones. My grandmother’s name is losing its edge to the lichen. A brown leaf, curled like a fist, rests on the shoulder of a stone angel who has forgotten what she was weeping for. The caretaker burns a pile of them in the far corner—the smoke is a blue thread stitching the afternoon to the dusk. I think of the dead not as sleepers but as a vast, patient audience, their hands folded, watching the slow arithmetic of rot. A leaf falls into the empty vase of a child’s grave. The vase is cracked. It holds the leaf perfectly.
